كريستا بايك.. قصة السجينة الأمريكية التي نجت من حقنتين قاتلتين. نُقلت بايك إلى المستشفى بعد أن نجت من محاولتين لإعدامها عن طريق الحقنة القاتلة الأسبوع الماضي.

شركة أرامكو هدف لهجمات الحوثيين، فما أهميتها للسعودية؟. في موازاة التصعيد الميداني، برزت منشآت شركة أرامكو السعودية ضمن أهداف الحوثيين، إذ أعلنت الجماعة استهداف منشآت تابعة للشركة، مؤكدة أن الهجمات تأتي رداً على الغارات السعودية على صنعاء ومحافظات يمنية أخرى.
الذكاء الاصطناعي يدعم فحوصات الموجات فوق الصوتية للجنين
احتجاجات الطلاب في فرنسا مستمرة.. فماذا نعرف عنها؟. شهدت الاحتجاجات أعمال عنف واندلاع حرائق وانتشار للغاز المسيل للدموع في الشوارع وحوصرت عشرات الجامعات وتم تعليق خدمات النقل العام في عدد من المناطق.

ساكن في بلا قيود: من حق أي قارئ أن يفهم الرواية بالطريقة التي يراها.. شدّد الروائي والكاتب السوداني عبد العزيز بركة ساكن على أهمية أن يكون الكاتب ملماً بما يكتب عنه وأن تكون لديه معرفة جيدة بالمكان والزمان وشخصيات روايته.

ما يمكننا أن نتعلمه من أخطر ظاهرة "النينيو الخارق" في التاريخ. بينما يستعد العالم لما قد يكون ظاهرة نينيو غير مسبوقة، في هذا التقرير نستكشف بالرسوم المتحركة والخرائط كيفية عمل هذه الظاهرة المناخية وأهميتها.

لماذا تشعر إيران بالقلق من تعمق العلاقات بين إسرائيل والإمارات؟. زيارة رئيس الوزراء الإسرائيلي بنيامين نتنياهو إلى الإمارات تثير مخاوف إيرانية متجددة من تحول الإمارات إلى شريك أساسي في منظومة أمنية تقودها إسرائيل، رغم استمرار الروابط الاقتصادية المهمة بين طهران وأبو ظبي
"كل يوم هناك قتلى": غزيون يواجهون غارات إسرائيلية رغم وقف إطلاق النار، مع تعثر اتفاق سلام. ما يزال العديد من الفلسطينيين يعيشون في مخيمات مكتظة، في ظل تعثر الخطة الأمريكية لإنهاء الحرب إلى حد كبير.

لماذا يستهدف الحوثيون مطار الرياض في السعودية وكيف تطورت التصعيدات؟. التحالف العسكري بقيادة السعودية يعلن اعتراض وتدمير صاروخ باليستي أطلقته جماعة أنصار الله في محافظة الخرج، بعد ساعات من إعلانه سقوط مقذوف في محيط مطار الملك فهد الدولي بالدمام شرقي المملكة.
الهجوم على مطار الرياض: حدث خطير آخر في صراع مشحون بالتوتر. تصعيد الهجمات الحوثية على البنى التحتية الحيوية في السعودية يؤثر على سمعة المملكة كملاذ آمن للاستثمارات.

ما أثر الحروب والنزاعات على الصحة النفسية للأفراد في الدول العربية؟. يصادف اليوم العالمي للصحة النفسية العاشر من شهر أكتوبر من كل عام، وفيه تذكر الأمم المتحدة ووكالاتها ذات الصلة بمعاناة الأشخاص الذين واجهوا تحديات تتعلق بالصحة النفسية.
التضخم في الولايات المتحدة يتجاوز التوقعات: لماذا ترتفع الأسعار؟. تسارعت وتيرة ارتفاع الأسعار إلى 3.7 في المئة خلال الاثني عشر شهراً المنتهية في سبتمبر/ أيلول، مدفوعة بارتفاع تكاليف وقود السيارات.

العلاقات المصرية السودانية: لماذا يثير التنقيب عن الذهب توتراً بين القاهرة والخرطوم؟. أعادت تقارير عن مقتل وإصابة عشرات المنقّبين السودانيين عن الذهب في ضربات جوية على الحدود المصرية السودانية فتح ملف العلاقات بين البلدين، بما تحمله من خلافات بشأن السيادة والحدود، ومصالح مشتركة تتجاوز السياسة إلى الأمن والاقتصاد والروابط الاجتماعية.

ستارلينك في أوكرانيا: لماذا تُعد شبكة ماسك عصب اتصالات مهماً جداً في ساحة المعركة؟. توفر أقمار ستارلينك الاصطناعية التي تديرها شركة "سبيس إكس" المملوكة لإيلون ماسك، خدمة إنترنت عالي السرعة، وهو أمر تعتمد عليه الحرب الحديثة بشكل كبير.

لماذا تحمل أنثى فيل صغيراً نافقاً ليس وليدها؟ قصة الصورة الفائزة بجائزة عالمية. تكشف الصورة الفائزة بجائزة مصور الحياة البرّية لعام 2026 سلوكاً نادراً لدى الأفيال، يسلّط الضوء على تعقيد مشاعرها وحياتها العاطفية.
بريطانيا تهدد بحظر دخول الإريتريين بسبب موقف أسمرة من إعادة المهاجرين. وقالت وزيرة الداخلية إنها لن تتردد في فرض إجراءات على الدول الأخرى "التي ترفض التعاون".

لماذا تحجب منظمة قرى الأطفال الدولية تقريراً عن دورها في قضية الأطفال "المخفيين" في سوريا؟. أقرّت منظمة قرى الأطفال الدولية (إس أو إس - SOS) بأن أكثر من 140 طفلاً تم نقلهم إلى مرافقها من قبل أجهزة الأمن السورية.

أنباء عن أن الولايات المتحدة تدرس استخدام "أم القنابل" ضد إيران في حال استئناف القتال. نقلت شبكة "سي أن أن" عن مصادر مطلعة قولها إن الجيش يدرس الاستخدام المحتمل لقنبلة "جي بي يو-43/بي" والمعروفة باسم "أم القنابل" ضد البنية التحتية للطاقة والمواقع النووية الإيرانية.

التحالف يعلن اعتراض صاروخ في المدينة المنورة، وجماعة أنصار الله تنفي. أعلن التحالف العسكري بقيادة السعودية، يوم الخميس، اعتراض صاروخ كروز بمنطقة المدينة المنورة، فيما نفت جماعة أنصار الله الحوثية هذه الأنباء

Congress Can Do More to Curb Kushner’s Conflicts of Interest. No one should be getting paid by the countries they are conducting diplomacy with, especially not the president’s son-in-law.
How JFK Helped Pave the Way for Trump’s Crackdown on Dissent. Warnings about transnational radicalism are rooted in the same accusations that sought to silence a renowned reporter decades ago.
Mapping Global Impunity. Press freedom setbacks are largely driving deteriorating scores around the world.
India’s Growing Cockroach Problem. Prime Minister Narendra Modi defends his country as a “mother of democracy” amid widespread protests.
The Limits of China’s Surveillance State. Today’s Beijing shows marks of how costly total control can be.
The Autumn Myanmar Turned Pretty. It’s been a week of diplomatic breakthroughs for the junta.
China and India Want Much the Same Things From South Asia. The two countries have reset bilaterally and internationally. Now it’s time to think regionally.
After Iran, Washington Needs a New Basing Strategy. The decades-old model has been upended by a war that favors movement and dispersal.
This Is Israel’s Haredi Election. The country’s coming election has become focused on the status of the country’s ultra-Orthodox at wartime.
The Painful Paradox of European Rearmament. Militarizing now may require even further militarization down the line.
Trump’s Diesel Deal Has No Winners. It won’t help consumers, won’t help Kyiv, and won’t mean riches for Moscow.
Why Hegseth Should Go. The defense secretary puts stunts over substance. The U.S. should send him on permanent leave.
Modi’s Crackdown Is a Strategic Error. The violent escalation is deepening public anger in India as voter list protests grow.
Environmentalists Are Wrong to Oppose the Senate’s Permitting Deal. America needs to build more to achieve its energy goals of lower costs, greater security, and more clean energy.
India’s Voter Roll Protests Swell. Modi’s government faces a growing challenge as Cockroach movement proves durable.
Surprise Starlink Cuts Blindside Kyiv. Signal failures have already disrupted several Ukrainian missions.
Now We’re Seeing the Extent of American Decay. From Hegseth’s plans to Trump’s theatrics, it’s hard to know what to be most outraged about.
Algeria Sets Its Sights on the Sahel. The North African country seeks to reclaim its status as a security mediator in the region.
Trump’s Midterm Strategy Harks Back to 1970. Forget hearts and minds, this path to power revolves around appealing to hate and anger.
The West Needs a Pax Biologica. Chinese firms are displacing Western competitors in one of the century’s most important and most overlooked industries.

Iran’s oil lifeline could run dry by mid-December, Kpler says. For the first time in Iran’s history, revenue from crude oil and condensate exports could dry up entirely by mid-December if the US blockade remains in place, according to the head of crude oil analysis at Kpler.

Iran may be restoring activity at nuclear-linked site struck by Israel. New construction and repairs at an Iranian compound previously targeted by Israel suggest Tehran may be moving beyond clearing war damage toward restoring operations at a site linked to nuclear weapons research, according to a Washington-based research institute.

War puts Iran’s nuclear ambiguity under scrutiny. A revisionist argument is emerging in Tehran over Iran’s nuclear strategy: that its longstanding policy of nuclear ambiguity failed its most important test when it did not deter the United States and Israel from attacking, and should now be reconsidered.

Zarif accused of aiding US, ‘suicidal attack’ on Iran’s security. Iran's hardline Kayhan newspaper accused former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif of undermining national security and helping Washington by depicting the Revolutionary Guards as a threat.

Russia fears a pro-Western Iran more than an Iranian atomic bomb. Moscow would rather live with an Iranian nuclear weapon than with a change of regime in Tehran, senior Russia scholar Mark Katz told Iran International, arguing that a pro-Western Iran is the outcome Russia actually fears.

Freight costs from Turkey to Iran surge fivefold in two months. The cost of transporting goods from Turkish ports to Iran has surged over fivefold in less than two months to about $8,000, Iranian media reported, as Washington pressures Turkey to help cut off Iran's overland trade routes to further isolate Tehran economically.

US weighs strikes on Houthis and Iran after deadly Saudi airport attack. A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s main airport drew a Saudi vow of retaliation on Saturday, as President Donald Trump raised the possibility of joining strikes on the group and resuming attacks on Iran.

US pressure threatens Iran’s political survival but may not bring concessions. The US blockade and tighter sanctions enforcement are cutting into Iran’s oil income and targeting financial networks that sustain the Islamic Republic, but may still fall short of forcing Tehran into concessions, experts said at an Iran International town hall in Washington.

World leaders condemn Houthi attack on Riyadh airport. An attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport drew condemnation from European leaders, the United Nations and regional governments on Sunday.

Machete-wielding men at IRGC-backed rally revive scrutiny of crackdowns. Footage and images showing men wielding machetes and swords at an IRGC-backed rally in the central Iranian city of Isfahan have renewed scrutiny of the Islamic Republic's history of using unofficial armed groups to suppress anti-government protests.

Iran-US diplomacy stalls as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify. Efforts to end the war with Iran and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained deadlocked Sunday, as military pressure continued at sea and the Iran-backed Houthis carried out increasingly deadly attacks inside Saudi Arabia.

Can US sanctions derail Iran’s China trade route?. Washington’s new sanctions are unlikely to stop a China–Iran freight train at the border, but may make the route Tehran has turned to under pressure from the US naval blockade costlier and less reliable.

Iran warns of wider risks as regional attacks intensify. Two commercial vessels were attacked near Oman on Sunday, two Indian sailors were left missing, and a drone struck an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp in Iraq on Monday, as Iranian officials warned that a renewed war could put regional infrastructure at risk.

Tehran seizes on Rubio’s Xerxes remarks to champion a past it once disparaged. Marco Rubio’s invocation of ancient Persia in a speech championing Western power has given Tehran an opportunity to present itself as a defender of Iranian identity, even as critics recall the Islamic Republic’s own record of disparaging pride in the country’s pre-Islamic rulers.

UK blames IRGC for RAF plot, vows crackdown on Iranian networks. Britain said on Monday that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had “almost certainly” directed a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, as it vowed to crack down on Iranian criminal networks, sanctioned two Iranian nationals and summoned Iran’s ambassador.

Over 90 killed in six months as clashes escalate in Iran's southeast - report. Armed attacks and security operations in southeastern Iran have left at least 94 people dead and 33 wounded since March 31, with fighting growing more frequent and involving heavier weapons, US-based human rights group HRANA reported Monday.

Suspect in plot to attack Iran journalists sought embassy visit, UK court hears. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain discussed an “embassy” visit with one contact and told another he had been promised £150,000 and help resolving his criminal case in Iran, a London court heard.

Meta, Google remove Iran matchmaking app after child marriage report. Meta and Google removed Iran’s “Adam and Eve” matchmaking app and related promotional accounts after an investigation found girls as young as 13 were being listed as prospective spouses, US-based rights group HRANA said Monday.

Iran hardliners back threats to strike Persian Gulf digital infrastructure. Iranian hardliners have backed security chief Mohsen Rezaei’s threat to strike data centers, undersea internet cables and artificial intelligence facilities in the Persian Gulf if the United States and Israel resume hostilities.

US military support against Houthis risks widening Iran war, expert says. Washington could support the Saudi campaign against the Houthis at little direct cost by lifting political objections to its operations, but deeper military involvement risks appearing to widen the Iran war, senior Middle East analyst Ryan Bohl told Iran International.

UKMTO warnings show 12 commercial ships attacked in one week. Twelve attacks on commercial vessels were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf between October 5 and 11, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) warnings.

Iran officials hinted at land incursions if US resumes strikes - WSJ. Some Iranian officials have privately suggested Tehran could send forces into neighbouring countries if the United States launches new strikes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the warnings.

‘Best advertisement for Starlink’ Iranians mock threat to subsea cables. The Islamic Republic’s threats to target undersea internet cables in the Persian Gulf drew mockery and criticism from readers who told Iran International that such attacks could deepen Iran’s isolation and damage its own connectivity.

Iran says six killed as armed clashes intensify in southeast. The Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that five members of an alleged kidnapping cell and one of its personnel were killed near Zahedan, while separate reports said more than 20 members of an Iran-backed militia were killed or wounded in the area.

Gunfire heard as county-naming protest turns violent in central Iran. A protest over the name of a newly created county in central Iran turned violent after security forces moved to disperse demonstrators, with videos sent to Iran International capturing gunfire, tear gas and injured protesters.

Amnesty urges global action after Iran executes five protest-linked prisoners in one week. Amnesty International on Tuesday condemned Iran’s execution of five men in cases linked to the January protests within one week and called for coordinated international pressure on Tehran to halt further executions.

Houthi airport strikes carry echoes of Iran’s aviation threats, experts say. The deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport mirror Iranian warnings to disrupt regional air travel in response to US sanctions, analysts say, while serving the Houthis’ own goal of pressuring Saudi Arabia over its support for rival forces in Yemen.

State TV calls Iran’s northern sea by its English name, citing Israeli agenda. Iranian state television has begun referring to the country’s northern sea as Caspian in Persian, a departure from the customary Khazar, after airing claims that the older familiar name serves alleged Israeli ambitions in the Caucasus.

Iran faces worse economic outlook than war-hit Mideast rivals, IMF says. The International Monetary Fund forecast Tuesday that Iran’s economy would shrink 7.6% in 2026, a worse outlook than for its main Middle Eastern rivals amid the war, with Saudi Arabia and the UAE facing smaller contractions and Israel and Turkey expected to grow.

Tehran raises the stakes, betting Washington will blink. Despite signs of movement in negotiations with Washington, Tehran is showing little inclination to ease military pressure, pursuing diplomacy while signaling that renewed US attacks could trigger a broader regional response.

Iranians' support for US pressure masks divisions over its cost. Nearly three-quarters of respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll backed continued US pressure on the Islamic Republic, while thousands of comments revealed deep divisions over its economic cost and whether it could bring political change.

Iran names new commander for renamed Quds Force assassination unit. The Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has appointed a new commander to its overseas assassination unit and renamed it to Unit 600 after its personnel and structure were exposed, two sources close to the IRGC-QF told Iran International.

Oscar-winning Farhadi says next film will be in Persian, without mandatory hijab. Oscar-winning Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi says his next film will be in Persian and set in Tehran but shot abroad to avoid Iran's mandatory hijab rules and government permit requirements.

Trump says Iran decision coming, suggests Tehran behind Houthi attacks. US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would make a decision on Iran “very soon,” as fresh attacks hit commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated.

Iran threatens to reconsider UK ties over RAF Fairford allegations. Iran on Tuesday summoned Britain’s ambassador and threatened to reconsider diplomatic relations after London blamed the IRGC for a suspected plot targeting a US-used airbase and Britain’s intelligence chief warned of growing Iranian threats to military sites.

Iran escalates Hormuz tanker attacks in gamble ahead of US midterms. Iran's surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz may be an attempt to exploit US restraint ahead of the midterm elections and undermine a recovery in Persian Gulf oil shipments, experts told Iran International.

Iran executes mountaineer after rights groups warn of imminent hanging. Iranian authorities executed Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a 38-year-old mountaineer from Kerman, the judiciary’s Mizan News reported on Wednesday.

Nowhere else to go? The puzzle behind Iran’s stock rally. Iran’s stock market is raising eyebrows with a sustained rally even as the country’s economy struggles with dwindling foreign-currency inflows, energy shortages and uncertainty over the war.

Iranian wheat farmers face planting cash crunch as payments lag, rial slides. Iranian wheat farmers told Iran International that delayed government payments for their previous harvest are leaving them short of cash for autumn planting, while inflation and the falling rial erode the value of money they are still owed.

Women’s Basij commander, police officer killed in southeast Iran. A women’s Basij commander and a police officer were killed in separate attacks on Wednesday in Iran’s southeastern Sistan-Baluchestan province, adding to a series of deadly shootings, bombings and armed clashes in the region.

Zarif under fire for dismissing nuclear deterrence before war. A resurfaced video of former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif saying Iran lacked enough enriched uranium to produce a nuclear weapon has ignited a fierce debate after successive wars with Israel and the United States.

Iran police killed brothers celebrating Khamenei’s death, source says. Iranian police fired 36 rounds at a car during a seven-minute chase near Tehran, killing two brothers aged 15 and 19 after its occupants honked their horn while celebrating the death of then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iranians report months-long waits for unemployment benefits. Iranians receiving unemployment benefits say payments have been delayed by up to two months, leaving some struggling to pay for food and service debts, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Tehran signals escalation in conflict IRGC likens to a ‘world war’. A senior Revolutionary Guards official has compared Iran’s conflict with the United States to a world war that could reshape the global order, reflecting a mindset in Tehran that appears increasingly resistant to backing down despite the risk of renewed US attacks.

Man in Iran International attack plot told police he was paid £2,000 to film. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain told police he had received £2,000 for filming, according to interview transcripts read at Woolwich Crown Court on Wednesday.

How Iran shielded forces over 2022 protest killings. Iran has built impunity for the killing of protesters into its laws and judicial system, Amnesty International said in an investigation detailing how security forces accused of deadly violence can help determine whether their own actions were lawful.

Ignore prices and economy is fine, Iran ex-minister says. A former Iranian labor minister has drawn ridicule after saying the country has no economic problems other than high prices and inflation, remarks that came as official data showed year-on-year inflation approaching 90%.

Shiraz and the wine industry Iran lost after 1979. Nearly five decades after the 1979 Revolution brought an end to Iran's legal wine industry, the country retains vast vineyards and a centuries-old winemaking heritage but remains absent from a global wine export market worth $37.8 billion in 2025.

Iran’s strikes on Persian Gulf water and power were deliberate - Reuters. Iran and its allies hit water plants, airports, refineries and a nuclear power station across the Persian Gulf with a precision that rules out the official story of falling debris, a Reuters investigation has found, showing the civilian damage was the aim, not a side effect.

‘We cannot bring America to its knees,’ former Tehran mayor says. Iran cannot bring the United States to its knees despite inflicting damage on American forces, a former Tehran mayor said in a state television interview, arguing that Iran's military capabilities cannot match Washington's and calling for an end to the war through negotiations.

Alger annonce avoir arrêté 61 « saboteurs » marocains, Rabat évoque une « affabulation ». Les 61 personnes arrêtées dans la région d’Oran ont été présentées par Alger comme constituant un groupe criminel venu commettre des actes de sabotages. Pour le Maroc, il s’agit de candidats à la migration vers l’Europe.

TotalEnergies, NNPC, Conoil… Au Nigeria, comment la méga-raffinerie Dangote redistribue les cartes du marché pétrolier. Les revenus pétroliers de la Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), la compagnie pétrolière nationale, ont chuté de près de 78 % en 2025. Le lancement de la raffinerie Dangote et la libéralisation complète du marché ont déclenché une guerre des prix féroce dans l’ensemble du secteur aval.

Centrafrique : les manœuvres de Touadéra pour contenir la colère populaire contre la vie chère. À l’appel de la société civile, une journée ville morte a été organisée ce 12 octobre à Bangui, marquant la première mobilisation de ce type contre le pouvoir depuis 2023. Mais Faustin-Archange Touadéra a tout fait pour en limiter la portée.

Pourquoi Aliko Dangote accorde un délai supplémentaire pour l’IPO de sa raffinerie. Les investisseurs ont jusqu’au 27 octobre pour manifester leur intérêt. Aliko Dangote insiste sur le nombre de personnes qu’il veut voir participer à l’opération.

Au Niger, une fuite de pétrole majeure met la gestion du champ d’Agadem à l’épreuve. Une éruption de pétrole brut et de gaz secoue le nord-est du Niger depuis le 25 septembre. Le ministère du Pétrole alerte sur un incident environnemental d’une gravité exceptionnelle.

En Guinée, le calendrier des élections sénatoriales et régionales désormais fixé. Il s’agit des dernières étapes du retour à l’ordre constitutionnel : ces scrutins doivent permettre à Mamadi Doumbouya de mettre un terme à la période de transition entamée après son coup d’État de septembre 2021.

Rwanda – Jean-Guy Afrika : « La Formule 1 s’inscrit dans une ambition beaucoup plus large ». La Formule 1 signe son retour sur le continent africain en s’installant pour dix ans sur le circuit de Bugesera, près de Kigali. Pour le directeur général du Rwanda Development Board, cet investissement est cohérent avec la stratégie d’attractivité du pays.

Accords stratégiques et tensions diplomatiques : 5 questions pour comprendre la position du Somaliland dans la crise dans la Corne de l’Afrique. Reconnue par Israël en décembre 2025, la République autoproclamée s’impose dans les équilibres géopolitiques de la région, entre diplomatie sécuritaire et deals économiques. Au risque d’accentuer des tensions déjà vives.

Côte d’Ivoire-Mali : le patron des renseignements ivoiriens attendu à Bamako. Face à la progression de la menace jihadiste dans le sud de son territoire et aux enjeux stratégiques du corridor Abidjan-Bamako, le Mali affiche sa volonté de relancer la coopération en matière de renseignement avec son voisin, après plusieurs années de tensions.

Sidi Ould Tah, Makhtar Diop, Jeremy Awori… À Luanda, la finance africaine veut convertir les profits en investissements productifs. Les 3 et 4 novembre, Luanda accueillera la sixième édition de l’Africa Financial Summit (AFIS). En rassemblant plus de 1 250 participants, le sommet, organisé pour la première fois en Afrique australe, entend transformer les succès individuels en investissements productifs.

Mines : comment la montée de Paris au capital d’Eramet peut rebattre les cartes avec Libreville. L’État français s’apprête à porter sa participation dans Eramet à 49 % pour renflouer le groupe minier en difficulté. Un sauvetage financier qui pourrait bouleverser les équilibres entre Paris et Libreville sur la transformation locale des ressources.

RDC : après le lancement d’une nouvelle rébellion, l’heure du choix pour les alliés de Joseph Kabila. En prenant la tête du Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), né de la dissolution de l’AFC/M23, l’ancien chef de l’État contraint ses soutiens comme les autres opposants à se positionner dans cette nouvelle donne politique.

Cameroun anglophone : le St Joseph’s College de Sasse, au cœur des luttes identitaires. Fondé en 1939 sous l’administration britannique, il a traversé les bouleversements du Cameroun anglophone, des tensions nées des indépendances aux violences de la crise séparatiste. Son histoire est celle d’une identité contestée, au cœur d’une décennie de conflit dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso).

Pourquoi l’ouverture d’Ecobank au yuan change la donne pour le continent. En se rapprochant du système de paiement chinois (CIPS), le groupe togolais veut permettre aux entreprises africaines de régler plus directement leurs échanges avec l’Empire du Milieu. Il rejoint Standard Bank et Afreximbank dans la course aux transactions en renminbi.

Maroc : qui est Ahmed Touizi, le nouveau président de la Chambre des représentants ?. Ancré à Marrakech et dans son arrière-pays, fort de trois décennies au Parlement, le nouveau président de la première Chambre s’impose au sommet du pouvoir. Retour sur le parcours méconnu de ce vieux routier de la politique marocaine.

« N’est pas Sankara qui veut ! ». Le bilan d’Ibrahim Traoré à la tête du Burkina Faso et la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri comme première femme Première ministre du Maroc sont au menu de ce Débat africain, une émission diffusée sur RFI en partenariat avec Jeune Afrique.

Niamey dénonce « un acte d’ingratitude grave » après l’expulsion de deux agents nigériens par la France. Selon une source diplomatique, Paris a déclaré persona non grata deux agents de renseignement nigériens en poste en France. La décision passe mal à Niamey, qui rappelle que l’un d’eux avait été blessé en 2014 lors d’une mission conjointe avec l’armée française.

En Côte d’Ivoire, comment Lionel Soulard est devenu l’incontournable visage de Cargill dans le cacao. Face à l’instabilité des cours du cacao, le secteur de l’or brun ivoirien, clé pour l’économie du premier producteur mondial de fèves, cherche un second souffle. Le patron de Cargill West Africa et du groupement des exportateurs appelle à un changement d’approche stratégique.

Tullow Oil : le lent effondrement d’un ex-pilier du pétrole africain. Plongé dans de graves difficultés financières, Tullow Oil replie ses ambitions africaines sur le Ghana. Fragilisée par un revers fiscal à 196,5 millions de dollars, la compagnie joue son avenir face à un État désormais en position de force.

Maroc : face à une nouvelle plainte pour faux, Rita Zniber dénonce un chantage. Frappée d’une interdiction de quitter le territoire marocain à la suite d’une plainte déposée par Mohamed Nabil Zniber, son beau-fils, la patronne du géant Diana Holding organise sa défense. Coulisses.

Remaniement en Mauritanie : pour Ghazouani, un pas de plus vers un troisième mandat ?. L’important changement gouvernemental effectué par le président mauritanien le 10 octobre a coûté son poste au ministre de l’Énergie, après l’incendie de deux postes de transformation d’électricité à Nouakchott. Mais la manœuvre s’avère bien plus politique.

Au Mali, l’armée reconnaît une bavure à demi-mot. Une frappe au Mali a fait près de dix victimes dont des femmes et des enfants, le 12 octobre. D’habitude prompte à nier les dommages collatéraux, l’armée malienne a reconnu sans précision un « incident tragique ». Est-ce le premier signe d’une reconnaissance du coût de la guerre supporté par les civils ?

Tchad-France : ce que Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno est venu négocier avec Emmanuel Macron. Après la rupture de leur partenariat militaire fin 2024, Paris et N’Djamena tentent de rebâtir leur relation sur de nouvelles bases. Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno et Emmanuel Macron excluent cependant le retour des troupes françaises sur le sol tchadien.

Affaire Martinez Zogo au Cameroun : un témoin dit subir menaces et tentatives d’influence. Un officier supérieur, témoin dans l’affaire Zogo, s’est invité au tribunal pour dénoncer des menaces pesant sur sa vie. Jeune Afrique a également pris connaissance d’un courrier d’alerte qu’il a transmis au ministre délégué à la Défense.

Cameroun anglophone : Francis Enwe, le sénateur RDPC qui parle aux séparatistes. Député puis sénateur du parti au pouvoir, cet homme d’affaires à succès vit depuis dix ans au rythme de la crise anglophone sévissant au Nord-Ouest et au Sud-Ouest (Noso). Il tente de promouvoir un dialogue avec les séparatistes, dans un pays où le pouvoir n’y est globalement pas favorable. Rencontre.

Burkina Faso : Ibrahim Traoré a-t-il confisqué l’héritage de Thomas Sankara ?. Le mémorial consacré à Thomas Sankara, érigé à Ouagadougou, change progressivement de vocation. Pensé par ses fidèles, il est aujourd’hui réinvesti par la junte dirigée par Ibrahim Traoré, qui se rêve en réincarnation du mythe révolutionnaire.

Formule 1 : le pari financier de Kagame peut-il être gagnant ?. En obtenant le retour de la F1 sur le continent, le Rwanda s’offre une vitrine internationale inédite. Et réalise un coup sportif d’envergure dont la facture financière reste un mystère.

Face à l’Éthiopie, que vaut l’armée de l’Érythrée ?. Alors que les tensions entre Asmara et Addis-Abeba ravivent le spectre d’un conflit régional, l’armée érythréenne est sous le feu des projecteurs. Quelles sont ses capacités militaires et son aptitude à tenir sur la durée ? Décryptage.

Éthiopie, Guinée, Bénin… Quels pays d’Afrique affichent la plus forte croissance économique ?. Dans son rapport sur les perspectives économiques régionales, le FMI table sur une croissance du PIB de 4,5 % en 2026 et en 2027 pour l’Afrique subsaharienne, malgré la guerre au Moyen-Orient. Une moyenne qui masque de grands écarts.

Gabon : 10 choses à savoir sur Brigitte Onkanowa, la fidèle ministre de la Défense d’Oligui Nguema. Elle est sans doute la plus discrète des membres du gouvernement gabonais, au sein duquel elle a été reconduite le 11 octobre. Générale de brigade, ex-membre du CTRI, Brigitte Onkanowa ne cesse d’affirmer sa grande loyauté au chef de l’État.

Au Maroc, la consécration de Fouad Ali El-Himma, homme de l’ombre au service de Mohammed VI. Conseiller très influent auprès du souverain, qu’il a connu élève au collège royal, il est aussi le fondateur du Parti Authenticité et modernité, la formation qui va conduire le prochain gouvernement.

Tyla au Zénith de Paris : le décevant virage pop d’une chanteuse sud-africaine incontournable. Lors de son concert, lundi 12 octobre, l’interprète de « Water » présentera, notamment, le répertoire de son deuxième album paru cet été et à la dimension pop peu inspirée.

Le Sénégal peine à dépêtrer sa compagnie aérienne nationale des scandales à répétition. Le chef de l’Etat, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, mise sur Air Sénégal pour faire de Dakar un hub aérien, à quelques semaines du lancement des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse. Minée par une dette considérable, la compagnie fait face à une nouvelle affaire qui met en cause l’éthique de ses employés.

Joseph Kabila, ex-président de la République démocratique du Congo, prend la tête d’un mouvement politico-militaire incluant les rebelles du M23. Condamné à mort par contumace en 2025, l’ancien chef de l’Etat a été désigné à Goma, alors que l’opposition accuse l’actuel président, Félix Tshisekedi, de vouloir modifier la Constitution pour briguer un troisième mandat.

A Ceuta, les migrants ont opportunément disparu du paysage pour la visite du roi Felipe VI et de la reine Letizia. Les souverains effectuent une visite inédite, mardi 13 octobre, dans la ville autonome espagnole d’Afrique du Nord où les immigrés ayant déferlé du Maroc fin juillet sont encore des milliers à dormir à la belle étoile ou dans des centres d’accueil d’urgence.

Au Niger, une éruption de pétrole provoque un incident environnemental « d’une gravité exceptionnelle ». D’importantes quantités de pétrole brut et de gaz sont projetées à plus de dix mètres de hauteur, ont expliqué les autorités. Les causes de l’incident, qui a commencé le 25 septembre dans l’est désertique du pays, « ne sont pas encore totalement établies », mais la « piste criminelle ou terroriste » est écartée.

En Libye orientale, l’ascension fragile de Saddam Haftar, le fils du maréchal. Saddam Haftar, le dirigeant de la Cyrénaïque, est parvenu à prendre le contrôle du Parlement de Benghazi début octobre, consolidant ainsi son pouvoir et renforçant son statut de successeur de son père. Non sans attiser des querelles fratricides au sein de son clan.

Images. L’annonce surprise de la création d’un nouveau mouvement politico-militaire en République démocratique du Congo. Joseph Kaliba préside dorénavant le Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), une alliance avec les groupes rebelles AFC et M23.

Au Nigeria, le milliardaire Aliko Dangote veut faire de l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie de Lagos une opération populaire. Le magnat nigérian des affaires a promis que l’entrée sur la place financière de Lagos de sa raffinerie serait « l’introduction en Bourse du peuple ». Il ambitionne de rassembler 10 millions de souscripteurs.

La formule 1 retourne en Afrique pour la première fois depuis 1993, avec dix ans de Grand Prix au Rwanda « au début des années 2030 ». La formule 1 a officialisé, mardi, sa venue au Rwanda à compter du début de la prochaine décennie. La discipline n’était pas venue sur le continent africain depuis 1993 et le Grand Prix de Kyalami, en Afrique du Sud.

A Paris, Emmanuel Macron et Mahamat Idriss Déby actent le renouveau de leur coopération militaire. Après la brouille provoquée par l’éviction de l’armée française du Tchad, les deux chefs d’Etat se sont rapprochés au cours de l’année écoulée. L’armée française reprend même discrètement pied dans son bastion historique.

Ceuta est « indissociable » de l’Espagne, déclare Felipe VI, en visite historique dans l’enclave. Le roi d’Espagne a affirmé la souveraineté « indiscutable » de l’Espagne sur Ceuta lors d’une visite historique mardi dans l’enclave du nord de l’Afrique, revendiquée par le Maroc.

En RDC, l’ancien président Joseph Kabila prend la tête des rebelles de l’Est. Le nouveau Front pour la refondation de la nation, dirigé par l’ex-chef de l’Etat, dénonce la « tyrannie » de l’actuel président congolais, Félix Tshisekedi.
Niger : les images d’une éruption de pétrole qui provoque l’inquiétude. Selon le ministère du pétrole, il s’agit d’un « incident environnemental d’une gravité exceptionnelle ».

Au Liberia, la création de plus en plus incertaine d’un tribunal pour juger les crimes de guerre. Plus de deux décennies après la fin d’une période de guerres civiles qui a fait 250 000 morts, aucune personne impliquée dans les conflits n’a été jugée au Liberia.

Pour la « gen Z » de Madagascar, un an après le putsch militaire, les lendemains qui déchantent. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (1/4). Lancé en septembre 2025, le mouvement de protestation de la jeunesse malgache, qui a conduit au renversement du président Andry Rajoelina, se heurte aux promesses d’une « refondation » du pouvoir par la junte restée lettre morte.

Le Maroc désapprouve en silence la visite du roi d’Espagne, Felipe VI, à Ceuta et à Melilla. Mohammed VI n’a pas publiquement condamné le déplacement du monarque espagnol dans les enclaves d’Afrique du Nord, mais les signes du mécontentement royal sont là.

A l’île Maurice, un couvre-feu décrété après plusieurs jours de manifestations et de violences, déclenchées par un tir policier. Un policier a grièvement blessé par balle une femme, vendredi, à Camp-Levieux, au sud de Port-Louis. Selon la police, 84 personnes ont été interpellées mardi. Les faits recensés comprennent des pillages, des incendies, des actes de violence et des infractions au couvre-feu.

Navanethem Pillay, Prix Nobel de la paix : sur Gaza, « on nous a accusés d’antisémitisme et de partialité. Mais je sais ce qui est constitutif du crime de génocide ». La juriste sud-africaine a présidé la commission d’enquête du Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme, qui a estimé qu’un génocide se déroulait à Gaza. Dans un entretien au « Monde », elle revient sur son travail, récompensé le 9 octobre par le prix Nobel de la paix.

« Les Damnés de la donnée » : les travailleurs du Sud, invisibilisés et pourtant indispensables au développement de l’IA. Au fil d’une enquête menée auprès d’annotateurs de données à Madagascar, le sociologue Clément Le Ludec met en lumière la centralité du travail de cette main-d’œuvre précarisée et invisibilisée, indispensable au bon fonctionnement des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle.

Turkey is hailing an 'Islamic Nato' it can neither afford nor deliver Submitted by Osman Sert on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 07:16 The Mecca pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan answers a real security need, but economic hardship and political repression threaten Ankara's ability to fulfil its commitments Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan stand together after a meeting of the Mecca defence pact’s committee in Riyadh on 5 October 2026 (Turkish Foreign Ministry/Reuters) Off To characterise the defence agreement signed in Mecca on 7 August between Turkey , Pakistan and Saudi Arabia as an initiative devised in response to a single threat that emerged overnight is both incorrect and incomplete. It represents a long-standing need for alignment, brought into sharp relief three years ago by Hamas's attacks on Israel and the genocide that Israel has carried out since with US support. Given Israel's boundless destructive role in the breakdown of global and regional systems, coupled with Iran's disruptive initiatives, which are in fact not particularly new, there was really no other viable path for these three countries. In an atmosphere where the global security architecture and the very perception of security are unravelling, many regions are seeking security structures of their own. As the European Union develops a defence approach relatively independent of the US and Nato , it is only natural for Turkey to pursue similar endeavours with countries it believes share a common outlook. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Consequently, there is no expectation that this pact will replace either Nato or the three countries' other defence commitments. It is, however, defining a mission for itself in the space left vacant by other alliances. The timing, content and practical implications of the agreement are, of course, open to scrutiny. In scrutinising them, one must not forget that none of the three countries possesses the capacity to balance the evolving security risks on its own. In fact, no country, including the US, has such a capacity. One factor making the Mecca pact inevitable is the lowered threshold for conflict between states. Armed conflict between states has never been closer The effort to establish an order represented by the Abraham Accords , which either exclude or antagonise most countries in the region, accelerated this alliance as it converged with global and regional dynamics. One factor making the Mecca pact inevitable is the lowered threshold for conflict between states. Armed conflict between states has never been closer. Rival countries once used proxy organisations rather than confronting each other directly. In the Middle East, the role of proxies has diminished significantly, and countries now engage in direct conflict without intermediaries. Israel's destructive policies and US President Donald Trump's lawlessness have played a major role in this. Iran has responded in kind, both to defend itself and to re-establish the control on the ground that it had long since lost. Otherwise, it would have been unthinkable a decade ago for missiles fired from Iran to head towards Turkey, only to be intercepted by Nato. This is now the new normal in global security. Not Nato, not a declaration It is rather ambitious to read the same meaning into the parties' references to Nato's "an attack on one member is an attack on all" clause in the Mecca agreement. The legal formula resembles Nato's Article 5, but the two structures differ widely in institutional depth, joint command, force structure and operational readiness. Nato is an organisation born in a different historical context, within a distinct geographical and demographic framework. It was established with a clear mission: to counter a bloc that threatened all its members simultaneously. Mecca Agreement: A Muslim Nato or yet another Baghdad Pact? Joseph Massad Read More » Although members have faced numerous direct and indirect attacks since its inception, Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US. Either the members did not call for it, or they deemed the tensions they experienced to fall below the threshold of armed attack or outside the alliance's geographical umbrella. Here, by contrast, each country must manage risks that do not directly threaten the others. It is therefore difficult to speak of a unified perception of threat. The accelerating pace of events has begun to test the Mecca pact sooner than expected. For now, the partnership, which is expected to progress through advanced defence industry cooperation, mutual technical assistance and shared diplomatic positions, must produce practical responses to developments such as those in Yemen , where Saudi Arabia has already invoked it against the Houthis. The Mecca pact is not Nato, but it is no longer merely a political declaration. While its members may perceive the risks they face similarly, it remains unclear what kind of common security and regional perspective they aim to establish to replace the current system. The alliance also needs time to deepen. The lack of geographical continuity, technical compatibility and coordination on threats and projections are gaps that will not be easy to close, though they may be partially overcome over time. Why now for Turkey Alongside these global and regional changes, it is essential to take into account that Turkey's own security scope has expanded. Where Ankara once based its security perception entirely on defending its borders, its interests now stretch from the Horn of Africa to the Caucasus. It would be incorrect to explain this solely through the expansionist strategy of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) or the perception of geography and civilisation once described as "neo-Ottomanism". The failure to establish a stable order in the post-Cold War era has compelled a country of Turkey's stature to extend its military presence across a vast area. In an environment where the regulatory institutions of the global economic system have become dysfunctional, the sustainability of commercial interests also depends on an architecture built through ports, bases and alliances. The AKP's contribution here lies in the framework it developed, particularly over its first 15 years in power, based on its reading of the world and the networks of relationships required to act on it. However much it may be denied today, the approach built during Ahmet Davutoglu's tenure as foreign minister, and the experience President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has accumulated over 24 years of dealing with other leaders, made this possible. Ankara's three dilemmas As for Turkey's dilemmas, the first is capacity. The country is going through one of the deepest economic crises in the history of the republic. A country whose citizens are struggling to make ends meet may still possess a strong defence, but only at the cost of additional burdens on every other area of public life. A budget channelled into defence means cuts to healthcare, education, agriculture and the already rock-bottom living standards of ordinary people. That, in turn, signals a serious crisis of sustainability. Secondly, the current government is struggling to establish the minimum level of social legitimacy required to sustain such ambitious security structures. As has been seen time and again, sending troops abroad or forming defence alliances has won support in parliament well beyond the ruling party's number of seats. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); At present, however, the government sees politics as a zero-sum game and has left no stone unturned in its efforts to eliminate its political rivals. Parliamentary approval is a necessity for international agreements and cross-border troop deployments, and a government bent on eliminating its rivals will find it harder to secure the broad support such commitments require. Labelling a three-nation alliance whose details are not even clear as an 'Islamic Nato' from day one amounts, if not to self-deception, then to telling lies to the public Attempting to bridge this gap with an authoritarian "I've done it, so it's done" mentality does not render the action democratic or lawful, even if the step taken is correct and necessary. The third area of concern is the hollow rhetoric that the government itself has fuelled. The fact that the agreement bears the name of Mecca, a city sacred to Muslims, undoubtedly carries great symbolic value, and it would be wrong to dismiss it. Yet labelling a three-nation alliance whose details are not even clear as an "Islamic Nato" from day one amounts, if not to self-deception, then to telling lies to the public. So does constructing highly problematic narratives by adding up the countries' military forces as if they were items on a grocer's list. Claims that the three together constitute the world's largest tank fleet, the second-largest inventory of military vehicles and the third-largest helicopter fleet are of this kind. Such rhetoric will always have an audience, but realism is the more sensible long-term approach, given the disappointments and traumas societies would otherwise have to endure. 'They're a selfish bunch': How Abu Dhabi shaped modern Manchester Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Thu, 10/15/2026 - 07:30 Manchester City's owners provided investment that fuelled 'Manchesterism' and helped propel Andy Burnham into Downing Street. But at what cost? At a foodbank ten minutes from one of the richest football clubs in the world, Niamh, a young woman in her 20s, has just lost her job. “I found out five minutes ago,” she says, standing behind a desk just inside the entrance to Feed My City in northeast Manchester. Run by a charity called the Manchester Sikh Foundation, Niamh was one of the few people employed by the foodbank, which depends on volunteers, two of whom are sitting down next to her as she tries to process the news. “The council refer people to us, but we don’t get any council funding,” she says, of Manchester City Council. “Anyone can come here and get a hot meal… But we are scrambling to keep afloat. I don’t know if we’ll survive.” A short walk up the road is the Etihad Stadium, home to Manchester City, the football club owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy prime minister and vice president of the United Arab Emirates . Mansour, who has owned the club since 2008 but been to just two games, is a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family and the brother of the emirate’s ruler Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, who is also the president of the UAE. “They’ve never helped us,” Niamh says of Manchester City’s owners in Abu Dhabi, who have been described by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as a “huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”. “We’ve never asked them. But we are right here,” Niamh says. In front of her, a plaque on the wall commemorates the opening of the foodbank by Burnham on 1 December 2021, when the Labour politician was mayor of Manchester. Burnham, a vocal champion of “Manchesterism”, seems like a remote figure to Niamh now. She was engaged with national politics when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader before becoming disillusioned with it in the aftermath of his resignation following the 2019 election. “Honestly, I’m one of many Gen Z’ers who has checked out,” she tells Middle East Eye, referring to the generation now aged between about 14 and 29. “I’m now directly focused on my local community and the difference I can make here.” Without her job at the foodbank, a cluttered space that sits between a fried chicken shop and a newsagent, Niamh will have to find another outlet for her care and dedication, which places like this are so dependent on. A plaque on the wall at Feed My City, east Manchester, marking Andy Burnham opening the foodbank (Oscar Rickett/MEE) Half a minute up the hill from Feed My City there’s another foodbank, which can only afford to operate on one Saturday every month from the Living Hope Christian Church. Next to the church in a food truck selling jerk chicken, Millie Brown, who was born in Jamaica but has lived in this part of Manchester for 20 years, doesn’t mince her words. “Does this area look like anyone is putting anything into it?” she asks, gesturing toward the dilapidated buildings and rubbish-strewn streets. “The people with money don’t care about this place.” Brown is a member of the Pentecostal church next door and what money she makes from the jerk chicken stand goes to its foodbank. “They don’t support us,” she says of Manchester City. “Even the fans who come to the area on match days don’t come here.” The church foodbank has never got any help from Manchester City, which has previously contributed to other foodbanks and whose supporters have a foodbank initiative . “I don’t mind them,” Brown says of Manchester City’s owners, “but I think they’re a selfish bunch.” Manchester City did not respond to Middle East Eye’s request for comment. Guilty verdicts for Manchester City The question of what Manchester City’s owners have or have not done for the city around them is in the spotlight right now, as is the relationships that exist between politicians like Burnham, who has made much of the supposed success of the “Manchester model”, and the UAE. On 29 September, after a nearly eight-year long investigation, an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges relating to serious breaches of the league’s financial rules and a failure to cooperate with the investigation. City was found to have disguised more than £830m ($1.1bn) in illicit funding, and the commission’s report referred on eight separate occasions to “sham” contracts, agreements, commercial deals and arrangements struck by the club. As recorded in internal Manchester City communications leaked by Portuguese hacker and activist Rui Pinto in 2018, Simon Pearce, Abu Dhabi’s branding guru, had wrote of the contracts: “We can do what we want.” The connection between the football club and the image of the UAE was also clear from the start. Garry Cook, who as then-CEO of Manchester City was central to brokering the deal that saw Mansour buy the club, told Abu Dhabi’s representatives: “If you're developing your nation and you're looking to be on a global stage, we are your proxy brand for the nation.” A banner at Liverpool's Anfield football ground before the game against Manchester City, Sunday 11 October 2026 (Reuters) Manchester City has appealed the verdicts and continues to maintain its innocence, saying it has a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” to support this. City Football Group CEO Ferran Soriano has referred to the verdicts as a “Premier League conspiracy theory”. On the international stage, successive British governments and local leaders in Manchester have been accused of ignoring – or covering for - the UAE’s sponsorship of genocide in Sudan , war in Yemen and human rights abuses at home because of Emirati investment in the UK . 'I don't mind them, but I think they are a selfish bunch' - Millie Brown, Living Hope Christian Church foodbank “The UAE has been amazing for Manchester – football aside,” a former British civil servant, who worked on bringing in Emirati and other foreign investment into the UK, tells MEE. “They won’t leave,” the source says of the Emiratis. “They are serious investors and won’t do things that destroy value. And they will continue investing in the UK – we are a great stable place to invest. But they won’t invest in the volume we have seen for the last 20 years, and that is a loss to the UK economy.” That investment was referenced by Burnham in his first intervention following the guilty verdicts. The prime minister, who was mayor of Manchester from 2017 to 2026, said he would be “really concerned” to lose Abu Dhabi United Group as owners and praised them for investing in Manchester. “I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city,” Burnham said, before having to make clear that football-related disciplinary findings should be handled separately from the UAE’s economic ties to Manchester. Since then, there have been reports of Emirati officials threatening to cancel investments in the UK over “the Premier League’s actions”. On Monday, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) revealed details of Burnham's meetings with Man City, including with the club's chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, but it did not mention two hospitality dinners the then-mayor had with the Emirati executive, which took place at matches in 2017 and 2018. Manchester Life Launched in 2014 with a “£1bn” deal between Manchester City Council and the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) – the investment vehicle owned by Mansour – Manchester Life, which did not repond to MEE's request for comment, is the most prominent manifestation of Emirati investment in the city. On a bright October afternoon, the marina at the heart of its Ancoats and New Islington development in east Manchester sparkles in the sun. Young people stroll along the banks of a canal dug to connect two already existing canals and a billboard celebrates a collection of “Manchester Brits” – “the raver”, “the northern soul”, “the lad”. Two-bedroom flats here in a part of Manchester once described as a “post-industrial wasteland” can be rented for between £1300 and £1600 a month, and residents say you can’t get a one-bedroom flat for less than £1000 a month, in a city in which the average annual salary is about £34,000. There are no affordable homes in the project, and a 2022 report by Jonathan Silver, Richard Goulding and Adam Leaver of the University of Sheffield, entitled Manchester Offshored , detailed the way in which public leaseholds and assets were transferred to Abu Dhabi-controlled subsidiaries registered in Jersey, a tax haven. A surviving piece of the Smith's Arms pub, built in 1775 and demolished for a residential development (Oscar Rickett/MEE) There is a 158-apartment building called Smith’s Yard, named in honour of the pub that was demolished to make way for it. The Smith’s Arms was built in 1775 and was Manchester’s oldest pub when it was bulldozed in 2016 to make way for the flats. In the lobby of the building a brick facade taken from the pub and bearing its name is on display close to a canvas on which the slogan “For Manchester is the place where people do things” is written in a bubbly font of different colours. These references to Manchester, its history and its public-facing civic culture as a city that was at the heart of both industrial capitalism and the radical resistance to that, can be found across this constellation of Abu Dhabi-backed new build flats. There is a co-working space called Colony, blocks of flats called Cotton Field Wharf and another called Weavers Quay, which has a dog drinking station (a small metal bowl) outside it. Then there’s Bengal Street, named in the Victorian era after the part of south Asia whose cotton industry was systematically destroyed by Britain’s East India Company, a wealthy, mercenary-deploying expansionist imperial force that one European diplomat tells MEE has been an inspiration to the UAE. The UAE in Sudan That expansionism is now most clearly on display in Sudan, where the UAE backs the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been found to have committed genocide in Darfur by the UN and US. The UAE continues to deny this support. Middle East Eye has reported on it extensively, and on the “political capture” that has seen the UK shy away from calling Abu Dhabi out on it. The New York Times has reported that Mansour is in regular, direct contact with Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, the RSF leader better known as Hemedti. For Mohannad Taha, who lived in Manchester for a decade and started the Manchester4Sudan activist group, it is “easy to decouple the football club from the ownership, which is an oligarchic, corrupt force”. Mohammed bin Zayed al-Nahyan and Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan of the UAE watching Manchester City's 2023 Champions League final game in Istanbul (Reuters) “I think the ownership is 100 percent complicit in what is happening in Sudan. I think the leadership of the club is somewhat complicit, the fans and the players not at all. “Our leaders are scared to confront Abu Dhabi’s complicity because of investment,” Taha says. Born in Newcastle to Sudanese parents, he is dispirited by what he sees as a failure to link Manchester City’s owners to the war in Sudan, which is the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. The premier league’s guilty verdicts “felt good in a small sense”, he says, “but then I thought: are people going to make the jump into Sudan? “If you tackle the Emirati leadership in a principled manner, then you will find them guilty. If you are beholden to them, you will find them not guilty.” From council estate to new build flats Looking out over the glistening marina in Ancoats, Isaac Rose, a tenant organiser and author of The Rentier City: Manchester and the Making of the Neoliberal Metropolis , describes what we see in front of us as “the original sin of Manchester”. “This nice scene was built on a destroyed and flooded council estate,” he tells MEE. "Abu Dhabi is a layer on top of what's already happened." This estate was the Cardroom, named after the card room in local cotton mills and demolished in the early 2000s. Initially, the Cardroom redevelopment, rebranded as “New Islington” after an old mill in the area but with a deafening echo of the London neighbourhood in which Tony Blair had lived before becoming prime minister, was handed to Urban Splash, a company founded by former 80s raver Tom Bloxham. 'This nice scene was built on a destroyed and flooded council estate. Abu Dhabi is a layer on top of what's already happened' - Isaac Rose, tenant organiser and author An intriguingly unfiltered Urban Splash promotional video from 2002 chronicles the company’s attempts to win the estate’s residents round to their vision of urban regeneration. Bloxham, with cropped bleached blond hair and The Fall’s Jerusalem as soundtrack, enthuses about turning “this dereliction into a world exposition of some of the best areas in the country”. “Look at this, the canals, aren’t they fantastic, the Ashton, the Rochdale, let’s put in some new canals," he exclaims, "let’s create a new Amsterdam, a new east Manchesterdam, a really special place in the city.” But as the video demonstrates, selling this vision to the Cardroom estate’s existing residents was another matter. In the now-demolished Cob o'Coal pub, one asks: “Where are the homes going to be to accommodate us?” There is no answer. “Yous have made your mind up what you’re going to do,” another says. “Let’s have it right. You have.” In the end, Urban Splash built just one building of significance in New Islington, a construction called Chips, made to resemble a chip. Then came the financial crash of 2008 and the election in 2010 of the Conservative-Liberal Democrat government which, under Chancellor George Osborne, instituted an austerity policy that would go on to cut over 60 percent of central government funding to local authorities. Luckily for Manchester though, the local football team had some new oil- and gas-rich owners from the Gulf, and for them the financial crash was an opportunity, not a setback. Andy Burnham and the Manchester model While Burnham has, as prime minister, taken credit for the perceived success of Manchester, for Rose and other chroniclers of the city’s fate, the former mayor is a bit-part player in a story that began in the 1980s and was driven by two men, Richard Leese and Howard Bernstein. “Burnham has staked his reputation on Manchesterism and now we see the compromises that have been involved in that,” Richard Goulding, co-author of the Manchester Offshored report, tells MEE. “The Manchester model is one in which you can have growth and redistribution without having to make hard political choices,” Goulding says. “What’s embarrassing for Burnham is that he’s been willing to take the credit.” 'Burnham has staked his reputation on Manchesterism and now we see the compromises that have been involved in that' - Richard Goulding, University of Sheffield As leader and chief executive of Manchester City Council from the mid-1990s into the 2020s, Leese and Bernstein, both Manchester City fans (Leese is now an honorary president of the club, while Bernstein died in 2024), were the principal architects of the Manchester model, which saw the council aggressively pursue public-private partnerships and outside investment. Leese, a former maths teacher from Mansfield, was part of a group on the left of the Labour Party that took over Manchester council in the “glorious revolution” of 1984. But with Margaret Thatcher winning the election of 1987 and Thatcherism cementing itself in Westminster, Leese, who did not respond to MEE’s request for an interview, pursued private investment for his adopted city. After an IRA bomb – the largest to go off in mainland Britain since the Second World War – went off in Manchester city centre in 1996, Leese and Bernstein set about rebuilding and redeveloping the city they ran. The City of Manchester stadium was built with public money for the 2002 Commonwealth Games and taken over thereafter by Manchester City Football Club, which renamed it the Etihad Stadium after Mansour’s arrival in 2008. “The financial crash is so traumatic for them because they’ve spent their life dragging Manchester out of industrialisation,” Rose says of Leese and Bernstein. Billboards at the Ancoats and New Islington development, Manchester (Oscar Rickett/MEE) For Abu Dhabi – as well as for Qatar and investors from China , Russia and elsewhere – the crash meant that British commodities and state assets could be gobbled up for bargain prices. In 2013, British ministers set up a secret unit, codenamed Project Falcon, that gave the UAE privileged access to the UK’s political elite, prime land deals and world-famous institutions in academia and the NHS. Tony Blair acted as a lobbyist for the UAE and Osborne pushed for Emirati investment in non-defence assets. The ownership of Manchester City meant that for Leese and Bernstein, there were investors already tied to their city who were “richer than God”. “Government doesn’t have the money nor necessarily the ideas to reinvigorate places – and to do so against market economics is both futile and a bad use of the money they do have,” says the former British civil servant. “Almost all major reinvigorations have depended heavily on private capital.” 'All was subjugated to the City, all served the interests of our lucrative status as a safe haven for corrupt, and corrupting wealth' - Carl Scott, former UK defence attache In a letter to the Financial Times, Carl Scott, a former UK defence attache in Moscow, described a related realisation he had when he returned to Britain from his posting in 2016: “All was subjugated to the City, all served the interests of our lucrative status as a safe haven for corrupt, and corrupting wealth.” “We take them as we find them,” said Bernstein, of the club’s owners, meaning that what they might or might not be doing at home or in the Middle East was not of Manchester’s concern. The owners from Abu Dhabi were also incentivised. The Manchester Offshored report found that nine sites sold to Mansour in the 2014 deal were done so at a fraction of their value, and well below what other plots nearby fetched. This was a deal that produced a “negligible” financial return for the public and in which the family silver was sold off cheap, the researchers concluded. Reporting from the Manchester Mill and the I Paper has also revealed that Abu Dhabi was given a “sweetheart deal” that afforded it first refusal on a broad stretch of land, and that the local authority has received less than £3m for building almost 1,800 homes under the agreement. “The deal is always too good to be true. They aren’t running Abu Dhabi United Group as a charity,” says Goulding. The Manchester of Engels In his play Comedians , the playwright Trevor Griffiths, who was from Ancoats, has one of his characters - a comedian-turned-teacher who fought in the Second World War - describe the devastation of the German city of Dresden after it was bombed to rubble. “It reminded me of Ancoats,” the character says. In the 19th century, Friedrich Engels, Karl Marx’s collaborator, described the “350,000 working people of Manchester and its environs” as living, “almost all of them, in wretched, damp, filthy cottages”. “One day I walked with one of these middleclass gentlemen into Manchester,” Engels writes. “I spoke to him about the disgraceful unhealthy slums and drew his attention to the disgusting condition of that part of town in which factory workers lived.” 'Mayfair means money': A walk through the Gulf elite's favourite part of London Read More » The gentleman listens patiently and then, as he and Engels part, tells him: “And yet there is a great deal of money made here.” Manchester’s redevelopment has, Goulding says, “brought in jobs and increased opportunity. But there is still a lot of severe inequality in the city”. “Look at the inequality and the foodbanks,” says Rose, who paints a wide, sweeping picture of Manchester that depicts its journey from the forefront of industrial capitalism in the 19th century to the forefront of rentier capitalism in the 21st century. “It reminds me of Disneyland,” he says, looking out over the Ancoats marina. “There’s a facade that’s really nice, but behind it…” Waiting at a tram stop a couple of minutes from the Feed My City foodbank, Janet and David, a Manchester City fan in his sixties, say that the owners from Abu Dhabi “have done a lot for the area”. But David is not defiant, is not revelling – like some fellow fans – in the label “cheat”. “If they’re guilty, we’ve got to take the hit. We can go back to our roots. We’ve been there before, we can do it again.” Their tram pulls into the station, its destination written on the front: Etihad Campus. Why have Saudi air defences failed to intercept Houthi missiles? Submitted by Paul Iddon on Wed, 10/14/2026 - 21:30 Geography, interceptor shortages and evolving attack tactics may help explain why Saudi Arabia's advanced systems have struggled to stop repeated strikes A US airforce member looks on near a Patriot missile battery at the Prince Sultan air base in Al-Kharj, central Saudi Arabia, on 20 February 2020 (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP) Off For years, Yemen 's Houthis have demonstrated their ability to strike some of Saudi Arabia 's most strategically important targets, from oil infrastructure to the kingdom's capital. But repeated missile and drone strikes on Riyadh's main international airport have raised fresh questions about the limits of the kingdom's sophisticated air defences. Since 6 October, the strikes have killed at least 20 people and injured almost 400. The deadliest attack so far happened on 10 October when 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded. On Monday, the kingdom vowed a "serious" response to the attacks and less than 24 hours later, Saudi strikes targeted energy facilities in Sanaa - causing massive fires and explosions that rocked the Yemeni capital. So why have the latest Houthi attacks repeatedly penetrated Saudi defences, and what do they reveal about the kingdom's ability to protect its most valuable assets? (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Riyadh has spent billions of dollars on some of the world's most advanced air-defence systems, assembling an arsenal designed to counter precisely these threats. Its equipment includes the American-made MIM-104 Patriot, including the advanced PAC-3 variant with hit-to-kill technology, and the even more sophisticated Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system. Both can intercept ballistic missiles and have demonstrated their capabilities in combat. Saudi Arabia also has a well-equipped air force, including advanced F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoons, capable of engaging drones and cruise missiles. Houthi strikes mark the end of Saudi Arabia's Yemen 'containment strategy' Read More » Yet Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly evaded or penetrated the kingdom's defences, exposing the difficulty of protecting a vast territory and its high-value targets from sustained attacks. Nicholas Heras, interim executive director at the Middle East Policy Council and senior director at the New Lines Institute, said Saudi Arabia’s vast territory leaves it "unusually exposed" to Houthi attacks launched from northern Yemen. "Much of Saudi territory is desert, which makes it challenging to fully defend because of the distances that must be accounted for - and it costs more to have personnel maintain early warning systems in that terrain," Heras told Middle East Eye. "The Houthis have a target-rich environment in Saudi Arabia that includes some of the most important oil infrastructure in the world that are more immediately exposed to the drone and missile attack capabilities that the Houthis possess." Heras said the attacks on Riyadh were intended to send a message to Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen. "The Houthis perceived a gap in Saudi capability and attention span and struck Riyadh to send a signal to Saudi Arabia that if Sanaa is hit, Riyadh will be hit," he said. 'Deliberate escalation' Federico Borsari, a defence expert at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (Cepa), believes the strikes represent an escalation in the Yemeni group’ willingness to attack the kingdom rather than necessarily demonstrating a fundamentally new capability. The group has possessed long-range strike capabilities for almost a decade and previously targeted Riyadh in 2017. "Since then, their arsenal has further expanded to include increasingly sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles built with Iranian help," Borsari told MEE. "But without evidence it is hard to tell whether some new capabilities were used." For Borsari, the more concerning development "is the Houthis' ability to conduct repeated, coordinated strikes against heavily defended targets." (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); He added that the timing appears consistent with "deliberate escalation intended to impose economic and political costs" on Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen. Freddy Khoueiry, lead Middle East and North Africa and defence analyst at risk intelligence company RANE, said it remained unclear whether the attacks reflected new Houthi capabilities. 'The escalation is significant because the Houthis are demonstrating both the capability and willingness to impose direct costs on the Saudi capital' - Freddy Khoueiry, RANE "Based on publicly available information, it is still difficult to determine whether the Riyadh attacks represent a specific new technological upgrade or simply a decision to employ existing capabilities more aggressively against civilian aviation infrastructure," he told MEE. "In either case, the escalation is significant because the Houthis are demonstrating both the capability and willingness to impose direct costs on the Saudi capital," he said. Mohammed al-Basha of the Virginia-based Basha Report risk advisory said the Houthis had spent years refining their long-range strike capabilities. "For years, the Houthis have used their attacks on Israel to refine their long-range strike capabilities," he told MEE. "What appeared to be failed attacks were also opportunities to learn and adapt." The group may have applied lessons from its regional attacks, as well as from Iran’s confrontations with the US and Israel, to improve its ability to challenge sophisticated air-defence networks. "Saudi Arabia has invested heavily in Patriot, Thaad, and other systems, but its vast territory makes comprehensive protection difficult," al-Basha said. "The Houthis do not need to overwhelm the entire network. One successful strike can cause significant damage and disruption." The repeated strikes also raise questions about whether Saudi Arabia has enough interceptors to sustain its defences during a prolonged campaign. The interceptor problem Saudi Arabia's interceptor stockpiles may have been depleted following sustained use during the wider regional conflict with Iran. Repeated missile and drone attacks can rapidly consume the expensive interceptors needed to stop incoming threats. The United States has also expended significant quantities of Patriot and Thaad interceptors during the conflict, putting pressure on supplies that could take years to replenish. 'Riyadh no longer feels safe': Houthi strikes shatter Saudi capital's aura of calm Read More » Borsari described interceptor depletion as a "credible explanation" for the breaches, although he cautioned against treating it as the only possible cause. He pointed to media reports from last month suggesting that Riyadh was running low on ballistic missile interceptors. "If true, this would create difficult operational trade-offs for air-defence commanders when deciding which threats to engage, how many interceptors to allocate, etc," he said. "These decisions become even more problematic during mass salvos." The Houthis could also be attempting to saturate Saudi defences by launching different types of weapons simultaneously, including one-way attack drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. Even sophisticated, multilayered air-defence systems cannot guarantee that every incoming projectile will be intercepted during a sustained bombardment. Borsari said it would be "naive to deny" that the Riyadh strikes raise "serious questions" about the effectiveness of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defences, particularly their ability to protect fixed, high-value targets under repeated attack. Khoueiry similarly argued that the strikes were less evidence of "a fundamental deficiency" in Saudi air defences than a reminder of the limitations facing even advanced systems. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "Saudi Arabia has to defend a very large territory and prioritize coverage around major cities, military sites and critical infrastructure, while interceptor availability is also under pressure," he said. "Direct ballistic-missile impacts could reflect those constraints, but on their own they do not prove a severe interceptor shortage." A costly game of adaptation "We don't know what the specific cause of this failure is," Borsari said of the attacks. He noted that an air defence network's effectiveness depends on several components. "The effectiveness of a defensive network depends not simply on the sophistication of its interceptors but also on sensor coverage and integration, proficient C2 (command and control), ammunition availability, etc. So it could be any of these, or - most likely - a combination thereof." Saudi Arabia's geography compounds those challenges. Its airports, oil facilities, ports and military installations are spread across a vast area, making continuous protection expensive and difficult to sustain. 'For years, the Houthis have used their attacks on Israel to refine their long-range strike capabilities. What appeared to be failed attacks were also opportunities to learn and adapt' - Mohammed al-Basha, Basha Report "The main challenge is detection, and for that you need to rely on various assets, including aircraft, to ensure proper early warning," Borsari said. "But maintaining such a detection regime over time is very costly and a sustainment burden on both the equipment and personnel." There are cheaper options for countering drones in particular, including automated anti-drone turrets equipped with heavy machine guns and low-cost short-range interceptors. But these require supporting infrastructure and careful integration with existing systems. "So I'm afraid we will continue to see drones penetrating Saudi territory for the foreseeable future," Borsari said. Khoueiry sees the latest Houthi strikes, alongside recent Iranian attacks on American and regional targets, as evidence of a wider effort to adapt to sophisticated air-defence systems rather than simply a matter of luck. "Iran and its partners appear to be learning how to operate against layered air defence networks, adapting flight routes and tactics to improve penetration and impose higher interception and economic costs," he said. "The lesson for Saudi Arabia and the wider region is that increasingly sophisticated air defences still need dense surveillance, sufficient interceptor stocks and constant adaptation to keep pace with evolving missile and drone threats."
