The journalists, which included two Leicester Gazette reporters and two union-accredited freelancers, were covering a demonstration outside UAV Tactical Systems in Leicester, a subsidiary of the Israeli arms manufacturer, Elbit Systems on 8 October. Participants held handmade signs expressing support for the proscribed direct action group, Palestine Action, an offence under Section 13 of the Terrorism Act. Emma Guy, Leicester Gazette editor, told MEE the journalists had been “blanket arrested” under Section 13 and detained by police for three hours before they were de-arrested after handing over their personal information, despite the reporters having identified themselves to multiple officers. “A decision was made by Leicestershire Police to blanket arrest journalists and then de-arrest them on a case by case basis,” Guy said. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The two freelance journalists told MEE that the protest began peacefully, and the police had agreed with the activists to disperse at midday. But when the participants attempted to leave a cordoned area around that time, they were stopped. “The police suddenly arrived in quite large numbers, and they formed a kettle,” said Matt*, a freelance photographer who used a pseudonym as he wished to remain anonymous. Shortly after, an officer announced through a megaphone that all protestors who were standing within the police cordon encircling the vigil would be arrested. 'They just arrested anybody that was in there. People that were just standing round holding banners, and people that had done nothing at all' - freelance journalist “I didn't think that necessarily would apply to press. I mean, it never does, press is always the exception,” Matt said. Both reporters who spoke to MEE said they had presented their press cards to the police in order to pass through a cordon around the protestors to do their work. “I showed them my press card a number of times in order to get through the cordon. Probably about four or five times, you know, to go out and then to come back in, and it was fine,” Matt told MEE. When he attempted to cross the cordon a final time, he was stopped and informed by a police liaison officer that he was arrested under Section 13 of the Terrorist Act for supporting a proscribed organisation. Both journalists were then informed they would be de-arrested if they handed the police their personal information, despite having already presented their press cards, which contain pin codes allowing police to verify the cardholder's identity. Police try to haul an elderly protestor into a police van outside UAV Tactical Systems in Leicester, 8 October (Martin Pope) “But they weren’t interested in that, and they didn't want to seem to check. I just think it was incredibly heavy-handed,” Matt said. “They just arrested anybody that was in there. People that were just standing round holding banners, and people that had done nothing at all.” Another freelance video-journalist who goes by the name “Barold" on social media told MEE that his arresting officer refused to speak with his representative from the National Union of Journalists. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Barold told MEE that “at one point the officer negotiating my de-arrest explicitly told me that part of the purpose of the arrest was simply to ascertain people's details and find out who everyone was”. Guy said that the Leicester Gazette reporters - Joseph Herbert and Devon Winters - had identified themselves as journalists to a press liaison officer as soon as they arrived on site, and later to their arresting officers. “So this wasn't a case of misidentification,” Guy said. Former government lawyer and spokesperson for the campaign group Defend Our Juries, Tim Crosland, told MEE: “There is no legal basis for police to demand members of the public provide them with personal information generally, and definitely not as a pre-condition for ‘de-arrest’". "Such oppressive and intimidatory police conduct is characteristic of a police state, not policing by consent," he added. 'A worrying precedent As they're local to the Elbit site, Guy and her team have reported on protests there repeatedly over the last five years, but without incident. “We've never had an issue, and the process is always the same - we approach the press liason officer and introduce ourselves,” she told MEE. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "This a concerning for us as a small newsroom. Like many others, we don’t go to work thinking that we’ll be arrested under the Terrorism Act. It sets a worrying precedent that journalists are being arrested for doing their jobs," she added. 'Such oppressive and intimidatory police conduct is characteristic of a police state, not policing by consent' - Tim Crosland, Defend Our Juries According to Guy, the reporters were informed by police that they were arrested under an expansion of the Terrorism Act, which includes live-streaming images or material in support of a proscribed organisation. A Leicestershire Police spokesperson told MEE in response to a request for comment that: “A number of people identifying themselves as journalists were at the scene of protest activity on Thursday 8 October in Meridian Way, Braunstone. “To affect a thorough investigation, due to the circumstances and number of people at the scene, everyone was placed under arrest and told to remain in the area,” the spokesperson said. “Once these individuals had been spoken to, details provided to officers and it was established that no offences had been committed, they were de-arrested," they said, adding that they had not been taken into custody. When asked by MEE whether officers had accused any journalists of live streaming the event, the spokesperson referred to a statement confirming that a total of 35 people had been arrested under Section 13, with one person "further arrested on suspicion of racially aggravated public order," and taken into police custody. It added that all 35 have been released on conditional bail. A woman surrounded by police holds a placard expressing support for Palestine Action outside UAV Tactical Systems in Leicester, 8 October 2026 (Martin Pope) Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said that union is "concerned" by reports of the arrests and has written to the National Police Chiefs' Council "over concerns of police overreach". Davison said that the union had emphasised following the government's ban that "covering Palestine Action protests and taking photographs or videos of the group's placards does not in of itself constitute support for the group". Defend Our Juries confirmed to MEE that, despite lots of filming and livestreaming of previous protests, no one has previously been arrested for doing so. ‘You don't know if you're gonna come home’ Both journalists who spoke to MEE said that they observed interactions between Elbit security staff and police officers. Matt, who has covered a number of protests at Elbit sites, said that he has noted communication between the arms firm's security staff and the police during previous demonstrations. “As a journalist, you don't feel entirely safe. You’re made to feel that you shouldn't really be there,” he said. 'As a journalist, you don't feel entirely safe. Israel’s 2026 election: Who are the main leaders and where do they stand on the key issues? Submitted by Daniel Tester on Wed, 10/14/2026 - 12:55 How Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Golan compare on Gaza, West Bank security, the ultra-Orthodox military draft, and future Knesset coalitions. On The Israeli election on 27 October is one of the most important in the country’s history, the first since 2022 and the Hamas-led attacks of 2023, the genocide in Gaza and the war on Iran. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , Israel’s longest-serving premier and now seeking a seventh term, faces wide criticism for his handling of the wars, which have isolated Israel internationally. Other issues facing Israelis include the security of the occupied West Bank, including the growth of settlements, and compulsory military conscription for ultra-Orthodox communities. Israel uses proportional representation to elect 120 members to the Knesset, although no single party since the nation was founded in 1948 has won a 61-seat majority. Instead, politicians and parties cut deals and form coalitions to win power. The anti-Netanyahu Change bloc, for example, led by front-runner Gadi Eisenkot, includes ex-PM Naftali Bennett (B’Yachad) and former deputy prime minister Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beiteinu) among others. Polls at the time of writing forecast a deadlock. Netanyahu or his rivals will need to once again reach out to smaller parties, such as those backed by ultra-Orthodox voters or the Israeli far right, to form a government. Millions of Palestinians in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, occupied by Israel for nearly 60 years, do not have Israeli citizenship and so cannot vote, in contrast to Israeli settlers living in the occupied territories. Arab parties that draw support from the two million-plus Palestinians living inside Israel were initially banned from entering the race in September, before the ban was overturned earlier this month. Arab voter turnout in national elections is usually below average amid boycotts . But for this election, more Palestinian citizens of Israel are predicted to vote than usual according to polls, with the Palestinian-led Joint List expecting 70 percent voter turnout. These are the main candidates and their parties. Benjamin Netanyahu / Likud Current seats: 32/120 Netanyahu, first elected in 1996 and prime minister for 20 of the last 30 years, faces his toughest election yet. His career has been built on hawkish stances against Israel’s enemies, expanding West Bank settlements and blocking Palestinian statehood. His current government, in power since 2022, is the most right-wing in Israeli history and has overseen genocide and war crimes in Gaza, for which Netanyahu faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivers a speech to members of the Likud party in Tel Aviv on 17 September 2026 (AFP) Many Israelis have questioned his decisions leading up to 7 October 2023, including playing off Hamas against Fatah to weaken the Palestine Authority; also whether he ignored warnings of the attack which killed 1,200 people. Netanyahu opposes an official commission of inquiry. The Israeli-US war on Iran has failed to secure a decisive victory. Tens of thousands of Israelis are still displaced amid attacks from Hezbollah in Lebanon . Controversial proposals to weaken the judiciary have mostly been shelved amid protests . But Netanyahu and Likud (which translates as “The Gathering”) still retain strong support among many on the Israeli right, where they are seen as no-nonsense protectors of Israel who have pledged to disarm Hamas and maintain “ security zones ” in Lebanon. The government is also seeking to push ahead with the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which will divide the West Bank, amid international condemnation. Gadi Eisenkot / Yashar Current seats: New party Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s biggest rival, heads Yashar (“Honest” in Hebrew), the party he founded in September 2025. An ex-chief of staff in the military (2015 to 2019), Eisenkot, 66, has served in the Knesset since 2022 but has limited ministerial experience save eight months in the emergency government formed after 7 October. Gadi Eisenkot (centre) holds a meet-and-greet at a coffee shop in Jerusalem on 12 August 2026 (AFP) He is of Moroccan Jewish heritage and, if elected, would be Israel’s first Mizrahi prime minister. His upbringing in Eilat, far from the elite of Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, and his faltering English , have added to his image as a political outsider. Many Palestinians and human rights campaigners question Eisenkot’s military past: during Israel’s 2006 invasion of Lebanon, he formulated the Dahieh Doctrine , which advocated “ disproportionate force ” in civilian areas to deter attacks. A self-styled moderate , Eisenkot has been critical of aspects of Netanyahu’s approach on Gaza, not least the long-stalled hostage talks. His personal story is well-known to many Israelis: Eisenkot’s son, Gal, and two of his nephews were killed in Gaza in 2023 and 2024, with Gal’s funeral broadcast on national TV. Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution, which he says is unviable after 7 October, and the formal annexation of the West Bank, which he says will only worsen security. Leading the polls, he has become the unofficial leader of the Change bloc but will likely need more parliamentary partners to govern. He has said that allies will need to agree that Israel is a Jewish and democratic state; that military service must be universal; and that Hamas is a terrorist organisation that must be dismantled. While Eisenkot has rejected the option of relying on the Palestinian parties, he also vowed to form a government "even if we don't have 61 seats". This, coupled with statements from some of the Palestinian parties, is seen as indicating there may be options for some form of cooperation. His conditions about military service likely rules out partnering with ultra-Orthodox parties who want to keep the Haredim’s draft exemption. Itamar Ben-Gvir / Otzma Yehudit Current seats: 6/120 Once shunned as too extreme for mainstream politics, Otzma Yehudit (“Jewish Power”), led by Itamar Ben Gvir , has pulled Netanyahu’s government further to the right since 2022. In September it avoided a vote in Israel’s Central Election Committee to bar it from standing. Now it is likely to increase its seats. A kippah-bearing a portrait of Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben Gvir, at a shop in Jerusalem on 4 October 2026 (AFP) It has heavy support from Israeli settlers, and it backs annexing the West Bank (Ben Gvir, 50, lives in the settlement of Kiryat Arba). Relations between Ben Gvir and Netanyahu have often been tense during the past two decades, with the Otzma Yehudit leader recently saying that the prime minister wants to form a government without him. A Knesset member since 2021, Ben Gvir became national security minister in 2022 when his party unexpectedly won seven seats, despite his criminal convictions for incitement to racism and support for terrorism. He has been sanctioned by the UK, France and others for backing the genocide in Gaza ; led invasions of al-Aqsa mosque , over which he proclaims Jewish sovereignty; and taunted detained activists from the Global Sumud Flotilla. Otzma Yehudit advocates the “ voluntary emigration ” of Palestinians from Gaza; rallies draw chants of “death to Arabs”. In government, it has sponsored judicial reforms and the death penalty for Palestinians. Its junior ministers have discussed nuking Gaza. But Otzma Yehudit has tense relations with ultra-Orthodox communities because it backs universal conscription. Bezalel Smotrich / Religious Zionism Current seats: 7/120 Once a marginal extreme-right faction, the Religious Zionist Party (RZP) has ascended as a partner in the ruling coalition. It had a strong showing in 2022 amid an electoral pact with Otzma Yehudit, but the parties have now severed this to run as competitors, despite Netanyahu’s pleas for an alliance. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich arrives at the Israeli settlement of Maale Arugot in Gush Etzion, occupied West Bank on 2 September 2026 (AFP) Leader Bezalel Smotrich, 46, the son of an Orthodox rabbi, draws support from a more religious base than Ben Gvir, wants the implementation of Jewish law (halacha), and says Torah scripture has underpinned his strategy as finance minister since 2022. Smotrich also wants a judicial overhaul, the abolition of the Oslo Accords , the dismantlement of the Palestinian Authority, and the Israeli settlement of Gaza and the West Bank. He calls himself a “ proud homophobe ”. Like Ben Gvir, prosecutors at the ICC have sought warrants for Smotrich’s arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians in the West Bank. RZP backs military conscription for ultra-Orthodox communities but, sitting alongside Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s fragile coalition, has voted for Haredi-backed laws, such as stopping arrests of Haredi draft dodgers. Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid / Together Current seats: 24/120 Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett (2021-22) and Yair Lapid (July-December 2022) announced a joint ticket in April, later named B'Yachad (“Together”). Bennett will be prime minister if the party wins. The pair unseated Netanyahu in 2021 amid an on-off political partnership that has lasted more than a decade. Yair Lapid, left, and Naftali Bennett hold their inaugural conference of their "Together - Under Bennett's Leadership" party in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 12 May 2026 (AFP) Bennett, 54, sits on the right, is a longtime opponent of Palestinian statehood and ex-leader of The Yesha Council that represents West Bank settlers. A software multimillionaire, he was Netanyahu’s chief of staff from 2006 to 2008, when they fell out. Lapid, already known as a TV host and writer, founded Yesh Atid (“There is a Future”) in 2012. A secular centrist, he opposes Palestinian statehood and, like many Jewish politicians, supports the settler movement in principle, while distancing himself from Ben Gvir and Smotrich. In April, Lapid, 62, said : “Bennett is a clear right-winger, but he is a liberal, decent, law-abiding right-winger, who did not sell his values - neither to Haredi extortion nor to corruption.” Both men oppose the ultra-Orthodox draft exemption and have pledged a commission of inquiry into 7 October. Yair Golan / The Democrats Current seats: 4/120 The centre-left Democrats, who regard themselves as a “liberal-democratic Zionist party” , formed in 2024 from the Labor Party and the smaller Meretz. They are led by Yair Golan, 64, one of the few Israeli politicians to criticise the killing of Palestinians in Gaza, calling it a “national psychosis”. The Democrats leader Yair Golan meets with potential voters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 24 September 2026 (AFP) Amid a massive backlash , he has qualified that he blames the government, not the military . He was deputy chief of staff from 2014 to 2017, re-enlisted on 7 October and is credited with saving several Israelis amid the Hamas-led attacks, for which many Israelis regard him as a war hero . The Democrats have led protests against judicial reforms, oppose annexing the West Bank, and back the two-state solution. They have an Arab candidate in Soumaya Bashir, and are the only major party to openly support joining Arab parties in a coalition. Avigdor Lieberman / Yisrael Beiteinu Current seats: 6/120 The right-wing Yisrael Beiteunu (“Our Home”), which relies on Israel’s 1.5 million Russian speakers for support, has been led since 1998 by its founder, Avigdor Lieberman , 68, an emigre from Soviet-era eastern Europe. The party has never finished higher than third, but has been in coalition with seven of the last 10 governments. Avigdor Lieberman, centre, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 26 September 2026 (AFP) Yisrael Beiteinu backs universal conscription, the expansion of settlements and tougher stances against Iran , Hamas and Hezbollah. Lieberman has held all the key cabinet roles, including deputy prime minister (2009 - 2012). He has faced probes over alleged corruption , allegations of an assasination plot , and was convicted of physically assaulting a 12-year-old boy in 2001. Known for his brash statements , he was an ally of Netanyahu and served under him in his first term. But their relationship is rocky and Yisrael Beiteinu is now outside Netanyahu’s ruling coalition. Lieberman claims he warned Netanyahu and Eisenkot of a potential Hamas attack ahead of 7 October. The Joint List Current seats : 5/120 Three of Israel’s four major Arab-led parties, Hadash, Ta’al and Balad, are standing together as the Joint List, led by Hadash leader Yousef Jabareen, 54. Avigdor Lieberman, centre, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 26 September 2026 (AFP) WRONG CAPTION The Central Electoral Committee banned the parties from participating in September amid claims that they denied Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, before that was overturned by the Supreme Court on 2 October. (Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh has dropped out of the election after the court signalled it would uphold the ban against him for an article he wrote regarded as celebrating the Hamas attacks). All three parties, which are secular, want greater rights for Palestinians in Israel, especially when it comes to crime and policing , condemn Israeli conduct in Gaza and settlements in the West Bank and supports a two-state solution. Jabareen said recently in a clear message to the Change Bloc: “Removing the threat called the Netanyahu-Ben Gvir-Smotrich government is our central goal, and we will act in every possible way to send this criminal government home." But past attempts within the List to present a unified front have collapsed over ideology. Hadash, led by Ayman Odeh until his retirement in May, includes communist and left-wing groups that back Arab and Jewish candidates, including draft refuser Ofer Cassif . Ta’al, led by Ahmad Tibi is regarded as a moderate Arab nationalist party. Balad has proposed a Jewish candidate. The Joint List hopes to gain enough seats to be a powerbroker in the Knesset, although none of its members have ever been invited to form a coalition. Most Jewish-led parties say they will not work with it. Mansour Abbas / Ra’am Current seats: 5/120 Ra’am (the Hebrew acronym for the United Arab List), is led by Palestinian citizen of Israel, Mansour Abbas, 52. It is the only Arab-led party to have served in government, during the short-lived Bennett-Lapid coalition from 2021-22. Alongside the Joint List, it was banned in September, before that decision was overturned. Leader of the Palestinian Israeli party Ra'am Mansour Abbas campaigns in Ka'abiyye-Tabbash-Hajajre, Israel, on 26 September 2026 (AFP) Rooted in political Islam, Ra’am is socially conservative, and criticises Israeli conduct in Gaza and illegal settlements in the West Bank. But it has more moderate stances toward Israel than other Arab-led parties and is seen by many Jewish Israelis as preferable to the Joint List. Abbas’ demands from potential Jewish partners include prioritising the civil rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel instead of the Palestinians in the occupied territories. For the first time it has put forward a Jewish candidate , former police chief and Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz. Aryeh Deri / Shas Current seats: 11/120 Two parties draw strong support from the Haredim, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up around 14 percent of Israel’s population. Each believes religious authority should govern politics and play a more decisive role in political life. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, left, and Aryeh Deri, of the Shas party at the Knesset, Jerusalem, in May 2023 (AFP) Shas is the bigger of the two, backed principally by Sephardic and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox. It has sat in seven of the last 10 Israeli governments and is part of the ruling coalition. In recent years it has moved further to the right, aligning itself with Ben Gvir. The party is chaired in the Knesset by rabbi Aryeh Deri, 67, who has had 10 ministerial roles since the 1980s. He served two years in prison for taking bribes in the early 2000s. Shas is focused on protecting Torah study and the rights of its ultra-conservative voter base. In government, it has demanded funding for Haredi institutions and welfare benefits: more than half of the Haredim do not work, prioritising Torah study. In exchange, it has voted with Netanyahu on issues such as the genocide in Gaza and West Bank expansion. Shas ministers quit the cabinet in 2025 over Netanyahu’s plans to end Haredim military exemption, although continued to back him on other key issues. Yaakov Asher / United Torah Judaism Current seats: 7/120 United Torah Judaism (UTJ) is heavily backed by Ashkenazi branches of Judaism and is itself a union between two groups that occasionally fall out : the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael and the Lithuanian Degel HaTorah. It is chaired in the Knesset by Yaakov Asher, although its ultimate authorities are more senior rabbis. The UTJ is chaired in the Knesset by Yaakov Asher, although its ultimate authorities are more senior rabbis (Creative Commons). Like Shas, its priorities centre around preserving ultra-Orthodox life. Although many of the party’s voters live in settlements, the party is officially not Zionist , instead believing that a Jewish state should only be established after the Messiah arrives. Some rabbis from the party have criticised the war on Gaza, citing the deaths of Israeli soldiers. But it is conscription that has all but undone the party’s alliance with Netanyahu. In May, UTJ pulled support and called for the collapse of the government after it failed to pass laws securing their military exemption. It had done so previously in 2025, though continued voting with Netanyahu on key decisions. The party now reportedly sees Eisenkot as a preferred coalition partner to Netanyahu. In a paper published on Monday by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), a think tank based at Tel Aviv University, Tamir Hayman set out 10 principles he said could be inferred from the policy now being implemented. Among them is the assumption that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”, and that “peace agreements are merely technical and temporary arrangements requiring constant reassessment”. Hayman, a reserve major general who led the Israeli army’s Military Intelligence Directorate between 2018 and 2021 and is now the institute’s executive director, wrote that this new concept “has not been formally articulated or presented to the public, nor is it bindingly defined within the defense establishment”. “In practice, however, its principles inform decision-making and dictate Israel’s approach to security,” he added. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hayman described his list as “a subjective, theoretical and deliberately exaggerated interpretation” of current policy, and said the paper was intended as a basis for public and professional debate. He argued that the change pointed to a shift in Israel’s national identity, and said his aim is addressing “the question of who we are" after 7 October. Hayman wrote that the premise underlying the concept was that the weakness of Arab states served Israel’s interests. “Consequently, undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process, one that Israel can manage more effectively than it can contend with strong nation-states, and one that it should even encourage,” he wrote. He linked this to another principle, under which security is pursued by establishing “communities and outposts in all areas of friction with the Arab population, in Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank], and in security zones in Syria , Lebanon , and the Gaza Strip ”. That deployment “further contributes to the destabilization of the ‘synthetic’ Arab states”. Peace as ‘naive error’ Hayman wrote that under the new concept, striving for peace is seen as repeating the error of the “conceptzia”, the Hebrew term for the prevailing strategic assumptions widely blamed for Israel’s failure to anticipate the 7 October attack. Netanyahu’s former aide alleges attempt to alter 7 October records Read More » “A meaningful peace agreement is unattainable in the Middle East, as peace agreements are merely technical and temporary arrangements requiring constant reassessment,” he wrote. “According to this view, peace is not an intrinsic value that generates security, but a means of achieving other policy objectives.” Politically, he added, peace is regarded as “a naive concept” associated with the left-wing “peace camp”, in tension with or in direct opposition to the right-wing “security camp”. The paper said the concept treats war as “essential to national security”, citing the line “silence is filth” from the anthem of Betar, the Revisionist Zionist youth movement founded in 1923 by Ze’ev Jabotinsky. “War is necessary, and preventive war is preferable because it secures a significant achievement at the outset. Its intensity may vary with circumstances, but its constant presence is an asset to national security,” Hayman wrote. Severing ties with US The paper also said the concept views the United States as a “declining power” that will “soon abandon Israel in any event”, and holds that severing ties with Washington is “essential to Israel’s independence and the resilience of its Jewish national identity”. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Other principles Hayman identified include the primacy of the state’s Jewish identity over its democratic system, “even at the cost of eroding its democratic values”. He wrote that the concept regards the Palestinian national movement as “an inauthentic Western narrative rooted in post-colonial guilt”, and leads to “principled opposition” to any separation between Israel and a Palestinian entity and to the establishment of a Palestinian state. Under this view, he wrote, security is to be achieved by expanding settlement “both within and beyond the ‘Green Line’ (which is regarded as fictitious)”, while Arab inhabitants who remain “will be granted residency rights and local self-governance”. ‘Self-fulfilling prophecy’ Hayman contrasted each shift with what he described as the founding principles of Israel’s traditional security concept, posing a series of questions for debate. On peace, he asked: “What is the strategic and moral price of a security concept that defines peace agreements as a ‘conceptzia,’ a flawed delusion to be inherently mistrusted, rather than a strategic asset that enables the state to prosper and should therefore be preserved?” Israeli press review: High-tech brain drain plagues Israel Read More » He asked whether treating peace as inherently temporary risked “becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy that undermines Israel’s long-term security”, and how Israel would address the risk of emigration, “including a brain drain on a scale that threatens its economy”. On the use of settlers in forward positions, he asked whether placing civilians as a front-line “shield” reversed the priorities of a sovereign state, which he said places soldiers before civilians, and exposed “noncombatants to precisely the risks that the state, through the Israel Defense Forces, sought to spare them”. How the unholy alliance of Big Tech and the far right threatens the world Submitted by Joe Gill on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 17:41 Far-right populists are the best chance for the tech oligarchs to hold onto power and wealth through the pursuit of ‘End Times Fascism’ Amazon executive chairman Jeff Bezos (C) and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (bottom right) with President Donald Trump in the White House, on 29 September 2026 (AFP) Off We are a decade or so into the age of bots – when the algorithms of social media created a new kind of attention economy that overhauled the way we see the world, spend our time and speak to each other. My birth, by way of example, was announced by old-style telegram. Today, Telegram is a social media platform where FPV drone footage of Russian and Ukrainian soldiers being killed is uploaded daily and watched by millions. Historian Eric Hobsbawm characterised the short 20th century from 1917 to 1989 as the age of extremes. It can also be viewed as the age of modernism, from the publication of James Joyce’s Ulysses (written between 1914 and 1921) to social revolution, industrialised war, and fascism. Rather than ending in 1989 with the fall of the Berlin wall, I agree with that other great Marxist writer David Harvey’s assessment that it ended earlier, in the late 1970s, with the arrival of the Apple II home computer, Deng Xiaoping’s reforms in China, and a return to free market ideology in the West. The 40-year age of globalised finance ended around 2016, with the widespread shift to machine-learning neural networks and a return to populist politics. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); This is a measurable social revolution. In 2015 the average UK adult spent just over an hour online – today they spend more than three hours. Young people led this shift, spending more time online using popular apps than watching traditional television as early as 2015-16. They now spend almost five hours on their phones daily. No wonder parents are going spare. But they are no role models. Average British adult mobile usage time has increased from 1 hour 17 minutes per day to 3 hours and 21 minutes per day in a decade. TV viewing has remained stable at just over three hours . This radical shift has also seen a revolution in political discourse in the West and across the world, driven by social media. Who controls the narrative In the uprisings of 2011, from Cairo’s Tahrir Square to New York’s Occupy, new forms of social media allowed insurgent movements to mobilise people around their demands for change. It felt like social media could be used for liberation. But by 2016, the ruling elites of the West and East had managed to seize back control of the technology, and find ways to target millions of voters. The results were seen in the campaigns of Donald Trump, the UK Brexit vote, and later in Boris Johnson’s “Get Brexit Done” election of 2019. While in 2017 Jeremy Corbyn’s social media outriders were able to break through the hostile right-wing legacy media narratives, within two years the situation was reversed. The Tories’ media strategists used targeted Facebook ads to devastating effect – millions were convinced that Corbyn was a demonic, terrorist-loving child snatcher. By 2016, the ruling elites of the West and East had managed to seize back control of the technology, and find ways to target millions of voters The mood on the doorstep, as I remember well, was sour and in some cases violently hostile. Old media played its part, but the algorithm was the critical ingredient in swinging the country to Johnson . This decade has seen the most dramatic advances for the far right, aided with platforming by Elon Musk’s X , the activities of shadowy media specialists like Cambridge Analytica, and Israeli , Russian and Emirati bots. From the political margins, populist nationalists have gone mainstream. In Latin America, the pro-Trump/pro-Israel right has swept away half a dozen left-wing governments that had governed for much of the 2000s. The difference from the rise of fascism a century ago in the age of radio is salient: Mussolini and Hitler were both elected by popular vote and then seized power and overthrew the democratic order. They saw democracy as inevitably favouring the left and socialism. Not so today. A century of mass politics has shown that effective political advertising can convince the electorate to vote for parties of the right and of capital. There is no iron law that says workers vote for working-class parties. Moreover, as traditional socialist parties became increasingly dominated by the graduate professional classes, and their organic links to trade unions diluted, it was no longer obvious that they represented workers. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mobilising left, voting right As long as a right-wing party can appeal to working-class voters – using fear of immigration, stirring division over issues such as gay or trans rights, and outright disinformation – the left can be defeated. This is the model that has been honed and mastered in Europe and the US over the last half century – first for Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, then for the populist right in the age of Instagram. Left-wing parties and movements are battling for attention in a social media ecosystem controlled largely by billionaire media owners and Instagram influencers. Still, effective social media operators of the left, such as Zohran Mamdani and Zack Polanski, have proven able to break through. Chin up, Zack! It was never going to be plain sailing for the new-look Greens Read More » There is a paradox at work here: the most mobilised groups – from the pro- Palestine movement, to the students protesting in France , and the millions on the streets of Brazil supporting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s latest presidential run – are from the left. But with the help of armies of bots , malign actors, including Israel and the US, can mobilise conservative voters, as seen most recently in Colombia . Nationalism today has its own favoured enemies – Muslims/Islam, the left, globalists, LGBTQ people. It denies climate change and loves fossil fuels, even as the planet reels from wildfires and deadly floods. So far, unfolding climate chaos is not denting this advance. Elections in Brazil this month, Spain in November and France next April are the far right’s to lose. Meanwhile, huge plumes of black smoke rise from the fuel depots and tankers targeted in wars for land, sea and oil – from Russia and Crimea to Saudi Arabia and the Strait of Hormuz. Fossil energy is the means and target of these wars. Collapse – first gradually, then suddenly System collapse unfolds first gradually, then suddenly, as Ernest Hemingway might have put it. It is worth recalling that the fascist epoch of the 1920s to 1940s only ended due to the catastrophe of World War Two. The apocalyptic fear today, encapsulated in a new book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor , is that the global right, from Washington and Tel Aviv to Brazil, will burn the world, through war, ecocide and pumping every last drop of the planet-frying oil that fossil capital sees as its birthright (and the funding source of the right's political campaigns). The right's call to end immigration needs an answer, such as 'Tax billionaires, slash rents and democratise AI to enable a three-day week' The Gaza genocide is the proof that they can and will do this – still largely supported by centrist parties who remain loyalists to the disintegrating western global order (as long as a garrison force like Israel does the “dirty work”). Until recently, the left’s promises have been insufficiently bold or easy to understand compared with those of the right – the call to end immigration needs an answer, such as "Tax billionaires, slash rents and democratise AI to enable a three-day week". Amazon’s owner Jeff Bezos is a recent, if unconvincing, convert to a three-day week, which he says will be made possible through the productivity gains of AI – a rather neat fulfilment of the prediction by John Maynard Keynes in his 1930 essay "Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren” . Keynes warned then that “there is no country and no people, I think, who can look forward to the age of leisure and of abundance without a dread. For we have been trained too long to strive and not to enjoy.” Keynes had not counted on the fact that the gains of productivity would not be spread widely but instead would go to a class of billionaires whose desire to accumulate is insatiable. The fear of the billionaire class that the masses are turning against them may be crystallising in these kinds of progressive-sounding pronouncements. But they are also pursuing other options. Far-right populism is the best chance for the tech oligarchs to hold onto power and wealth through the pursuit of “End Times Fascism” , in which genocide, ecocide and evangelical end times are all part of the plan, as described in Klein’s latest work. Meantime, there are signs that the structures of established democratic politics can no longer contain the frustrations of millions of people, as seen in the mass protests over unaffordable housing in Spain, and students in revolt in France over underfunded education. German revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg famously wrote from prison in 1915 that the world faces “either the triumph of imperialism and the collapse of all civilisation as in ancient Rome, depopulation, desolation, degeneration – a great cemetery… Or the victory of socialism...” Klein and Taylor insist the majority who oppose the far right tech lords “must break the doom loop, and find a new way of living together, rooted in our existence on this Earth, in the here and now”. For now, we are well into the doom loop, with no clear way out. The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye. National Assembly, Senate pass resolutions endorsing Centre's imposition of emergency in KP. ISLAMABAD: Shortly after the National Assembly passed a resolution endorsing the federal government’s imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Wednesday, the Senate also gave its approval for the measure. The Centre had imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Sunday, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the motions regarding the proclamation of emergency before both Houses. Senate proceedings In the Senate, the resolution was passed amid the opposition’s outcry, with PTI senators staging a walkout. The Senate’s approval followed a heated debate between treasury and opposition members, during which Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar defended the procedural propriety presenting the resolution in the House and getting it approved. He argued that a “constitutional resolution” had been laid before the House in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Senate. “Under Article 232, a copy of [the proclamation of] emergency has been laid before the House. An attempt to bypass the constitutional procedure cannot succeed,” he said, adding that the requirement of a seven-day notice for tabling a resolution did not apply to one presented under a constitutional necessity. “If its opponents have any objections, they should reject the resolution through their vote after the debate. We cannot deviate from the Constitution and rules of the House,” he said. As opposition voiced opposition to the resolution, Senate Chairperson Yousuf Raza Gilani asked them to exercise patience. “This is not a classroom, do not make noise,” he remarked as senators from the opposition benches continued sloganeering. Among them, PTI’s Humayun Mohmand said independent Senator Faisal Vawda had said months ago that governor’s rule would be imposed. He alleged that terrorism being cited as the reason for the measure was just an excuse and the actual “target is the PTI”. “The decision to impose governor’s rule and emergency was taken months ago,” he alleged. Seemingly referring to the creation of Bangladesh, he said the federal government’s decision since 1970 had proved wrong. PTI-backed Senator Hamid Khan also argued that there “seems to be some other objectives behind governor’s rule and emergency”. Referring to the talks between the Centre and the opposition ahead of governor’s rule and emergency in KP, he alleged that negotiations “were just a drama” and were held “only to deceive the people”. “The real decision was taken elsewhere long ago,” he claimed. He further said that Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who tried to mediate between the Centre and the opposition, had stated that while the negotiations were taking place, “a decision came”. “Governments formed on the basis of Form-47 do not have the real mandate,” he added. He further regretted that after the 26th Amendment, “there is neither any Constitution nor an independent judicial system”. “The judiciary has been stripped of its independence, which closes the avenues to challenge unconstitutional steps,” he said. Khan went on to say: “Article 232 has to be presented before the House for debate, not just for saying yes. Decision was taken by those whom Constitution does not allow to take the decision, but they have complete dominance over Constitution. At this time, neither is there any Constitution nor any court in the country.” PTI Senator Mohsin Aziz railed against federal ministers, who have been accusing the PTI of facilitating terrorism. “You talk about terrorism, what do you know about terrorism? People of KP sacrificed their children and picked up bodies. […] Did we support Pakistan or terrorists? Those calling people of KP terrorists should be ashamed. These are valiant people who saved this country,” he said. Aziz said terrorism was a result of unemployment, hunger, non-availability of hospitals, water and education. Senator Zeeshan Khanzada, also from the PTI, said he condemned the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. He accused the federal government of “abducting” Sohail Afridi, who has been rendered non-functional as the KP chief minister following the imposition of governor’s rule, and other PTI MPAs. JUI-F’s Kamran Murtaza said the opposition’s resolution against governor’s rule should have also been included in the agenda for the day, but it was returned with objections. Murtaza argued that the relevant material required for endorsement of enforcement of Article 232 and 234 — constitutional provision related to imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — had not been presented in the House. Despite letters and applications, the government had not provided documents and material related to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, he said, adding that senators had to obtain that material through social media. Members could not be satisfied with a decision until complete information came forth, he said. NA proceedings The NA question hour session was suspended due to discussions on the emergency. The motion in the lower House of Parliament was adopted with a majority vote after a discussion opened by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar. “The National Assembly approves the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on the 11th October, 2026 in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution,” read a post by NA’s official X account. According to Article 232 , if the “president acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days. Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months. Throughout Wednesday’s proceedings, opposition members participated calmly and did not stage any loud protest, unlike past instances when the PTI objects to the Centre. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also attended part of the session, with pictures released by the NA showing him shaking hands with Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif shakes hands with leader of the opposition in the National Assembly, Mehmood Khan Achakzai, on Wednesday. — Photo courtesy NA Facebook Federal ministers defended the emergency imposition while assailing what they described as the PTI-led KP government’s lack of will to combat terrorism. In tune with that, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari blamed the PTI for the circumstances that compelled the Centre to impose emergency in KP and termed it a “political suicide attack” for the party. However, he also urged the treasury and the opposition to get back on the path of dialogue and make joint efforts against terrorism. At one point during the proceedings, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq noted that the Oct 3 dialogue was held in a cordial atmosphere. Sadiq praised both sides for “attempting more than their capacity so that the matter is settled”. However, he said some matters were beyond the parties’ control and voiced his support for forming the same committees for negotiations if ever needed in the future. Addressing PTI lawmakers, the speaker said, “Everyone’s response was that this [process of dialogue] should continue, but you also understand that your hands were tied.” He took note of the PTI’s complaints regarding the jail conditions of party founder Imran Khan, adding that he had even provided details of facilities provided to the jailed ex-premier. The session was adjourned to meet again at 11am on Oct 16 (Friday). ‘Political suicide attack’ Bilawal began his speech by highlighting that emergency and governor’s rule in KP were measures taken under the Constitution . Reading the relevant provisions, he asserted that the Centre tried its best to “engage the opposition so this step did not have to be taken”. “They will have to accept, even if not publicly, but the responsible leadership of the opposition knows that the PTI itself carried out a political suicide attack on its KP government,” he remarked. The PPP chief maintained that the PTI could not deny that its “leadership, particularly in the province had a key role in the political, constitutional and legal circumstances” at present. Bilawal emphasised that the PPP’s stance was that “before employing this constitutional atomic bomb, we must engage with PTI and the opposition and try to address the federal government’s reservations that they were not supporting them in the war against terrorism”. He observed: “If political space is restricted for one political party, it is impossible that it remains restricted for that particular party; it is limited for every political party, political worker and Pakistani citizen. “We are responsible for this, but you cannot deny that you are also responsible for it,” he said. Terming the imposition of emergency a “difficult decision”, Bilawal recalled alleged remarks by Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional — that he would not combat terrorism the way the Centre wanted. “If this was not a political suicide, then what else was it?” The Bhutto scion wondered if the opposition and Afridi had left any reason for President Asif Ali Zardari, who he said prides himself on passing the 18th Amendment, to “refuse to sign” the emergency proclamation. He argued that due to the PTI’s actions and statements, neither the president, the Centre, nor he had any legal or political reason left for not imposing emergency in KP. “But even today, I would recommend to the federal government that we extend our hand forward once again for negotiations, political discussions and try to find a resolution and a middle path,” Bilawal added. The PPP chairman noted that emergency was “always a stopgap measure”. “We cannot sustain the emergency forever,” he added, emphasising that while the counterterrorism fight would be better than before, an “all-of-society and all-of-country response” was needed to eradicate it completely. Regarding the Oct 3 talks of a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition, Bilawal said, “Late at night, I was informed that congratulations, negotiations are succeeding.” He said the PTI was willing to declare the areas in KP with surging terrorism as “terrorist areas”, and the opposition was about to agree that the federal and KP governments would sign a pact on joint efforts against terrorism. However, the dialogue collapsed. The former foreign minister pointed out that the security challenges Pakistan was facing were “way more complicated” than before, adding that India “could still not digest […] its embarrassment” from the May 2025 conflict . Referring to remarks by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that its ‘ Operation Sindoor ’ was still ongoing, Bilawal said: “It means that India is still sponsoring terrorist incidents in Pakistan, sometimes in the form of TTP (Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan) and sometimes in the form of separatist terrorist groups.” He reiterated Pakistan’s stance that India was involved in terrorist activities being conducted from across the Afghan border. The ex-foreign minister then highlighted Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran war. “But there is a state — which we do not recognise as a state — that will neither be happy nor ever forget that you took this step. And those Zionist forces will and are interfering in Pakistan’s internal politics and state.” Concluding his speech, the PPP chairman emphasised the need for building consensus on “some fundamental issues” for an empowered lower house. “Even today, we are saying, come and at least begin from this house,” he said while addressing the opposition benches. Gohar demands implementation of NAP Speaking in the NA, PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan said his party “rejected” the Centre’s move to impose emergency in KP. He asked what “terrorism” Imran’s wife or sisters had allegedly been involved in that they had been put behind bars, or what the accusations were against the PTI MNAs and MPAs who he said were detained. Gohar further said, “One person is not present in the house currently. When he comes during a joint session, then I will reveal the reality of the negotiations.” He affirmed that the PTI had raised its voice against terrorism, adding that measures against the scourge must be taken according to the National Action Plan (NAP). Gohar argued that the PML-N opposition during the PTI’s tenure carried out “14 long marches in two years, but you did not let us stage even one long march”. Presenting his version of the Oct 3 talks with the government, the PTI leader said his party was being asked to immediately call off the long march . “I said where did [the topic] of terrorism arise from suddenly.” Noting that the government had put forward “five reservations”, Gohar said PTI was willing to make the KP Police Act similar to that of Punjab and Sindh. The PTI leader reiterated his party’s request for the production of certain MNAs it says were taken into custody. Gohar also welcomed Bilawal’s proposal to continue dialogue. Responding to Gohar’s remarks, the PPP chairman said the PTI was busy in its long march while the people of KP were being targeted by terrorists. Bilawal reiterated that the opposition could keep arguing against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, but no one could deny that the decision was grounded in the Constitution. “I cannot insist on the government to continue talks with PTI despite being defrauded multiple times,” the PPP chairman said. Pointing towards Gohar and Achakzai, Bilawal said: “I believe that none of them is allied with terrorists. I believe that they will definitely want to combat terrorism; however, they cannot deny the fact that their former chief minister contradicted this fact.” Bilawal again requested all the stakeholders to unite and combat terrorism collectively. He also called for the provision of all facilities to the incarcerated PTI founder. ‘Threat to national security’ Addressing the house, the law minister explained that emergency was imposed in KP as the security situation there was becoming a threat to “national security”. Tarar noted that after the Proclamation of Emergency was issued, the Constitution’s Article 232 required that both houses of the parliament approve the measure. He recalled that the federal cabinet examined “material” regarding terrorism in the province during its Oct 11 meeting and then advised PM Shehbaz to recommend the imposition of emergency. He noted that some people compared the measure to the emergency imposed by former dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf on Oct 12, 1999. The minister particularly noted “internal disturbances” and cross-border infiltrations. He contended that the situation since Oct 15, 2025, when Sohail Afridi’s government came into power in KP , was “turning into a threat to national security to an alarming extent”. He went on to highlight that there was a rise in terrorism in KP, especially after 2021, due to the approach of the provincial government. “Perhaps there might be foreign, diplomatic and political reasons behind it, which got inflamed due to a political party’s point of view.” Tarar stated that 2,911 incidents of terrorism took place between 2021 and 2024 in KP, but they surged to 3,787 incidents between Oct 15, 2025 and Oct 9, 2026. He criticised the KP chief minister for ignoring martyred security and police personnel, and for instead preferring to promote his political designs and make visits across the country. “Even this was announced that the federal capital will be conquered,” he said, referring to the party’s plan to hold a protest long march towards the federal capital. The PML-N leader expressed his government’s gratitude to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq for providing a platform for dialogue between the Centre and the opposition. He reiterated the government’s stance that the PTI had the agreement draft changed multiple times, but even then backed off from it. Tarar observed that the PTI demanded the release of their party founder Imran Khan and his treatment in a private hospital despite knowing that only courts could provide such a relief. He said two days would be “remembered in the country’s democratic history with regard to misfortune and a political party”. On the emergency measure, the law minister noted that a special mechanism has been introduced for 12 districts of KP. Speaking after Tarar, Achakzai criticised him for trying to prove that terrorism was not tackled in KP. The opposition leader questioned the government’s mandate in the February 2024 general elections, quipping that the opposition would “surrender” if the minister could swear that the government won those polls fairly. Achakzai alleged that the incumbent ruling coalition was formed “illegally”. ‘You do not have clean hands’ Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif went on to recall the tenure of the PTI government in the Centre and assailed the party’s past actions. Referring to ex-prime minister Imran Khan’s plan to resettle members of the TTP, he said PTI tried to convince the then-opposition that “bringing these terrorists back would be better for Pakistan”. The PML-N leader mentioned the 2019 episode of an Indian pilot’s capture in Pakistan: “They had threatened and we were surrendering. The then-prime minister was saying, ‘What should I do? Attack India?’” Asif urged the opposition to reflect on its past actions, adding that Imran often used to praise former army chief retired General Qamar Javed Bajwa. “As long as this contradiction remains in our words and actions and in our society, the circumstances of this country will not fix.” He narrated his time behind bars during the PTI government, when Shehbaz “smuggled a blanket” to him to brace the low temperatures. “I used to eat the jail’s food,” he said, claiming that orders were given to remove the geyser when it was installed. “But we did not hold rallies or mourn at D-Chowk or dig graves. We did not martyr police and law enforcement personnel,” Asif remarked. “You demand equity when you have clean hands. You do not have clean hands, you cannot demand equity; this is a thousand-year-old principle,” he contended. “You know very well what Gen Musharraf did to me. There was a 4x6 cell in Attock jail,” the PML-N politician said, emphasising that he stood with his party and ex-PM Nawaz Sharif. Speaking on the current political situation, Asif alleged that Afridi used to “take directives […] from a person sitting in Afghanistan”. He referred to a statement by the TTP condemning the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops in certain places. “Who is their ally and who is their rival?” he said. The minister further countered the PTI’s stance that its leaders have not been able to meet Imran, who is imprisoned in the Adiala jail. “Meetings are held, [but] a lot of them are not publicised or brought on record,” he maintained. Farooq Sattar urges PTI to ‘openly condemn terrorism’ In his remarks on the floor of the lower house, Farooq Sattar expressed Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan’s (MQM-P) confidence in the decision taken by the prime minister. “This was an extremely difficult decision, but so unavoidable that you had no other option,” Sattar said about imposing emergency and governor’s rule. “We trust your decision as we trust your experience, capabilities, political acumen, and that you made this decision in the interest of the nation,” he added. The MQM-P lawmaker contended that the PTI was “on the wrong side and does not have concrete arguments” to declare that the decision was baseless or made with political motives. “The main issue is of the mindset,” he declared, adding that Imran had “publicly said that the war on terror is not ours”. “This is their policy. This is their mindset.” Sattar questioned whether the KP government had ever published reports to expose terrorist hideouts and extremist trends. He further raised questions about the government’s pursuit of cases against suspected terrorists. “Openly condemn terrorism; else, the allegation of backing [it], if a commission is formed and God forbid, it is proven in the inquiry that there is political extremism and terrorism complicity, there is a nexus, then where will you go?” Sattar recounted his past MQM experiences, saying, “I have also suffered such times. A lot of times, the narrative coming from the top was difficult to defend. Today, I feel that Barrister Gohar is also not in the position to defend his [party’s] position on KP.”

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs393.86 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.65 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 15 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Lawmakers, govt differ over Discos’ privatisation. • Muhammad Ali claims CCI nod not required, says Discos caused over $30bn in losses over 15 years • Panel seeks records of council’s decisions, other consultations • Questions Rs2.6tr federal spending on devolved subjects ISLAMABAD: The propo­sed privatisation of power distribution companies (Discos) stirred controversy on Wedn­esday, as a Senate panel maintained that the matter constitutionally fell within the domain of the Council of Common Interests (CCI), while the government’s top privatisation official insisted that no fresh CCI approval was required. Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali told a subcommittee of the Senate Functional Committee on Devolution that no new CCI approval was needed for the privatisation of Discos. He added that the companies had caused losses of more than $30 billion over the past 15 years. He said the CCI had approved the privatisation of three power generation companies and nine distribution companies in 2011. It also approved the National Electricity Policy on June 21, 2021, which recommended that the government explore various privatisation options to improve the efficiency of state-owned entities where applicable. Both decisions remained valid, he said. On the validity of the decisions, the law division, in a Sept 25, 2026 letter, reconfirmed that in light of the 2011 CCI decision, fresh approval was not required for the privatisation of Discos. Accordingly, the privatisation division maintained that no fresh CCI approval was required in light of the 2011 decision and the 2021 National Electricity Policy, Mr Ali said. The adviser told the subcommittee that legal and procedural requirements for the privatisation process had been fulfilled. He said the National Electricity Policy 2021 had been formulated after obtaining recommendations from the provinces and that the privatisation programme had subsequently been approved, with further work undertaken during 2023-24. Referring the matter back to the CCI at this stage could cause significant delays, affect investor confidence and adversely impact the financial position of power distribution companies, he argued. Highlighting substantial losses faced by the power sector due to electricity theft and operational inefficiencies, he stressed that privatisation was necessary to improve performance and reduce burden on the national exchequer. Responding, subcommittee convener Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro emphasised that the constitutional position and role of the CCI could not be overlooked. He questioned whether the proposed privatisation was consistent with the constitutional distribution of powers under Article 157, observing that electricity distribution and related matters involved provincial interests. Referring to previous judicial decisions and privatisation initiatives, he stressed the importance of transparency and protecting provincial interests, and asked authorities to provide relevant decisions and supporting documents for examination. He said provinces, being represented in the CCI, should have an opportunity to consider matters falling within their domain. Officials informed the committee that the CCI had taken 11 relevant decisions and that, according to available record, no province had formally recorded reservations. They assured that relevant documents and details of provincial consultations would be shared. The minister reiterated that all necessary legal requirements had been met and referring the matter back to CCI was not considered necessary at this stage. The chairman reiterated that the committee’s examination was intended to ensure constitutional compliance, transparency and effective parliamentary oversight, and directed authorities to furnish decisions and supporting documents so the matter could be assessed in light of the Constitution and previous judicial pronouncements. He said constitutionally the matter was related to CCI and necessary documents must be submitted to examine the process from all aspects. The subcommittee met under the convenorship of Senator Ghumro to review federal expenditure on ministries, institutions, organisations, statutory bodies and corporations retained by the federal government despite provincial matters following the 18th Constitutional Amendment. It also examined compliance reports and status of matters concerning the CCI. The meeting was attended by Senators Jan Muhammad Buledi and Poonjo Bheel, secretaries of cabinet, CCI, Establishment Division, special secretary establishment, additional secretary establishment and senior officers. At the outset, the report of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP) and the Accountant General on expenditure incurred by the federal government on ministries relating to provincial subjects was taken up. The chairman observed that despite 16 years since the 18th Amendment, concerns persisted regarding federal expenditure on devolved subjects, including education and health, which had been notified as provincial matters by the Implementation Commission. Referring to Articles 168 and 169 of the Constitution and the legal framework governing the audit of public expenditure, he questioned the authorisation and constitutional basis for expenditure of approximately Rs2.6 trillion on the health and education ministries over the past 16 years. He termed the expenditure of Rs2.6tr by the federal government on the two ministries, which he said had been de-notified in 2010, a misuse of taxpayers’ money, arguing that the Centre could spend only on federal subjects. He said the amount could rise to several trillion rupees once expenditure on other ministries created for provincial subjects was included. Mr Ghumro expressed concern that the details sought by the committee had not been submitted within the stipulated timeframe and stressed that parliament was the primary authority for authorising public expenditure, and that such expenditure should be confined to federal subjects. He maintained that expenditure from the Federal Consolidated Fund could not be authorised for devolved provincial matters. AGP officials explained that the audit process was guided by budgets approved by the competent parliamentary forum and acknowledged certain limitations in coverage. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

Israeli settlers set fire to mosque in occupied West Bank. MIKHMAS: Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque and graffitied its outside walls on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank village of Mikhmas, Palestinian sources and the Israeli military said. Atta Kanaan, a Palestinian resident of Mikhmas who lives 50 metres from the mosque, told AFP that he heard the sound of breaking glass shortly after midnight on Wednesday and immediately went to the building. “A fire was burning fiercely, and we called the fire brigade. Young men rushed to help us with fire extinguishers, and we managed to contain part of the fire before the flames engulfed the entire mosque,” he said. Israel’s military told AFP that soldiers were dispatched to Mikhmas following a report of graffiti and arson at the mosque, as well as damage to a vehicle. “No suspects were identified,” it said, adding an investigation had been opened. AFP video footage showed that the fire had burned down the mosque’s interior carpeting and blackened the walls. An AFP journalist reported that slogans were spraypainted in Hebrew on the exterior walls, including “just because we are quiet doesn’t mean we are asleep”. 'No time to recover': UNDP chief sounds alarm on growing poverty after Iran war. Millions could be thrown into poverty by surging energy costs, the impact of an intense El Nino phenomenon and higher interest rates, with vulnerable countries being pushed to the brink by repeated crises, the UN’s development chief told AFP. Global fuel prices have soared since the United States launched its war on Iran in late February, with Tehran’s retaliations against Washington’s Gulf allies curtailing major oil and natural gas supplies. Fiscal deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios around the world have ballooned since the 2008 global financial crisis, with governments firefighting against a series of shocks including the pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, UN Development Programme (UNDP) head Alexander de Croo said many developing countries had responded to the current spike in energy prices with blanket subsidies, but a succession of crises had left them with limited resources to keep that up. “You have to repair your roof while at the same time your home is on fire,” he told AFP, adding governments in the developing world did not have time to rebuild buffers or resolve previous shocks before being hit by new crises. The IMF warned this week that while global growth had held up in the face of the energy crisis, that resilience was highly dependent on the boom in AI technology investments, and poorer countries not exposed to that were still struggling. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva had warned that “winter is coming” — an allusion to popular fantasy book series “Game of Thrones” —implying that a cataclysm was around the corner if the world did not prepare for it. And De Croo added: “Some countries have a well-insulated house with money in the bank. Other countries have a house without a roof and no money in the bank. “We’re stumbling from one crisis into the other, and what countries need is some space, and some time, and access to financing.” Not getting the response right could be devastating. The UNDP warned in a new report that about 130 million people were at risk of being pushed into poverty this year if energy and food price increases were fully passed on without subsidies. People in South and East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are at particular risk, the agency said. ‘Difficult to manage’ With advanced economies seeing bond yields surge — owing to elevated inflation expectations, surging debt ratios and AI capital-raising activities — global borrowing costs have been rising. That in turn, de Croo warned, had tightened space for developing countries to access the capital they needed to combat the shocks, with rising interest rates feeding into increasing debt payments. According to UNDP, the median developing country now spends about 9.5 percent of government revenue on interest payments — the highest in a quarter of a century, and more than three times that of high-income countries. “It starts to be a difficult situation to manage, and it takes away all their margin for policy,” de Croo said. The former Belgian prime minister said he would spend the week in Bangkok — where world economic policy leaders have gathered since Monday —pushing for advanced economies and multilateral agencies to invest in economic growth, resilience and job creation in the developing world. He also said recent stark cuts in international aid were having an impact on those countries. The UNDP warned there was potentially more pain to come, with this year’s El Nino climate phenomenon forecast to be the strongest on record. That is expected to have widespread effects including flooding, droughts and other extreme events that are estimated to peak in early 2027. De Croo also said private capital needed to step in to help fight some of the worst consequences of climate change. “We see that the impact of climate has an economic cost. Avoiding that cost has a business case,” he said.
