FCC declares plea against KP CM’s appointment infructuous after governor’s rule. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Thursday disposed of a challenge to the appointment of non-functional Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, deeming it infructuous after the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were imposed on Sunday. The federal government cited the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism as the reason for the measures. At present, Afridi remains in preventative custody along with some of his cabinet members. The PTI had reported their detention shortly after the Centre imposed emergency and governor’s rule. “The petition has become infructuous following the imposition of state of emergency and the governor’s rule,” observed FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, who headed a two-judge bench also comprising Justice Ali Baqar Najafi. The bench took up a petition moved by estranged PTI leader Sher Afzal Khan Marwat against the resignation of former KP chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur in October 2025, who preceded Afridi. At the outset of the proceedings on Thursday, the chief justice wondered whether the petition could be heard given recent developments in KP concerning the chief minister and added that proceedings on the petition could not continue in light of these events. However, petitioner Marwat said he also intended to challenge the imposition of governor’s rule and the emergency and, therefore, needed a short adjournment in the case. Justice Najafi, however, observed that the case against the now non-functional chief minister was no longer a live issue, adding that governor’s rule and the emergency were separate and independent matters. The petitioner pointed out that if governor’s rule and the emergency were lifted in the near future, Afridi would be restored to his position. At this, the chief justice observed that if the chief minister was restored in the future, the petitioner was free to file a miscellaneous application for the restoration of his petition. “At present, Sohail Afridi does not hold the office of the chief minister,” the chief justice observed. Later, talking to the media, Marwat said he would challenge the state of emergency and governor’s rule. “I will have the challenge ready by tomorrow,” the petitioner announced, adding that all evidence would be compiled for legal action against the decision. He also rubbished allegations that the PTI patronised terrorism, adding that PTI leaders were elected representatives who had themselves been victims and targets of terrorism. He said the failure of PTI leaders to attend the funerals of the martyrs was not justifiable, as they had avoided attending the funerals out of fear of threats and vitriol on social media against them. He regretted, however, that if a party allowed itself to be driven by its social media presence, it would inevitably face such situations. Marwat also offered to steer the party if the PTI leadership was unavailable to lead it, adding that when there was no one else in the party, he was there, but when others came, he stepped back. The petition Through his petition, Marwat had sought a declaration that the resignation letters submitted by Gandapur on Oct 8 and 11, 2025, were made under the unconstitutional dictation of a convicted and disqualified individual and therefore lacked legal volition, rendering them legally ineffective. The petition alleged that the entire process of replacing Gandapur as the KP chief minister was initiated pursuant to directives issued by jailed PTI founder Imran Khan, who, it claimed, stood convicted and constitutionally disqualified under Articles 62 and 63 of the Constitution. It argued that a person subject to constitutional disqualification was legally incapacitated from exercising control over state functionaries or issuing binding political directives. The petition requested the FCC to quash and set aside all consequential actions, including the Oct 15, 2025, notification regarding the installation and continuation of Afridi as chief minister. It further requested the court to restore Gandapur as chief minister, declaring his resignation invalid and his de-notification legally ineffective. The petitioner had argued that, as an elected representative from KP, he was directly concerned with preserving constitutional governance in the province and said any unconstitutional disruption of Gandapur’s government would undermine the public mandate. The petition raised questions concerning the independence of high constitutional offices, the legal limitations on disqualified individuals exercising influence over state machinery and the enforcement of Articles 2A, 4, 5, 17, 25 and 130 of the Constitution. “It is an established principle that when the functioning of an entire provincial executive is subverted by external dictation, the rights of the public at large under Articles 9, 17, and 2A are directly infringed, creating an imperative for this honourable court to exercise its constitutional jurisdiction,” the petition argued. It further questioned whether an individual who stood convicted and constitutionally disqualified under Articles 62 and 63 could lawfully issue directives that influence, alter or dismantle elected provincial governance structures. The petition also asked whether instructions from a disqualified individual or defunct political entity had any constitutional validity, arguing that the governor must reject a chief minister’s resignation if it was not voluntary and lacked constitutional legitimacy.

The 21-year-old made a strong impression on the international stage in the recently concluded three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries in the first two matches to help Pakistan clinch the series. His performances were more than just individual milestones, signalling a shift towards a more aggressive batting approach in T20 cricket, with Maaz emerging as a key figure in the change. He scored 50 off 29 balls in the opening match, helping Pakistan recover from an underwhelming powerplay alongside captain Sahibzada Farhan. In the second T20I, Maaz took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers, smashing 96 off 51 balls, including seven sixes and six fours, to come close to a maiden international century. His impressive run, however, will have to wait for another opportunity to continue in Pakistan colours, with the batter left out of the ODI squad despite having featured in six matches in the format, including his debut, earlier this year. Maaz had made an immediate impact in only his second ODI against Bangladesh, scoring 75 and taking three wickets with his left-arm spin. However, he struggled to maintain that form in the subsequent home series against Australia in May-June, managing scores of eight, zero and 27 on difficult surfaces. The reasons behind his omission from the squad for the upcoming tri-series remain unclear. The break, however, offers him an opportunity to refine his game with the 2027 World Cup in mind. “I am targeting the ODI World Cup and I am preparing for it,” Maaz said in a video interview released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday. “I have a 15-20-day window coming up which I am going to dedicate to working on myself for the World Cup.” The youngster, who rose from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to become a franchise T20 sensation, has continued to build his reputation on the domestic and international circuits. He also struck two centuries in the recently concluded Caribbean Premier League season. Maaz believes the key to his progress lies in strengthening his natural game rather than focusing excessively on his weaknesses. “[In training] I try to work as much as I can on my strengths and less on my weaknesses, because if the ball is out of my range, I’d still be able to push it for a single or two,” he said. “However, if it is in my range, then I can hit it for six with my eyes closed. “If you watch both my CPL and international knocks, I keep a positive intent from the very start. “And if the ball comes in my range then I don’t spare it. And when a ball is a bit here or there, I try to rotate the strike.” That clarity of approach also extends to his preferred batting position. Although Maaz has previously said he is open to batting anywhere in the order, he admits he is most comfortable opening the innings. “I feel the most comfortable playing as an opener,” he said. A place in Pakistan’s squad for the 2027 World Cup would put Maaz in contention for an opening slot alongside Saim Ayub, who is averaging nearly 47, and experienced campaigner Fakhar Zaman. Maaz, however, views the competition for places as a challenge rather than a setback. “Even if I am asked to bat lower in the order, I’ll try to bat so well that they [team management] are forced to push me higher,” he said.

Joint parliamentary session debates resolutions on emergency, governor’s rule in KP. A joint session of the Parliament is currently discussing two resolutions regarding the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The joint session of the National Assembly and the Senate is taking place a day after both Houses of Parliament, in separate sittings, passed resolutions endorsing the imposition of emergency in KP. According to Article 232 , if the “president acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days. Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months. The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. During Thursday’s joint sitting, opposition members turned up carrying placards inscribed with slogans, such as “emergency na manzoor (emergency is unacceptable)”. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who attended part of the session, shook hands with opposition leaders of both the Senate and the NA, pictures and footage showed. At the outset of the proceedings, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry presented a motion under Rule 232 of the Parliament (Joint Sitting) Rules 1973 to suspend certain sub-rules so he could move the resolutions. As loud noes echoed and opposition members chanted “emergency na manzoor ”, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq again put the motion to a vote by asking the members to stand up, which was then adopted with 214-56 votes. Subsequently, Chaudhry moved two resolutions before the joint sitting — one for the Proclamation of Emergency under Article 232 and the second for the proclamation of governor’s rule under Article 234. Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar then opened the discussion on the two resolutions. Noting that a resolution regarding the imposition of emergency also required to be passed by a joint sitting, Tarar said a special mechanism has been put in place in KP to run its affairs during the emergency and governor’s rule. He said members of the treasury benches were ready to reply to any query raised by the opposition. The law minister highlighted that the PTI-led government in KP, which now stands non-functional, was advised time and again to tackle terrorism. He again lamented that PTI leaders did not attend any funeral of martyrs who lost their lives in terrorist attacks. Tarar went on to stress that governor’s rule was imposed under Article 234, which allows the move if any provincial government was being run against the Constitution. Explaining the constitutional process to approve the resolution for emergency, he said the joint sitting could reject it by a total majority, ie 51 per cent. Similarly, the resolution for governor’s rule also required a total majority of votes for approval. At the outset of the sitting, the Parliament offered prayers for the lives lost, mostly of children, in a roof collapse in Peshawar. Gohar objects to allegations of ‘backing terrorists’ Speaking later during the proceedings, PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan said the country was going through a “very fragile situation”. He lamented that the KP government was accused of “backing terrorists”. “The prime minister has alleged that we are supporting terrorists. We are disappointed to hear that. You have to apologise to the entire population of KP and us,” he said. “Prime minister, you have given a message to the entire world that one of the federating units of the country was backing terrorists,“ Gohar added. He highlighted that the opposition stood with the government during a war with India. “But today we are called supporters of terrorists,” he regretted. Barrister Gohar rejected the proclamation of emergency and declared that the PTI will make the country stronger and eradicate terrorism when it comes into power again. He also rejected the government’s claims that PTI leaders did not attend funerals of martyrs, recalling that he himself had attended multiple funerals in KP. Gohar said the PTI was willing to engage in dialogue with the government provided that its demands were met. He lamented that speeches of opposition members were not shown in the media. Achakzai blames ‘faulty decisions’ Speaking in the Parliament, NA Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai blamed “faulty decisions” of the country’s rulers for the current situation. He enquired about the whereabouts of Sohail Afridi, the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional and was reported to be in preventative custody . Achakzai, who leads the opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), accused PML-N’s Sadiq of not running the house judiciously as the speaker. He said the opposition was ready for dialogue on issues such as empowerment of Parliament and eradicating terrorism of all kinds. “If you hold dialogue on these issues, we will give unconditional support,” he added. The opposition leader compared the KP imbroglio to the 1971 separation of East Pakistan, noting that Afridi was called a “terrorist”. “Were multiple attacks on the heads of different political parties in the past in KP committed by Sohail Afridi?” he asked. Achakzai said terrorism was introduced by those who had brought fighters for the Soviet-Afghan war. “When the Afghan war was over, these terrorists were left free in the tribal areas of the country and they started killing Pakistanis,” he added. The opposition leader then mentioned the reported deaths during the July unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). The TTAP chief sought meetings of incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan with his family, friends and party workers. He questioned who had “sent” ex-premier Nawaz Sharif to exile in Saudi Arabia and who “murdered” ex-PM Benazir Bhutto. The NA speaker took exception to Achakzai’s remarks on his chairing of the session. “You are saying to me that I am not running the House correctly. You have not read Rule 30. Someone takes their mobile phone; someone disrupts [the proceedings].” Sadiq further said recordings of members’ speeches that were “anti-state” would not be uploaded on the NA’s social media accounts. Meanwhile, Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas accused the government’s delegation of derailing the dialogue with the opposition, including the Oct 3 talks . The Majlis Wahdat-i-Muslimeen (MWM) chief said some more time should have been allowed to make the talks successful and called for resolving the public’s issues instead of blaming each other. The senator contended that people voted for the PTI in large numbers during the February 2024 general elections in reaction to Imran’s imprisonment. Noting that this was his first tenure as a parliament member, Abbas said he realised that the Constitution was a safeguard of the rights of people. He further claimed he did not receive a salary or any perks and privileges from the Senate. ‘We kept waiting’: PPP’s Rehman recounts Oct 3 talks In her remarks, PPP Senator Sherry Rehman asked the PTI to define its agenda and reasons for its long march , which the party had announced to stage towards Islamabad but remained within KP. Rehman added that President Asif Ali Zardari and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had insisted on resolving issues through dialogue because terrorism was a red line for them. She called on the opposition not to dictate to the government and to avoid giving lectures on patriotism. Rehman emphasised that everyone was trying to find common ground and “a path of action”. The PPP leader objected to the opposition’s claims that the government delegation left the Oct 3 talks. “We kept waiting for you. The speaker and I ordered food for you as leaving was not being considered. We could have sat till 5am or 6am,” she said. Rehman asserted, “We had said we would wait further […] This is not fair to say that we said ‘we are leaving’. Definitely not. Opposite.” Speaking on the topic, the NA speaker — who chaired the talks — also remarked, “What was the hurry in launching the long march?” Sadiq referred to a post on X made by Afridi about going ahead with the long march even as the negotiations were underway. “You said to ignore it, so we kept ignoring it till 3am, so I think, if you want to sit again [at the table] then do not go into further details. Those things took place in confidence; bury them here.” The PPP vice president remarked that the country faced several emergencies, including those regarding education and poverty, that needed to be seen holistically. “If you think PPP is going to support any sort of emergency which is against the Constitution, you are wrong,” she declared. “This Constitution has bound the country together through difficult times. We remember the lessons from the fall of Dhaka,” she said. “PPP has seen many phases of the path towards democracy. It (martial law) was a dark chapter in history; we do not want the country to go through such an experience again,” Rehman said, recalling “sacrifices” made by her party. JUI-F says no ‘evidence’ presented Senator Kamran Murtaza of the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F), who had earlier submitted a resolution opposing the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, contended that no documentary evidence was presented before the Parliament for the decision. He argued that the proclamation under Article 234 required a report from the KP governor, but in this case, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi had not presented a report explaining why governor’s rule was necessary. The JUI-F senator said the security situation in Balochistan was also grave and pointed out that a provincial government now had its writ in the Katcha areas without an emergency being imposed there. Murtaza stressed that free and transparent elections under a fair election commission were the only solution to the existing problems.

School collapses in Pakistan: A timeline of incidents since 2021. The roof of a private school in Peshawar’s Afridi Abad collapsed on Thursday, killing 33. The deceased included 32 students — between the ages of seven and 14 — and a female teacher. Pakistan has witnessed several incidents of structural collapses at educational institutions in recent years, resulting in the deaths and injuries of students, teachers and other staff members. Here is a timeline of reported incidents over the past five years. Sep 11, 2026 — Karachi, Sindh Five people were killed and two others injured when a wall of a dilapidated government school building collapsed on them in Orangi Town’s Sector 11. The school was closed at the time of the incident. July 2, 2026 — Lahore, Punjab A child died and at least five others were injured after the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in the Baghbanpura neighbourhood . The school administration was constructing a two-marla structure to expand its existing 14-marla building. The roof collapsed during the construction work, sending debris onto the boy and others, including a motorcyclist and several labourers. June 30, 2026 — Lahore, Punjab In Lahore’s Kahna area, 14 children were killed while several others were injured when the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed. A statement by the Edhi rescue service, which took part in the rescue operation, said that the roof “collapsed suddenly”. Lahore District Education Authority Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Tariq Mahmood said the building housed a private tuition centre and was run by a woman resident of the area. June 30, 2026 — Umerkot, Sindh Three girls, aged 3 to 13, were killed after a portion of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed and the rubble fell on them. The girls were returning home after attending a nearby seminary. While they were passing by the wall, it suddenly collapsed, locals said, adding that the girls died before they could be rescued from under the rubble. May 7, 2026 — Dera Ghazi Khan, Punjab At least four children were killed and 20 people were injured after the roof of a classroom at a private school collapsed. The injured included 16 students, two teachers and as many labourers. A probe into the incident revealed that construction for an extension of the building was underway when the roof of the classroom collapsed. February 2026 — Sialkot, Punjab A student of Government Girls Higher Secondary School Bediana in Sialkot district was buried under the rubble of an under-construction structure that collapsed on her. The authorities registered a case against District Education Authority Chief Executive Officer Mujahid Hussain, school principal Kalsoom and the contractor following the incident. June 30, 2025 — Multan, Punjab Several girls were injured when the roof of a madressah collapsed. Rescue personnel pulled the girls trapped beneath the rubble out. Four girls were treated at the site, while five others received first aid before being shifted to Nishtar Hospital. Sep 26, 2024 — Muzaffargarh, Punjab A student died while six of his class fellows were critically injured when the roof of a private school collapsed in Wesandywali village . The incident happened at the Aligarh Public School. The owner had started the construction of a room on the upper floor without seeking permission. The ceiling of the old classroom could not bear the weight and collapsed. Aug 30, 2024 — Khairpur, Sindh Twelve students suffered head injuries when a large chunk of concrete plaster fell from the ceiling of a government high school classroom in Basiro village , Khairpur district. A viral video showed large, brick-sized chunks of concrete scattered across classroom desks, while students with bloodied heads and faces were being rescued and taken to hospitals. July 2, 2024 —Swat, KP Six children were injured when the roof of a classroom collapsed in Tangaar village , in Gwalerai Union Council of Swat’s Matta tehsil. The incident occurred in a nursery classroom at a private school. One of the walls collapsed before the roof caved in. May 9, 2024 — Layyah, Punjab Eight children were injured when the roof of their classroom collapsed at a private school in Chak 344/TDA, in Chaubara tehsil of Layyah district. The children were attending a pre-school class at Al-Rahman Grammar School when the roof collapsed on them. Feb 21, 2024 — Jacobabad, Sindh Four young students were injured when plaster fell from the ceiling of their classroom at the main government primary school for boys in Jacobabad . Teachers at the school said that plaster had fallen from the ceiling of a Grade Three classroom. The school building was in a dilapidated condition. July 4, 2023 — Okara, Punjab The roofs of three rooms and a portion of the veranda at the Government Elementary School collapsed just days before Eidul Azha, during summer vacation. The village school catered to 900 students. The affected area consisted of three rooms and a veranda used by the middle section students, totaling 300 in number. June 27, 2023 — Bannu, KP Three seminary students were killed and two others injured when a room’s roof collapsed in Bannu . The roof caved in when some workers were busy spreading clay over it to prevent leaks during rains. An official said many parts of the district had received heavy rain the previous night, and the roof of the seminary collapsed due to absorption of rainwater. Aug 26, 2022 — Muzaffargarh, Punjab At least 14 students were injured, 12 of them seriously, when the roof of a classroom collapsed in a private school in the Jinnah Garden locality. At the affected school, 65 students were studying from nursery to 5th grade. Oct 22, 2021 — Jhelum, Punjab Two students were killed and 20 other people — 16 students and four teachers — were injured when the wall of a school collapsed during an event inside the school situated along the GT Road in Jhelum . The students who died were both aged 15. June 7, 2021 — Lahore, Punjab A schoolboy was killed and three others were injured when the boundary wall of a private school collapsed on College Road in the Green Town area. A police official said the children were playing near the wall when it collapsed. Four of them were trapped under the debris. One died on the spot, while the other three suffered injuries. Header image: Residents gather during a search operation after a roof collapsed at a school in Peshawar on October 15, 2026. —AFP

India expected to overtake Japan as world's 4th largest economy in 2027: IMF. India is expected to become the world’s fourth-largest economy by 2027, overtaking Japan, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) projections that on Thursday laid out the Asian nations’ contrasting trajectories. The IMF said Japan would remain the fourth-largest country by nominal gross domestic product this year, but in 2027 India is set to take its place, with a GDP reaching $4.52 trillion. Japan is slated to slip to sixth place that year, falling behind both India and the United Kingdom, the projection showed. India has shown strong growth in recent years despite global economic headwinds, with the IMF this week raising its forecasts for 2026 growth to hit 7.0 per cent. Japan, by contrast, is plagued by an aging population and other structural problems that have seen the Asian giant’s growth stagnate. The United States is the world’s largest economy, followed by China and Germany. Releasing the IMF’s regional economic outlook for Asia-Pacific on Thursday, Asia Director Krishna Srinivasan said India entered the current energy price shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran from a strong position. “India entered this with very strong fundamentals,” he said. “Growth was strong, fiscal prudence was pretty much enshrined, they had lots of reserves and so on. And so in that context, they have responded well to the shock.” Growth in Japan, by contrast, is projected to slow to 0.7pc in 2026, with the country hard hit by an increase in energy prices —and wider inflation— that has seen the Bank of Japan raise interest rates to their highest level in three decades. The country, long haunted by deflation, has seen a sustained increase in consumer prices since the spring of 2022, and spiking energy prices from the Iran war have further fuelled those rises. The fall of the yen, which hit its lowest level in 40 years against the dollar over the summer, is further driving up the cost of imports. Japan’s aging population is also weighing on economic activity. The IMF’s Srinivasan said Japan’s economy was benefiting from the boom in artificial intelligence investments, but not as much as its regional neighbours. The benchmark Nikkei index in Tokyo fell by nearly five percent on Thursday, dragged down by a plunge in tech stocks amid doubts over the profitability of the AI sector.

Pakistan worst hit by hunger in South Asia. • Economic instability erodes household purchasing power; heavy rains, floods trigger acute crop losses • ​South Asia remains in the ‘serious’ category; ​global hunger rises after two decades ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia on the 2026 Global Hunger Index released on Wednesday, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks and global conflicts. Published jointly by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and the Swiss organisation Helvetas under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, the report reveals that progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018. In Pakistan, economic instability and sharp food price inflation have eroded households’ purchasing power and constrained access to food. Undernourishment in the country has climbed from low in 2018 to medium, while child wasting has risen toward the high threshold. Across South Asia, the situation remains serious with a regional score of 23.5. Although the region’s score has fallen substantially from an alarming 37.5 in 2000, most of that progress occurred before 2018. While Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved from the alarming to the serious category since 2000, child stunting remains very high. Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall, whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. Child mortality rates in both nations have declined from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels today. The report warned that high levels of acute food insecurity will persist across the region. Heavy rains and flooding caused localised crop losses in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures negatively affected Afghanistan’s 2026 cereal-growing season. According to Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates, 218 million people in South Asia, including Iran, were undernourished between 2023 and 2025, representing roughly one-third of the global total. Globally, hunger is rising again after nearly two decades of progress. The 2026 global score stands at 18.1, worsening from 17.6 in 2018. Hunger has increased in 32 countries since 2018, and 57 countries are on track to miss achieving even low hunger levels by 2030. Three of the index’s four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — have worsened, while only child mortality has continued to decline slightly. State-based armed conflicts, now at their highest level since World War II, alongside frequent extreme weather events, are major drivers of this reversal. The war in Iran and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are driving up fuel, transportation and fertiliser costs. Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea export restrictions threaten higher wheat prices, making basic supplies unaffordable in the Global South. Compounding the crisis, international spending on food security has fallen to 2016-2017 levels, forcing cuts to aid programmes and emergency rations. The report urged governments to reverse funding cuts for humanitarian assistance and data collection to prevent and manage future crises. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

TTAP says 'no talks' with govt until meeting with Imran Khan is arranged, health details are provided. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Thursday announced that it was suspending all negotiations with the government, saying there would be “no talks” until a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan was arranged and information about his health was provided. The alliance, in a statement, said all negotiating authority would rest solely with its chairman, Mehmood Khan Achakzai. The announcement was made at a leadership meeting held at Achakzai’s residence, where the political situation arising from the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in KP, as well as the situation in the province, was reviewed in detail. In the days preceding the development, political tensions between the federal government and the opposition, mainly the PTI, had remained high after the party announced a long march to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. However, the march, initially planned for Islamabad, remained confined to KP until it fizzled out with the imposition of governor’s rule in the province. The alliance strongly condemned the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in KP, describing the move as a “robbery” and a midnight assault on the Constitution and the people’s mandate. It demanded that the decision be withdrawn immediately, saying the step was not only an insult to the people of one province but to those of all provinces. The statement added that the alliance would also file a petition against the decision in the Peshawar High Court (PHC). The TTAP also condemned all forms of terrorism, including state terrorism against the public, actions by state institutions against political parties, and violence by one sect against another. Expressing full support for the National Action Plan, the opposition alliance demanded that, instead of adopting new policies, the joint resolution of the Aman Jirga approved by the KP Assembly be implemented immediately. The participants also demanded the immediate release of non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, PTI provincial president Junaid Akbar, and all arrested members of the National and provincial assemblies and other leaders. The PTI had reported their detention on Oct 11, shortly after the Centre imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province. The alliance also demanded the release of Imran Khan’s sisters, who have been in detention for nearly three weeks under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance, as well as a meeting with the PTI founder and access to his doctors. The TTAP attributed the deteriorating law and order situation in Balochistan to the unrepresentative provincial government and the federal government’s failed policies, saying the provincial government had not been formed on the basis of the people’s genuine mandate. It called for the province’s issues to be resolved through dialogue with its people rather than the use of force. The alliance also announced plans to approach international human rights organisations and the United Nations over what it described as restrictions on judicial independence, media curbs and violations of human rights and the Constitution. Emergency over terrorism concerns On Sunday, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234. The decision came during a meeting of the federal cabinet, which deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP and noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Subsequently, the prime minister sent a summary to the president, who approved the move. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. On Monday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the governor’s rule, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

India voter purge. THE purge of millions of voters from India’s electoral rolls has sparked widespread demonstrations , spearheaded by young protesters calling for justice. The Cockroach Janta Party is at the forefront of the movement, while more established opposition parties, such as Congress, are also participating actively. The thread uniting these groups is their suspicion that the Indian election commission has been tinkering with the rolls to benefit the ruling BJP. Earlier this year, the youth-led CJP organised a massive anti-government campaign calling for the resignation of the education minister over exam irregularities. The movement succeeded in ousting the minister, with the youthful energy of its participants catching the BJP government off guard. This time too, India’s rulers have responded with brute force, bundling away thousands of protesters, including Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders, and cutting off access to the iconic Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi. Around 130m names have been removed from the electoral rolls. The Indian election authorities say the deleted names include voters who have died, relocated, or could not be traced. But the Indian opposition has dismissed this explanation. It is believed that many of the deleted voters were Muslims, as well as those belonging to other marginalised groups. Moreover, media reports say that the Indian election commissioner — whose resignation is being demanded — ignored objections from within the commission to the deletion of such a large number of voters. Such purging of the rolls is in keeping with the BJP regime’s marginalisation of vulnerable groups. It has employed lawfare and dubious means in the past as well to delete Muslim votes; millions have been disenfranchised through the National Register of Citizens. Earlier, the BJP and its Hindutva cohorts could get away with trampling the rights of Indian Muslims. But now, their shenanigans are not working. It appears that India’s other communities are also tired of Hindutva’s empty promises and its attempt to remake India in its own image through fair means and foul. The Sangh Parivar has run out of ideas, and its fantasies about a glorious Hindu past will not buy the people bread, or give them jobs. Hopefully, a fairer order can emerge from the tumult, in which all of India’s communities are treated equally. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

Palestinians fear violent olive harvest ahead of Israeli elections. With a black eye and a bandage covering his face, Palestinian farmer Abdellatif Bazzari looks out at his rows of olive trees that are half harvested before the season has even started. Bazzari, who was injured in a raid on the fields by Israeli settlers that killed his cousin, is afraid to return to harvest the other half without some sort of army protection, fearing a new attack. Like many olive farmers in the plains nestled between the occupied West Bank’s sinuous limestone hills, Bazzari decided to harvest as early as possible this year, hoping both to save his crops and avoid beatings. A Palestinian man is seen at an olive tree field during the harvest season, near the controversial Israeli separation wall, in the village of Beit Awwa, west of Hebron City in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Oct 15, 2026. — AFP With Israel heading to elections on Oct 27, some farmers believe the violence will escalate as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, locked in a tight race, seeks to shore up his right-wing base. “I think the prime minister of Israel is worried about the results of elections and he doesn’t want to take any action against the settlers as he hopes to receive their votes,” Bazzari told AFP . “If he loses, things will get better,” he hoped. Olives are as important economically to Palestinians as they are a symbol of their attachment to the land, accounting for an estimated 15 per cent of the West Bank’s agricultural GDP. A Palestinian man scoops a handful of olives at an olive tree field during the harvest season, near the controversial Israeli separation wall, in the village of Beit Awwa, west of Hebron City in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Oct 15, 2026. — AFP On Oct 7, a group of about 15 to 20 settlers raided the field where Bazzari and his family were picking olives by hand, beating them, before the army intervened and shot dead Bazzari’s cousin Ali Bazzari, he said. “My cousin bled to death right under this olive tree, irrigating the soil of Palestine with his blood,” Bazzari said, pointing to a tree in the field. Palestinians pick their olives during the harvest season at a field, near the controversial Israeli separation wall, in the village of Beit Awwa, west of Hebron City in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 15, 2026. — AFP ‘Don’t go out’ Bazzari said the Israeli army, which had been dispatched to the site of the raid, an isolated field near the West Bank village of Burqa, kept the ambulance from reaching his cousin after he was shot. The Israeli military said troops and border police forces were dispatched after reports of “rock hurling toward an Israeli civilian, who was injured”, referring to a settler. During the confrontation between dozens of Palestinians and Israeli settlers, “a commander operating in the area identified a terrorist running toward him while carrying a suspicious object and neutralised him”, it added. A Palestinian woman scoops a handful of olives at an olive tree field during the harvest season, near the controversial Israeli separation wall, in the village of Beit Awwa, west of Hebron City in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 15, 2026. — AFP Israeli leaders also highlight violence against Israelis, including the shooting death of a settler by a Palestinian last month. Bazzari, like other West Bank Palestinians whom AFP spoke to, said danger areas for the olive harvest have grown in recent years as settlements multiplied and expanded. “They don’t want us to plant, to farm anything. Punjab proposes holding local government elections in three phases in April. LAHORE: The Punjab government appears set to delay the long-awaited local government elections in the province once again, despite the polling schedule proposed by the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP), it emerged on Thursday. Earlier this month, the electoral body proposed holding local government elections in Punjab on December 14 and sent a draft of the suggested schedule to the Punjab chief secretary for consultation. The Punjab cabinet has instead proposed holding the elections in phases on April 4, 11 and 18, following recommendations by a ministerial committee formed to consult the ECP on the conduct of local government elections in the province. In this regard, the Punjab Local Government and Community Development Department wrote to the ECP on Wednesday. The letter, which conveyed the ministerial committee’s decision, cited smog, dense fog and adverse winter weather conditions expected during December and January, followed by the commencement of Ramazan in February, as reasons for not holding the elections as scheduled. The letter said the cabinet’s ministerial committee had held its second meeting on October 5, during which it deliberated at length on the ECP’s draft election schedule. The committee discussed scenarios arising from the likely tough weather conditions and Ramazan, the letter stated. It proposed holding the local government elections in phases to facilitate the effective deployment of election staff and security personnel, the efficient transportation of polling materials, better administrative oversight and improved accessibility for voters. The phased approach would also help avoid adverse weather conditions typically experienced during December and January and the period immediately following Ramazan, the letter said. The letter added that the Punjab cabinet considered the committee’s recommendations early on Wednesday and approved a proposal to hold the elections in three phases on April 4, 11 and 18, 2027, all of which fall on Sundays. The cabinet also decided that the allocation of districts among the three phases may be deliberated and thereafter mutually agreed with the ECP in a dedicated meeting, keeping in view administrative, logistical, security and geographical considerations as well as weather conditions, the letter said. On October 5, the ECP, in a meeting, upheld that it was prepared to hold local government polls across the province. The ECP letter stated that the commission had held a consultative meeting with the provincial cabinet committee on Aug 20 to discuss the poll date and had agreed to the Punjab government’s proposal to hold the elections between Dec 15 and Jan 15, 2027. The letter also stated that the ECP had held a consultative meeting with the provincial cabinet committee on Aug 20 to discuss the poll date. During the meeting, it had agreed to the Punjab government’s proposal to hold the elections between Dec 15 and Jan 15, 2027. On August 6, the Punjab cabinet had approved an allocation of Rs12.5 billion for holding local government elections in the province. The last local government elections in Punjab were held in 2015 under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2013 . Polling took place in phases between October and December 2015, and elected councils assumed office in 2017 after indirect elections for mayors and chairpersons. Since then, local body polls in Punjab have experienced repeated delays. The PTI government had dissolved the elected local bodies in April 2019 before they completed their tenure. The move was later struck down by the Supreme Court, which restored them. They eventually completed their term on Dec 31, 2021. Successive provincial governments repeatedly amended or replaced the Punjab Local Government Act. Each legislative change required the ECP to restart preparations, including delimitation and election planning. Changing laws and administrative delays by successive governments contributed significantly to the postponement of the local body elections. Under Article 140A of the Constitution and the Elections Act, local government elections should be held within 120 days of the expiry of local bodies’ terms. Since the councils’ term ended in Dec 2021, elections were due by April 2022, but they have been repeatedly postponed.

Patrick T. Fallon / AFP Commentary / United States 01 October 2026 20+ minutes Five Energy Market Factors That Could Tip the Scales in the Middle East War Oil, gas and fuel prices are central to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, with Washington striving to lower them and Tehran to keep them high. With both sides determined to prevail, five market-shaping developments in particular could affect whether fighting ramps up or de-escalates. Share BlueSky E-mail Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Salva Stampa Related Tags Global Order and Peacemaking United States Iran Israel/Palestine As Iran and the United States trade blows in the Gulf, they are both trying to sway at least one shared audience: global energy markets. The public and private companies that produce, refine, move and consume oil and gas around the world are listening rapt to what the belligerents say and watching every move they make in an attempt to understand where the war is headed. These commodities have many prices: for instance, what a barrel of crude oil is fetching today; how much customers are paying for derivative products like diesel or jet fuel in major markets like East Asia, the European Union or the U.S.; and what future delivery of such items is projected to cost. Together, these actual and estimated prices serve as a rough indicator of what the market thinks about the conflict’s likely trajectory. In turn, the price fluctuations are monitored in both Tehran and Washington, which factor them into strategy. U.S. President Donald Trump is plainly keeping one eye on the markets at all times. In June, when he signed a now defunct memorandum of understanding meant to end the war, he noted a market motivation, saying, “We run out of [oil] reserves at about four weeks”. On 13 August, with November’s midterm elections getting closer, Vice President JD Vance cited low fuel prices as Washington’s main war aim, saying “That’s goal number one – keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country”. Preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – Washington’s ostensible motive for launching its airstrikes in February – was apparently, at least for a time, goal number two. Iran, for its part, is trying to maintain the clout it obtained by asserting control of the Strait of Hormuz, for which it is willing to pay a big price. The Iranian economy is being hammered by intensifying sanctions and a resumed U.S. naval blockade that has halted exports from Iran’s southern coast. Washington has repeatedly hailed the impending death of Iran’s oil industry, due to lack of export and storage capacity. While these predictions were overblown, Iran is still reeling economically. As both the U.S. and Iran pin their hopes on being able to manage prices, the energy markets have proven unpredictable. Despite disruptions, the markets have displayed unexpected resilience, helping dilute the conflict’s economic consequences. Apocalyptic prophecies that oil would reach $200 a barrel have so far been incorrect. Instead, the price of the global benchmark, Brent crude, has risen from below $75 before the war to peaks that have not yet topped $130. These prices are high, but adjusted for inflation, they pale in comparison to previous spikes. Part of the explanation owes to buffers that have kept the markets from careening out of control. It helps that the world had an oil surplus when the war began, the U.S. had a few hundred million more barrels in its federal stores, Russia had more functional refineries and export terminals, China was building up rather than depleting its reserves and the Red Sea was largely open to tanker traffic. Since the war began, higher prices have pushed demand lower and raised production in some countries while new workarounds – in part orchestrated by the U.S. and Gulf states like the United Arab Emirates – and growing risk tolerance are sending a significant amount of oil through Hormuz despite Iran’s attacks. [T]he question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. Still, the question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. The feared tipping point at which a shortfall in oil supply causes a rapid price increase until demand falls has seemingly been forestalled by greater crude flow through Hormuz. But surging diesel and other fuel prices may now matter more than crude oil alone. U.S. retail diesel prices are soaring to record highs, generating support for a 90-day U.S. diesel export ban and even a measure of dissent from the war among members of Trump’s Republican Party (in many other parts of the world, rising fuel prices are already stoking significant public anger). Iran is cognisant of the correlation between fuel prices and the Republicans’ political fortunes; with the November midterm elections approaching and major Republican losses a significant possibility , Iran may think that such a result would produce new constraints on Trump’s war-making, in the form of more vigorous oversight from a Congress controlled by opposition Democrats. For this reason, many Iran watchers believe Tehran, along with its allies, will seek to prevent the U.S. from stabilising prices, even if it involves a mutually hurting re-escalation of the conflict. Indeed, in September, the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels advanced in Yemen, positioning themselves to more effectively threaten shipping in the Red Sea, a major energy corridor. But while Iran looks for ways to keep oil and gas bottled up in the Middle East, Washington and its partners continue to work on means of getting these items out, with the outflow of crude through the Strait of Hormuz reportedly hitting its pre-war baseline by the end of September, though refined products like fuel lagged far behind. Efforts are under way to keep raising this Hormuz outflow, and land routes add a few million more barrels. The U.S. conundrum now is that crude needs to reach refineries, and the resulting products to hit global markets, for the world to get out of its growing fuel crisis. As the U.S. increasingly looks to others to help manage the fallout of its war with Iran, it is also pursuing a number of costly mitigation measures, whose sustainability is questionable. This Crisis Group analysis examines the relationship between global energy markets and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. It looks at the cushions that have helped absorb war-related shocks to oil markets so far and the extent to which they are under pressure. It identifies five particular factors that could contribute to re-escalation or de-escalation of the conflict. U.S. concerns began with crude oil, but diesel may be the Trump administration’s undoing. Only Beijing knows how quickly and by how much China’s oil imports and fuel exports will recover. Ukraine’s strategic achievements threaten its patrons’ energy supplies. The Houthis have moved into Bab al-Mandab. The contest over the Strait of Hormuz has intensified. 1. U.S. concerns began with crude oil, but diesel may be the Trump administration’s undoing. The first factor to consider is U.S. energy security. The U.S. has developed several layers of protection from the worst market consequences of its own coercive action against major oil exporters like Russia (on which it has slapped Ukraine-related sanctions) and Iran (which it has both sanctioned and attacked). These include substantial increases in the efficiency with which oil is converted into economic output since the 1970s energy shocks and advancements like the shale revolution , which have made the U.S. itself the world’s top oil producer. Abundant natural gas production and Washington’s forcibly acquired control of Venezuelan oil export help, too. So does the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve. Yet these buffers are being put to the test. As part of a 400-million barrel release coordinated through the International Energy Agency to help keep a lid on oil prices, the U.S. is finishing up a drawdown of 172 million barrels from its strategic reserve. If completed, its holdings will drop to 243 million barrels. When the reserve draws down, private companies take the barrels as a loan, with repayment deadlines varying from early 2027 to mid-2029, and move the oil directly into markets. The releases to date have bolstered domestic refining, but they have also resulted in U.S. stores of oil falling to their lowest level since 1982 . The reserves are approaching what many analysts consider the minimum volume needed for the network of salt caverns and pipes the U.S. government uses for oil storage to stay functional. While the U.S. government has stated that the operational minimum of its reserves is 70 million barrels, a federal audit found that more than a quarter – implying an estimated 103 million barrels – likely cannot be withdrawn due to ageing storage facilities. Industry analysts have repeatedly put the operational minimum within a much higher range of 170-200 million barrels, with several experts warning of dangers to the salt caverns’ structural integrity below 300 million barrels, a threshold passed in early August. (The U.S. Energy Department disputes that any such problem exists.) U.S. strategic reserves could therefore be functionally empty in weeks to months, depending on the pace of withdrawals, with long-term risks to the viability of the entire system growing if they continue. Once this stockpile is depleted, U.S. concerns that need oil beyond that available from domestic production will need to look to commercial stockpiles and imports. Here uncertainty reigns. Aggregate estimates of a national operational minimum vary widely, and at least some analysts believe that a single U.S. figure is unknowable . Inventory at Cushing, Oklahoma – the storage and distribution hub for the U.S. domestic benchmark grade, West Texas Intermediate – has ebbed and flowed over the course of the war. Cushing storage rose in late September as refinery runs fell amid talk of a diesel export ban, after nearly hitting “ tank bottoms ” in June and July. Cushing does not represent the entire private U.S. oil or energy market, but its stock is an important signal alongside the status of strategic reserves, and it has shown real strain during the war. Nor is the demand side of the equation fully easing. U.S. crude exports, especially to East Asia and Europe, surged by some two million barrels a day or more through the first three months of the war, though in recent months they have started to fall, in part because of surging freight costs linked to the war. As to whether Venezuelan production can help soften the blow to global energy supplies or to U.S. stocks, it has likely done as much as it can already, at least for the short term. As to whether Venezuelan production can help soften the blow to global energy supplies or to U.S. stocks, it has likely done as much as it can already, at least for the short term. Following its January ouster of President Nicolás Maduro, the U.S. took control of Venezuela’s oil exports, and though the details of the arrangement remain unclear, Venezuela has consistently shipped 900,000 to over 1 million barrels per day in recent months. Its monthly crude exports peaked in May and declined through September as storage was drained, but they are still higher compared to the period just before the U.S. removed Maduro. The U.S. has been one of the largest destinations for Venezuela’s oil exports of late: its share rose to about two thirds in July, even as total exports fell slightly, before dropping to just under half by September. This flow from Venezuela is helpful to the U.S. at the margins but not by itself transformative. Average daily U.S. imports of Venezuelan oil in September were equivalent to under 3 per cent of the crude used daily by U.S. refineries (as of the week ending 18 September). In this way, Venezuela’s state oil company PDVSA has essentially become an unofficial if modest buffer alongside the dwindling U.S. strategic reserve. Over time, the U.S. government’s machinations could lead to greater output, though at a cost to Venezuela and its sovereignty. But significant short-term increases are unlikely, given years of reduced production and underinvestment. Trump has stated that he intends to fill U.S. strategic reserves with Venezuelan oil, but heavy Venezuelan crude is unsuitable for the reserve and would need to be swapped for lighter grades with the private sector. There are many hurdles to clear before that would be possible, suggesting that Trump’s statement is more intended to allay concerns about U.S. oil supply than to communicate real short-term solutions. Beyond inventory depletion and the limits of what Caracas can be compelled to do for Washington, the global market for fuels derived from crude oil is in much worse shape than when the war began and is now a more urgent issue for Washington than crude. As of August, global diesel exports had dipped by a third from mid-2025, while China’s fuel exports remain uncertain , Russian refineries are getting pummelled by Ukrainian aerial attacks and most other refiners around the world are already running at full capacity. Major maintenance work is looming for many. Russian and Gulf fuel exports were down over half from March to mid-August, spurring increased refinery production elsewhere such as in the U.S. and Europe; these heightened runs are far from making up the shortfall. Diesel supplies are especially tight, with U.S. prices up over 75 per cent from a year ago and still climbing. With national diesel inventory reaching a multi-decade seasonal low , the state of Texas declared an emergency over diesel prices, despite producing a third of U.S. diesel as of June. The squeeze has prompted one of the longest periods of running U.S. refineries near maximum capacity in a quarter-century – a “ super-refining ” spike that wears on equipment. Refineries will eventually need downtime for maintenance, or major breakdowns could occur. While the average U.S. consumer may not care about crude oil itself, rising fuel prices are felt intensely. Trump gathered executives from leading fuel refining and distribution companies at the White House on 1 September to ask them to lower fuel prices, but to little avail. Expensive diesel means higher costs for freight, such as the long-haul trucking and rail on which the U.S. economy depends, as well as for construction and agriculture . While the average U.S. consumer may not care about crude oil itself, rising fuel prices are felt intensely. Fuel accounts for up to 30 per cent of food costs in the U.S., for example. A barrel of crude is an abstraction; gasoline and food are survival. As noted, a 90-day diesel export ban is reportedly under consideration – one that may bring relief to some parts of the country at the considerable expense of others, as well as the global market, before refinery output falls. Previous warnings about being weeks away from domestic operational minimums helped persuade Trump to accept the memorandum of understanding with Iran back in June, but the recovery during the lull in hostilities that followed was not enough to push the timeline back significantly. Now energy markets – especially for fuels like diesel – are again showing major strain. 2. Only Beijing knows how quickly and by how much China’s oil imports and fuel exports will recover. The world’s largest oil importer, China, may have done more to stabilise the global market than the U.S. as the top producer. Surprising many, Beijing tamped down its oil imports by, at the peak, 5 million barrels per day, nearly half the pre-war volume, absorbing much of the initial shock of the U.S. attack and Iran’s retaliation in the Strait of Hormuz. By reducing its imports, Beijing kept global supplies from plunging further, protected itself from a price spike and burnished its image as a responsible actor. The world is now intently watching for signs that China will ratchet its imports up again and, if so, when and by how much. A modest increase in July crude imports, once thought to reflect an uptick from the brief June reopening of Hormuz, instead continued at a comparable level in August before dipping again through 24 September. Even in August, bullish estimates continued to project China returning to near 10 million barrels, or about 80 per cent of its pre-war imports, within months. Independent, or “teapot”, refiners, accounting for about one quarter of China’s refining capacity, were scouring crude markets for cargoes as fuel export restrictions eased, though the teapots are threatened by the most recent spike in oil prices and declining domestic inventory. China’s emergence as a swing consumer has ... drawn attention to its capacity to hold down imports. Historically, oil market observers focused on spare production capacity as an important indicator of stability, but China’s emergence as a swing consumer has instead drawn attention to its capacity to hold down imports. No one outside Beijing’s innermost councils knows how long China can continue to do so, but its restraint appears to have staying power. It was heavily stockpiling before the war, so no longer doing so accounts for some of the reduction in its demand. But the rest was achieved through a combination of commercial stockpile depletion, export controls and domestic demand reduction. Estimates vary, but China probably had something like 1.2 - 1.4 billion barrels in storage at the war’s start, giving it the world’s largest reserves. It drew down this inventory by some 100-200 million largely or entirely commercial barrels into August, still leaving the state with control of perhaps up to a billion more barrels than the U.S. Its estimated onshore crude stocks were far above the five-year average in August despite recent usage. Beyond the usual government and commercial holdings, China’s 2025 Energy Law requires commercial companies to maintain Corporate Social Responsibility Reserves, in effect a commercial extension of China’s strategic reserves. Fuel export restrictions beginning in mid-March also helped conserve stocks, which Beijing relaxed on a month-by-month basis starting in July. China’s development of the world’s largest coal-to-chemicals sector and heavy investment in electrification , particularly electric vehicles and renewable energy, has also helped keep oil demand much lower than it may otherwise have been. An additional, though rapidly diminishing buffer has been Iran’s oil. Beijing invoked its 2021 blocking law for the first time in May, instructing five refineries to ignore U.S. sanctions barring them from purchasing Iranian oil, while Trump reported that President Xi Jinping told him that China would continue buying oil from Iran at their May summit in Beijing. China has indeed continued these purchases throughout the war. By late September, Iran still had full tankers beyond the U.S. blockade line, carrying a volume of oil equal to maybe a few weeks’ worth of its recent daily deliveries to China. While the U.S. is blockading Iran’s coast and has chased down its tankers in the Indian Ocean, it has not touched the floating stockpile spread across the western Pacific from near Malaysia to the Yellow Sea, presumably to avoid a standoff with China. Hence, China has been able to keep buying oil and Iran to keep selling it despite all but halting loadings since the U.S. blockade was reimposed. These continued Chinese purchases of Iranian crude also loom over any deal that the U.S. may cut with Iran. Besides the blockade, U.S. sanctions are depressing Iranian oil sales. The June memorandum of understanding briefly eased these measures, allowing Iran to resume exports. It quickly hawked its oil to a range of potential customers, but few were willing to bite because a sanctions waiver is inherently temporary (and, as events subsequently proved, quickly reversible) and many had already contracted for alternative supplies. For now, the lack of other buyers means that China in effect controls the market for Iran’s oil. For now, the lack of other buyers means that China in effect controls the market for Iran’s oil, whether shipments already on the water outside the U.S. blockade line or others awaiting export. Beijing’s decisions about whether to increase its oil imports, how much of these imports will be Iranian and, absent credible, durable sanctions relief, what price it will demand as Iran’s only buyer will continue to largely set the value of renewed Iranian oil sales. Enticing other buyers would probably take even greater discounts – before the U.S. blockade, China had been buying at $7-12 per barrel below global benchmarks. At the moment, the lack of alternative buyers also means that Beijing can just let Iran’s remaining oil outside the blockade float at sea for as long as it needs to, comfortable that others are unlikely to snap it up. All these realities leave the U.S. in an uncomfortable spot: its ability to maintain its current course could well be linked to whether China maintains its massive import reduction while not reimposing deep fuel controls. While August fuel exports were up year-on-year, Beijing is rumoured to be considering new restrictions. But whichever way China goes, the U.S. is unlikely to push it too hard on its choice. Both because of Beijing’s influence over the energy markets, and because of its proven ability to retaliate for U.S. economic coercion by withholding rare earths, Washington has not gone beyond symbolic action in trying to stop Chinese purchases of Iranian oil, just as it has not reached for comparable tools regarding China’s purchase of sanctioned Russian oil. When asked why the U.S. was not imposing secondary sanctions on those still trading with Iran, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned of the consequences if the effort moved too quickly: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” China’s interests would seem to be best served by riding out the energy shock without rapidly and substantially raising its oil imports as long as it can comfortably do so, letting the U.S. fritter away its own oil reserves, munitions stockpiles and international reputation. Like any consumer, China does not want expensive oil and fuel, and it might be able to hold out for months, but probably not indefinitely. Beijing’s evergreen concerns about its “ Malacca dilemma ”, a vulnerability stemming from reliance on another maritime chokepoint, the Strait of Malacca, mean that it is unlikely to burn through its strategic reserves as the U.S. has done without a more urgent threat like a direct attack on its supply lines. There are already signs that China’s import recovery has begun – the question is how quickly it will progress and how far it will go. The same goes for its fuel exports, which may yet be restricted again. 3. Ukraine’s strategic achievements threaten its patrons’ energy supplies. “Diesel, diesel…diesel” was how a Ukrainian official described the subject of a late September call between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Russia-Ukraine war is one of the places where Trump is seeking solutions for a growing fuel crisis, though Kyiv shows no sign of letting up in its drone and missile strikes on the Russian energy sector. As of early August, “ the most dangerous commercial shipping environment in the world ” was in the view of some in the shipping industry neither the Strait of Hormuz nor the Red Sea, but the Black Sea. As it strives to fend off Russia’s all-out invasion for the fifth consecutive year, increase the costs of war for Russia and encourage de-escalation before winter, Ukraine has broadened its aerial campaign to the maritime theatre, attacking hundreds of ships in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov to paralyse Russian exports as well as Crimea’s supply lines and, in effect, lock Russia out of these water bodies. This wave of attacks is part of an effort to disrupt Russia’s energy sector and thereby cut off government revenue while raising the war’s costs for the average Russian. Meanwhile, Russia has stepped up its own air war, ordering more strikes on ships linked to Ukraine as well as export facilities like ports and grain terminals, as it did earlier in the conflict. The Black Sea campaign has severely restricted both countries’ grain exports, which together typically account for more than a quarter of annual global wheat exports, as well as Russian oil shipments. Thus, as the belligerents square off, global food and energy markets are taking collateral damage.
