Kyiv has been increasingly successful in its maritime disruption effort as its missile and drone capabilities improve. Meantime, while Russia’s air defences are spread ever thinner, its strikes on Ukraine are becoming more effective as Ukraine exhausts its own air defence munitions. Russia’s refinery capacity was down nearly a third by the end of July, and almost half by the end of August, as Ukraine’s attacks became more precise, hitting critical equipment that is difficult to repair. As a conservation measure, Moscow banned diesel exports in July, adding to existing restrictions on gasoline and jet fuel exports, later extending its restrictions on fuel exports and beginning to import fuel itself. These measures took more than 10 per cent of global seaborne diesel off the water, contributing to surging global prices (though Gulf diesel export losses remain much higher than Russia’s in recent months). Despite the impact its attacks are having, Russia spurned a Ukrainian offer of a Black Sea ceasefire in mid-August. Ukraine’s attacks included at least five at or near the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal on the Black Sea coast, through which about a million barrels of Kazakhstan’s oil pass a day – 80 per cent of its oil exports – alongside a small volume of Russian oil. That terminal is near the Russian port of Novorossiysk, which handles a share of Russian oil exports and a larger one of its grain exports, and became the main home for the remnants of Russia’s Black Sea fleet after it was mauled by Ukraine. It is not entirely clear why Kyiv would repeatedly target the CPC terminal, given that the main consumers of Kazakh crude are European refineries , little Russian crude typically passes through the terminal – though more might be diverted this way – and the transit fees earned by Russia are modest. Whether through miscalculation or intention, the attacks certainly got Washington’s attention. Not only did the forced suspensions involve typical exports equal to about 2 per cent of global daily oil demand, but U.S. oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron own almost a quarter of the pipeline, and both have sizeable stakes in large oil fields in Kazakhstan. Chevron’s investment in Kazakhstan production accounts for about 12 per cent of the company’s global output, and its CEO quickly complained about Ukrainian strikes on CPC to the White House in late July. Washington soon called on Kyiv to stop firing at the CPC terminal and non-Russian ships, though the wider aerial campaign continued. The impact of Ukraine’s missile and drone strikes has been blunted by, among other things, Russia’s ability to continue routing some of its exports through other ports, such as those on the Baltic Sea. Ukraine’s focus on refineries has freed up additional Russian crude for export, with July seaborne crude exports up 26 per cent year-on-year and total crude exports remained up 12 per cent in August despite further attacks on Black Sea terminals, though the increase means little for the availability of fuel if the crude does not reach refineries with spare capacity. Yet Ukraine’s attacks still raise energy costs, and Washington connected Ukraine’s aerial campaign to energy prices in early September, suggesting that the latest U.S. push to get Russia and Ukraine to the negotiating table may be partly motivated by the growing economic fallout of Kyiv’s war effort. As fuel prices continue to surge, Washington may lean harder on Kyiv to lay off the Russian energy sector. As fuel prices continue to surge, Washington may lean harder on Kyiv to lay off the Russian energy sector, an action that would help the movement of oil and give a psychological boost to traders looking for evidence of an easing crisis. In mid-September, Trump unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, though it was not immediately clear that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to the arrangement and strikes on energy infrastructure continued in the following days. Trump pressed Zelenskyy again at the UN General Assembly in late September, and the Ukrainian president (with the blessing of Kyiv’s European backers) again committed to a moratorium on attacking energy and grain facilities if Russia could credibly reciprocate. Even if such a truce came to pass, however, which is in doubt, refinery repair would take time. Washington’s most potent leverage over Kyiv is probably the missile interceptors Ukraine desperately needs to shield itself from Russian attack, especially as winter approaches. Trump previously said Ukraine could produce them domestically before reneging on the offer on the same day Vance asked Ukraine to back off the CPC. Ukraine hit a Greek-run tanker that reportedly loaded Russian oil at the CPC terminal on 16 August as well as a ship engaged in CPC terminal repairs in early September. Strictly speaking, these attacks did not violate its commitment to the U.S., even if they disrupted CPC operations. In the near term, Kyiv will likely keep firing at Russian refineries and export terminals, and keep the CPC terminal in its sights as well, unless the U.S. presses Ukraine harder or a Ukraine-Russia ceasefire is reached. 4. The Houthis have moved into Bab al-Mandab. The first weeks of September brought a flurry of news from the Arabian Peninsula that roiled global energy markets. The Houthis – an Iran-backed rebel force that has been fighting a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for more than a decade – were advancing rapidly down the Red Sea coast after breaking through their Saudi-backed opponents’ lines. At the same time, drones reportedly from Iraq struck several pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, forcing the pipeline’s suspension ; following repairs, a partial resumption began less than two weeks later, though complete restoration could take another six weeks. That pipeline ends at the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Prior to the war, it typically accounted for less than a million barrels per day of Saudi Arabia’s oil exports. From the war’s onset through July, it was carrying 3.3-4.3 million barrels per day of Red Sea crude exports. Those numbers began dropping once the Houthis shifted their attention to Saudi Arabia in late July, before the full suspension after the pipeline was hit. Any disruption to this flow is damaging to Riyadh and alarming to the global energy market, given the possibility of large drops in Saudi oil production if repairs are not fast or alternatives are not found. Earlier in the conflict, Iran briefly knocked out a pumping station on the pipeline, but otherwise operations had been smooth until the Houthis issued a 20 July warning to shipping companies not to load or discharge cargo at Saudi Arabian ports – in effect announcing a blockade. The Houthis then stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and government-aligned Yemeni forces. Like Iran in Hormuz, the Houthis appear to want to act as gatekeepers, allowing transits linked to friendly or at least non-hostile states. Strictly enforced, the Houthi blockade would end Red Sea exports, which have allowed Riyadh to reroute millions of barrels per day that would have gone through the Strait of Hormuz. Within weeks of the blockade’s announcement, Saudi Arabia’s oil exports nearly halved from late July to late August as tanker arrivals at Yanbu dropped by more than a third . The kingdom’s oil shipments through Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, fell from more than 3.5 million barrels per day in early July to near-zero in August. In response, Riyadh began sending shipments of oil through Hormuz on “shuttle runs” (see below). Yet a number of ships still appear able to safely pass by Houthi-controlled territory, like those connected with Russia and China, even when the China-affiliated tankers are carrying Saudi crude. The group also reportedly told Washington that it had no intention of attacking U.S. shipping and had previously informed the EU that it would refrain from targeting European ships. Like Iran in Hormuz, the Houthis appear to want to act as gatekeepers, allowing transits linked to friendly or at least non-hostile states, rather than ending all trade through the Red Sea. The Houthis demonstrated their ability to threaten shipping in their previous Red Sea campaign , launched after Israel began its Gaza offensive in response to the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas in southern Israel. Houthi fire at Israel and later Red Sea shipping prompted two spates of U.S. bombardment in 2024 and 2025, alongside airstrikes by Israel. These efforts did considerable damage in Yemen, but they neither crippled the Houthis nor forced them to cut a deal with Saudi Arabia or the Yemeni government. The rebels agreed to a ceasefire with the U.S. in May 2025, though the deal applied only to U.S. naval forces and U.S.-affiliated merchant vessels. Their Red Sea attacks in that phase of hostilities ended in September 2025. Nevertheless, their actions left a mark that has endured into the present conflict. When the Houthis again began firing at Saudi-affiliated tankers on 23 July, traffic through the Red Sea was down some 60 per cent from before 7 October 2023. A number of things have changed, however, since the 2023-2025 campaign. Then, the Houthis included much of the world’s commercial fleet on their ever-expanding target list. This time around, when they were late entrants into the conflict, they have hit comparatively few ships. Instead, they have focused on their domestic adversaries and infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, such as with repeated strikes on the Jizan refinery, one of the kingdom’s largest. That refinery showed no shipments in August. As with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refining, these attacks may prompt Saudi Arabia to export more crude oil because it is unable to refine the latter given the reduction in capacity. At the same time, the new escalation has expanded the battlefield. On 10 September, the Houthis reportedly seized Mokha , the government’s only major Red Sea port, and several Red Sea islands, followed the next day by the remainder of the coast, including Perim, a key island in Bab al-Mandab. Mokha was previously a launchpad for the government’s efforts to interdict Houthi supply chains that now criss-cross the Red Sea. Perim may be an even greater prize, because it enables tighter control of Bab al-Mandab and Red Sea traffic than could be achieved from Houthi-administered territory farther north. That said, taking these areas is one thing; effectively weaponising them under fire is another. To exert greater influence in these waters, the Houthis would need to deploy the right capabilities throughout their new coastal and island territory. The Houthis’ southward blitz suggests that their maritime interests lie in controlling Bab al-Mandab and much of the Red Sea rather than sealing off the Saudi Arabian coastline. If the group can hold the islands, cities and flat, hard-to-defend plains of the western coast – likely by taking territory within the Kahboub mountains further inland – then they will have stolen a march on not only Yemen’s government, but also Saudi Arabia and the U.S. They will have enhanced their ability to project power in the strait and the Red Sea overall at a critical juncture in the U.S. war with Iran. The Houthis may have gained greater leverage over the kingdom’s Red Sea exports, but by doing so against the backdrop of the East-West Pipeline attack, the group has helped force those exports back east. In particular, the suspension of the pipeline immediately compelled Riyadh to either curtail production exceeding domestic consumption once storage was filled or to heavily increase the volume of oil it sends through the Strait of Hormuz under threat of attack by Iran. It quickly chose the latter, and its oil exports through Hormuz rose by over 2 million barrels per day by mid-September, or around half of the lost exports through Yanbu, and appeared to keep climbing thereafter. Though the pipeline is being quickly repaired, with roughly half its flow reportedly restored as of mid-September, using Hormuz to send oil to the Gulf region’s typical Asian customers is a much more efficient route than going through Yanbu and around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Houthis’ missiles and drones. There are few options for quickly reopening the Red Sea, anyway. Washington previously failed to restore freedom of navigation there through serial bombardment of Houthi positions, and its sanctions against the group and its supply chains are already severe. It has reportedly met with Houthi representatives in Oman to lower tensions, and it is reluctant to more deeply involve itself in Yemen as its war with Iran proceeds. So far, the only U.S. response to the Houthis’ latest territorial gains and salvoes against Saudi Arabia ... has been to increase intelligence and targeting support. So far, the only U.S. response to the Houthis’ latest territorial gains and salvoes against Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh itself, has been to increase intelligence and targeting support . Despite having elevated Riyadh to the status of a major non-NATO ally in 2025, Trump has reportedly rebuffed Saudi requests to strike the Houthis. Diverting naval and air assets from protecting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or maintaining the blockade on Iran would benefit Tehran, with no promise of success against the Houthis. Trump could change his mind, but for the time being Saudi Arabia has been looking elsewhere for aid. It has yet to receive concrete assistance, however, whether from regional states like Egypt, the other parties in the newly formed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement alliance (Pakistan and Türkiye) or the new, thirteen-state Red Sea coalition . Several European countries either were already supporting Saudi Arabia – such as Greece, with its air defence deployment in the vicinity of Yanbu since 2021 – or have pledged other help, like the UK’s offer of what it characterises as “defensive” air-to-air refuelling. With no obvious options for finding barrels of oil and fuels elsewhere, the Houthis’ disruption of Saudi Red Sea oil exports is likely to continue forcing more exports through Hormuz via the “shuttle runs” discussed below, with all the risk that entails, for the foreseeable future. 5. The contest over the Strait of Hormuz has intensified. A top concern for global markets is if Gulf oil can find ways out of the Middle East despite Iran’s attacks on shipping and its neighbours. Two major pipelines bypass the strait, the damaged East-West pipeline and the UAE’s Habshan-Fujaira line that ends just east of the Strait of Hormuz. That UAE line is both operating and expanding , with work on a parallel line that will raise capacity from 1.8 to 3 million barrels per day more than halfway complete under the country’s “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy. “Shuttle runs” through Hormuz, despite Iran’s attacks, have increasingly succeeded in getting oil out through a lane along Oman’s coast in the southern half of the strait – though the risks and costs are significant. These runs account for most of the oil moving out of the strait. The battle over the southern corridor is a critical test of Iran’s capacity for preventing or raising the costs of shipping as well as the resolve of the U.S. and its Gulf allies, particularly the UAE. Finding a Way Out From the beginning of March into early May, the flow of non-Iranian crude fell to an average of 500,000 barrels per day – a far cry from the nearly 14 million barrels of non-Iranian crude and condensate just before the war, but not quite zero. Iran’s early attacks were enough to bring shipping to a near standstill as insurers, shipowners, charterers and seafarers were all wary of transiting the strait. Over time, as the financial and strategic costs have mounted and diplomacy has faltered, risk tolerance has grown, at least for oil (and double-hulled oil tankers that can weather a measure of damage). Scarcely a month into the war, oil tankers began transiting the strait seemingly without Iran’s permission. Those willing to risk Iranian attack are making short back-and-forth runs across the strait using the southern corridor, which, unlike its northern counterpart, is outside Iran’s territorial waters. A senior Gulf official suggested to Crisis Group that, in effect, the strait was open for those with sufficient nerve. These vessels are travelling with their location broadcasting turned off – or sailing “dark” – typically at night (though daylight slots were recently added) and often during periods when satellites are not capturing images of traffic on the route. The “shuttle runs” take place under U.S. protection that may involve a mix of aircraft and drones, though not escort by manned ships. There are also at least some U.S. military personnel operating within the strait. Oil is then transferred to more risk-averse ships waiting east of the strait in the Gulf of Oman. This model amounts to several oil producers – and a handful of shipping companies – assuming most of the hazards of transiting Hormuz. They charge a premium for doing so. The U.S. claimed that by early August oil flows were approaching pre-war volumes through the shuttle runs and bypass pipelines, with almost 9 million barrels per day going through Hormuz. Leading energy and freight analysts were dismissive of the U.S. government figure at that time. (U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright later clarified that the number was from all “waterborne routes”, suggesting a more expansive definition than some other Hormuz-specific tallies.) The true figure was probably closer to 6 million barrels per day for crude as of mid-August, though estimates vary, and a number of oil traders claimed it was between 6 and 8 million by the end of the month. To be sure, counting outbound barrels is as much art as science. It is complicated by ships going dark, even though industry estimates also draw on other signs of export activity like changes in Gulf oil storage, ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz and import data from oil buyers. It often takes days to weeks to get this information, meaning that early estimates are often later revised. There are a variety of reasons for such discrepancies (like double-counting ships or barrels, not discounting very small ships or not differentiating between crude and products). Aside from disagreement on the overall number of barrels, most observers concurred by early September that the volume was trending upward prior to the latest escalation, which may have briefly held outflow below 7 million barrels per day. The mid-September addition of more Saudi barrels reportedly brought crude exports through Hormuz near or back to the volume seen before the war, which has already helped lower global crude prices because of diminishing fears of further Saudi production cuts. Saudi Arabia has committed to maintaining its increased use of the strait, having sold almost 100 million barrels for delivery to Asian buyers in October and November, reportedly all via Hormuz. The growing volume of crude and products on shuttle runs is nearing the operational limits of regional capacity to service the ship-to-ship transfers that enable the runs. Combined with bypass pipelines, the gap between pre-war crude exports through Hormuz and outbound crude by late September may have been down to around one fifth or less . At the same time, the growing volume of crude and products on shuttle runs is nearing the operational limits of regional capacity to service the ship-to-ship transfers that enable the runs. Recent outflow may reflect a ceiling, or even have surpassed the ceiling, of what can then be moved beyond the U.S. blockade line by more risk-averse shipping, contributing to a growing bottleneck in the Gulf of Oman. Getting even more oil and fuel out of the southern corridor has already started to require longer distance shuttle runs, farther into the Indian Ocean, that increase costs or may otherwise force more crude back to the Red Sea. Yet with energy concerns increasingly shifting to fuels, even a few more million barrels of oil per day may not be enough to lessen Washington’s energy woes – or bring down spiking costs – unless Gulf Arab refineries are repaired or return to full capacity and are thus in a position to export. Some of those refineries are still under direct attack, and refined product exports remain down by around half to three quarters compared to pre-war figures because of refinery damage and a lack of means of export. These products are not moving on shuttle runs at scale, with movement through Hormuz still down around 80 per cent compared to before the war. Risky Business Shuttle runs are first and foremost about strategic concerns. The U.S. and the Gulf states feel compelled to find ways to move oil because they need to contest Iran’s claims to the strait and these exports are (in the case of the Gulf states) essential for national revenue. There is also a collective desire to protect oil infrastructure from damage due to prolonged shutdowns. Every convoy that makes it through the southern corridor weakens Iran’s hand, and so, to an extent, the cost of the transit is a secondary concern. Private companies tend to be motivated by skyrocketing tanker rates – the highest in the history of the supertanker market and at times surpassing $1 million per day for Hormuz transits, about double a month ago – alongside huge pay increases for seafarers and heightened oil prices. The players in shuttle runs and other dark oil transits have ranged from national oil companies like the UAE’s ADNOC to trading houses like Mercuria . ADNOC became a driving force behind the shuttle runs, even moving the exports of other Gulf producers , alongside the Korean-Italian owned shipping company Sinokor and a handful of others. ADNOC’s leading role is a demonstration of the varying risk tolerances among the Gulf states and Iraq. Other Gulf state companies like Saudi Arabia’s Bahri have also gotten involved , though at least one Gulf official has suggested that more states need to participate to further undermine Iranian claims and raise the costs if they continue attacks. Specialised crews commanding substantial wage premiums are also increasingly used for these runs, with rotations occurring after the vessel passes through the strait. The transits are expensive but not yet cost-prohibitive, though more successful Iranian attacks could change that. The transits are expensive but not yet cost-prohibitive, though more successful Iranian attacks could change that. Sinokor was at one point offering six months of extra pay to sailors to make a single shuttle run, while war-risk insurance was around 10 per cent of a ship’s value in early August – up from 0.25 per cent before the war – and rates specific to shuttle runs could be higher. It is also possible that the UAE (which was exporting more oil than pre-war in recent months ) and other shuttle operators will begin struggling to find tankers and crews for them as Iran damages those used for shuttling. Vortexa reported in August that only a few dozen tankers were making most of the shuttle runs. The largest, two-million-barrel tankers were handling about 60 per cent of shuttle activity. Every tanker that Iran disables thus makes a sizeable dent in the collective capacity for these runs, given the difficulty of rapidly replacing tankers that can cost hundreds of millions apiece. The costs of making these shuttle runs under duress are high enough, and the war has so distorted the global tanker market, that rising shipping costs are affecting routes far away from the Middle East. Indeed, U.S. crude exports have dipped recently in part because the cost of export is becoming prohibitive . A sustained increase of Saudi export of oil through the southern corridor via shuttle runs would, by one estimate , require a nearly 50 per cent increase in participating supertankers under certain conditions. Meanwhile, Iran is still trying to stop transit through Hormuz, with fresh ship attacks toward the end of September. On 24 August, Iran’s recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority published a (largely ignored ) list of 45 ships it claimed had violated its protocols for the strait, with most of the listed ships involved in shuttle runs. That list grew in September to 77 ships as Iran stepped up tanker attacks, while the U.S. launched its own “ tanker-for-tanker ” policy by pledging to hit one or more tankers for each one struck by Iran, beginning with strikes on two vessels linked to Iran’s state tanker company. Eight tankers – five of them laden, a major shift by the U.S. – were hit from 5 through 8 September. These U.S. strikes were followed by Iranian attacks on U.S. warships and other military assets in the region. U.S. officials have told Crisis Group that the shuttle runs prove Tehran cannot control the strait, in part because it often does not know when they are taking place. But while there are clearly limits to Iran’s capacity, they should not be overstated. Given how narrow the strait is and the slowing pace of tanker transits and ship-to-ship transfers (among other things), it seems unlikely that Iran has ever been wholly ignorant of the shuttle runs. It may not spot every ship, but it surely knows the southern corridor is handling a greater volume of traffic – whether from open-source satellite imagery showing the increasing number of ship-to-ship transfers east of the strait or the dhows and other small craft (including Iran-flagged fishing and other vessels) regularly moving in the strait, as the U.S. itself acknowledged in mid-August. Iran also continues to curtail other shipping, even as it loses its grip on the passage of oil and other tankers. The southern corridor is a risky oil route, not a functioning all-commodity trade route. Even as oil moves through it, cargo shipping has not returned to the strait to the same extent, including other products like liquefied natural gas (LNG). Container ship traffic was down 94 per cent as of September. Exports of other critical commodities like sulfur and nitrogenous fertiliser were still down about 90 per cent and 70 per cent, respectively, from January to August. This overall lack of maritime trade continues to strain the Gulf economies even as they steadily increase oil exports. Still on the Escalation Ladder? The risk of a new round of escalation centred on the Strait of Hormuz remains. Forcing the suspension of the East-West Pipeline was an achievement for Iran and its allies, but it is not a clear strategic win on its own – even setting aside the speed with which it is being repaired. Instead, the suspension set up a new test of capabilities and wills in Hormuz, as Saudi Arabia shifts millions of barrels back to the strait. If Iran does not counter increased flow through Hormuz, the temporary blocking of Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route will have achieved only a considerable expansion in southern corridor throughput. This gambit puts more of Saudi Arabia’s crude exports back into Iran’s field of fire, but it also raises the costs for Iran of failing to bar passage through the southern corridor because it would further demonstrate that Tehran can no longer enforce its claims upon the strait. If instead Iran is willing and able to suppress southern corridor transit and strand even more Gulf oil, potentially forcing a large reduction in Saudi production, then it will have notched a major, if not necessarily permanent, strategic achievement. In this way, good news for energy markets today – more tankers through Hormuz – may herald new risks of Iranian escalation tomorrow. Indeed, further escalation by Tehran now would fit a familiar pattern. Past spikes in Iran’s attacks on shipping have typically followed efforts to decisively shift traffic from Iran’s northern corridor to the southern corridor. For example, Iranian attacks jumped following the 3 May U.S. announcement of Project Freedom (an effort to guide ships through the southern corridor). They also increased after the 18 June declaration by a naval coalition under U.S. leadership that Hormuz was open and the southern corridor mine-free. They went up again in early July as traffic in the southern corridor surged, diminishing transits through Iran’s corridor. These July attacks caused a short, sharp dip in the volume of crude oil passing through the strait, though they did not stop shuttle runs from proceeding. If U.S. protection proves too effective within the corridor even as more oil moves through it, then Iran may decide to widen the scope of its targeting beyond the corridor itself. If U.S. protection proves too effective within the corridor even as more oil moves through it, then Iran may decide to widen the scope of its targeting beyond the corridor itself. It may strike more ships at or near regional ports, as it apparently did with a laden tanker in Iraq’s territorial waters on 9 September, or hit those engaged in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, which it has not done to date. Its announcement of a planned “restricted zone” stretching from within the Gulf to the U.S. blockade line and its growing list of “sanctioned” ships point to these risks. Such measures could force ship-to-ship transfers farther from Iran’s shores, raising costs and transit times. Costly U.S. overwatch is presently concentrated on the southern corridor itself, but ensuring blanket protection of tankers from Iraq’s coast out to the Arabian Sea could strain the capacity of the stretched U.S. forces, particularly since Iranian attacks have largely pushed U.S. troops out of the nearest military bases. In early September, as Iran intensified its fire at shuttle runs, the U.S. had already reduced its air defence coverage to a few daily time slots, down from a longer overnight period, in an effort to make its protection more sustainable and because, according to the U.S. military, “darkness has not proven to be the most secure time of day”. Yet it is not a foregone conclusion that Iran will escalate. It could show restraint for several, overlapping reasons: it may be satisfied with where prices of crude and especially fuels are hovering, observing the headaches afflicting the Trump administration as the November elections approach; it may want to calibrate rather than maximise – for now – the pressure on Saudi Arabia and other neighbours, leaving room for negotiations; and it may be under Chinese pressure to not escalate too far, including because of the risks to China’s own energy supply. Indeed, China reportedly requested that Tehran lean on the Houthis to de-escalate, following an entreaty from Riyadh to Beijing. Iran has consistently sought control of movement, and not a prolonged end to transits – now likely only achievable through comprehensive, hard-to-reverse mining of the entire strait, not only the original central corridor – which would leave Tehran with less room to negotiate. Tehran has at times shown more pragmatism than would be expected if its public statements about closure were literal policy – with some similarity to Washington’s exaggerated claims of the strait's openness or U.S. control. Instead, Iran has selectively permitted ships, crews and cargo to pass, depending on its immediate goals, making its efforts more akin to the checkpoints ubiquitous in conflicts around the world than a blockade. Its approach to Qatari LNG shipments is illustrative – it has at times permitted , attacked or otherwise blocked these transits depending on its objectives at that moment and Qatar’s engagement with Iranian unilateral arrangements for the strait, despite Doha’s role as a mediator. Arguably, the heavier toll is not financial, but strategic, as its adversaries chafe at accepting a newly imposed maritime order. If Iran manages to curtail shuttle runs, including by incapacitating a large number of tankers, it could reclaim greater leverage over time. The battle for Hormuz is not the Battle of the Atlantic during World War II, when the U.S. government and its allies along with their private sectors were willing to absorb huge losses of merchant ships. The private sector generally has little interest in a direct role in an attritional maritime campaign. Even state oil companies like ADNOC will have their limits. Conversely, for the U.S. and its partners to achieve their goals via shuttle runs, the latter would have to become so effective that – together with intense pressure on Iran’s economy – they lead Tehran to agree to lower its demands to reach a deal, at which point regular traffic would resume and a durable revival of Gulf refining would proceed. At a minimum, that appears far off. A Crude Compromise? Iran may still be willing to find a modus vivendi with its neighbours concerning Hormuz, especially if it is unable to deter traffic through the strait absent significant escalation. From Iran’s perspective, negotiations should be focused on the conditions under which movement takes place. A short-term compromise on the strait – such as the option under discussion in which the original central corridor is in effect divided between Iran and Oman, ensuring movement through the territorial waters of each – would help move crude and other commodities without the constant threat of attack, as the memorandum of understanding fleetingly did in June. But Iran’s initial asking price for Hormuz stability – recognition of its expansive maritime claims – is too high for other littoral states, even if the alternative is that oil exports remain under threat and other seaborne trade stays near rock bottom. (The Gulf states are engaging with the Oman-Iran track on Hormuz, though a 14 September meeting was postponed and has yet to be rescheduled.) There are further considerations that could shape efforts to reach a working arrangement. One is that any new agreement would be politically meaningless and likely short-lived in the absence of a wider deal involving the U.S. Another is that any arrangement for the strait that contravenes international legal protections for freedom of navigation, as Iran’s actions are widely seen to do, both implicates the rights of third-party states and could set a precedent that risks undermining global commerce. It is therefore likely to face high levels of international pushback. A related dilemma is that an arrangement intended to be temporary could remain indefinitely if negotiations on a new, permanent mechanism stall. Until a Hormuz-specific or a wider agreement is reached, the U.S. and Gulf producers have little choice but to continue the shuttle runs, which are as much freedom of navigation operations as economic activity. At the same time, Iran continues to occasionally crash drones and missiles into the bridges, engine rooms and hulls of ships – even at the cost of retaliatory U.S. strikes on its own tanker fleet and military installations. Oil is moving, but its price is still elevated. Diesel prices continue to reach new highs, especially in the U.S. The status quo is painful, and while both sides have incentives to find a way out – whether through inflicting more pain or through another attempt at negotiation, each may keep waiting for the other to blink. Diplomacy is the Best Bet for Restoring Affordability So, what will settle the energy markets? None of the first four factors listed above is likely to break in the direction of durable stability. Venezuela probably cannot quickly deliver major relief for a U.S. running short of strategic reserves and facing unprecedented diesel prices. China’s oil imports have begun rising (which puts upward pressure on crude prices), and its fuel export controls easing (which puts downward pressure on fuel prices), though these mixed trends both face headwinds. Russia’s refinery output and fuel exports continue to suffer under Ukraine’s aerial onslaught, which has also disrupted oil loadings at Russia’s Black Sea terminals. The Houthis are in Bab al-Mandab and pushing into the mountain range needed to secure their new coastal territory. Considerable uncertainty hangs over all these theatres, but events there mostly bode ill for fuel prices. One bright spot from the U.S. perspective is the shuttle runs through the Strait of Hormuz, where more oil has been moving over the last two months. That is an achievement, but for the increased flow to have a large impact on fuel prices, the crude oil needs to find its way to refineries with spare capacity and then that refinery output needs to be exported. There are few such destinations outside the Middle East. China is chief among them – and it will look to its own declining fuel inventories first. The status quo may also be unsustainable, as Washington runs the risk of a major Iranian escalation or a politically intolerable fuel crisis. On the other hand, Iran may be overestimating its leverage over the strait (and, by extension, the U.S.), leading it to overplay its hand in negotiations. In late September, Iran offered to reopen Hormuz as part of a phased deal. But an unblocked strait is not the incentive it was in June, because of the southern corridor’s success to date. Trump rejected the proposal, letting it be known that he expected U.S. military action to escalate after midterm elections. The export ban Trump is entertaining may temporarily drive down consumer prices in parts of the U.S., but it will cause prices to spike elsewhere. Nor would an unblocked strait – on its own – be the solution for rising diesel prices and other refined products that are eating away at paychecks in the U.S. and elsewhere. Here the problem can only be addressed by bringing capacity back online – and Washington has few levers within its reach to achieve this end. Most directly, it could lean harder into efforts to negotiate an end to the war; more indirectly, it could make a more serious investment in diplomacy to temper or halt the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Such options would not bring instantaneous relief, either, given the time it will take for damaged or shuttered refineries to resume operations and for their output to reach destinations with high prices. The export ban Trump is entertaining may temporarily drive down consumer prices in parts of the U.S., but it will cause prices to spike elsewhere – especially in Latin America and Europe. Its domestic effects also may well prove disappointing because, faced with a sudden drop in demand once cut off from the global market, U.S. refineries will produce less fuel. The bottom line is that neither side has a whip hand when it comes to bending the markets to their will, not least because neither has control or complete influence over key outside actors – including China, the Houthis, the Gulf states, Russia and Ukraine – when it comes to affecting the world’s refining capacity. As U.S. reserves dwindle and prices rise, the status quo leaves Iran and the U.S. under mounting pressure, with the Trump administration feeling political pain and Tehran groaning under mounting economic stress. Yet it is not clear if either has fully committed to reaching a near-term diplomatic off-ramp. Absent such a deal, the road ahead will be rocky. A prolonged standoff between the U.S. and Iran promises to bring economic hardship to both even if it does not trigger a resumption of all-out war. But there is also a chance that it brings both – with an extended period of uncertainty simply the prelude to another major escalation. The New Red Sea Wars mloukili Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:25 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Africa 06 October 2026 1 minutes The New Red Sea Wars Originally published in Foreign Affairs Conflicts in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa Have Become Inseparable Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Alan Boswell Project Director, Horn of Africa https://twitter.com/alanboswell Related Tags Horn of Africa Gulf and Arabian Peninsula On June 3, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the U.S. Congress that the fighting that had raged for three years in Sudan was now a “proxy war” and blamed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) for frustrating American efforts to bring the conflict to an end. Rubio was saying out loud what many observers already knew: what started as a domestic power struggle has morphed into a wider regional war, drawing in outside powers and spilling across Sudan’s borders. The spread of the conflict in Sudan is part of a larger geopolitical transformation. For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on one side of the sea increasingly alter the military calculations on the other. This entanglement is only deepening in the wake of the United States’ and Israel’s decision in February to launch a war on Iran, driving a deeper wedge between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh (which were already at odds), weakening the American-anchored security order in the region, and underscoring the importance of securing the Red Sea for shipping. For the past decade, the UAE has been the most aggressive outside player in the Horn of Africa, establishing ports and military bases, offering large financial packages to key allies, and involving itself extensively in Sudan’s civil war. But the recent war in Iran, along with the breakdown of the Emirati-Saudi security partnership in Yemen last December, made Riyadh less confident of Washington’s protection, more anxious about the UAE’s security ties to Israel, and more intent on controlling the Red Sea’s security picture. And so as Saudi Arabia has leaned into an alignment with Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, it has also brought that alignment to bear to strengthen key partnerships in the Horn. It is trying to counter factions in the Horn that are backed by the UAE or Israel even as it struggles to manage threats from Iran and its allies—including the Houthis, who have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Myanmar Military Steps Up Airstrikes in Rakhine as Ground Offensive Stalls cmoore Wed, 10/07/2026 - 12:46 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Asia-Pacific 07 October 2026 2 minutes Myanmar Military Steps Up Airstrikes in Rakhine as Ground Offensive Stalls Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean examines why the Myanmar military’s faltering counteroffensive and escalating air attacks have further dimmed prospects for a ceasefire in Rakhine State. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Myanmar The Myanmar military carried out one of its deadliest airstrikes against civilians on 28 September, hitting a busy market and bridge in Kyauktaw, a town in Rakhine State administered by the Arakan Army, a predominantly Rakhine Buddhist armed group that now controls much of the state. Local reports put the death toll at 50 people, with another 58 wounded. Military airstrikes have continued in the region since then, including attacks on two camps for internally displaced people that left eight civilians dead. Military targeting of civilians and non-military infrastructure is hardly new. The UN documented 982 civilian deaths from military airstrikes last year, and Rakhine has been among the hardest hit regions. Since the 2021 military coup, Naypyitaw has increasingly used airpower to punish communities in areas it does not control and destroy its opponents’ ability to govern effectively. This latest bombing campaign comes as a multi-front military counteroffensive in Rakhine appears to have stalled. On 4 September, the military began ground operations from its main remaining footholds in the state – the capital, Sittwe, and Kyaukphyu, home to Chinese infrastructure projects – while simultaneously attempting to push into Rakhine from the east, across the mountains from central Myanmar. Despite deploying drones, artillery, aircraft and gunboats, the attacks have made little headway. Recent peace overtures make the military’s escalation in Rakhine appear somewhat incongruous. After the military-controlled parliament appointed Min Aung Hlaing president in April, his administration invited ethnic armed groups for peace talks “without preconditions”. Several groups have since met his negotiators, but the Arakan Army has not been one of them. Although a tactical ceasefire would benefit both sides – removing one of the military’s most formidable opponents from the battlefield, while bringing relief to the armed group after years of intense fighting and an economic blockade – the two remain far apart on what a deal might look like. A truce along existing front lines would require Naypyitaw to acknowledge the loss of around 90 per cent of Rakhine State – a humiliating outcome for a military that firmly controlled the state under a decade ago. Even as a temporary arrangement, military leaders would fear such a deal could solidify into a permanent autonomous enclave. To make a deal acceptable to Naypyitaw, the Arakan Army would have to cede some of its current territory, which it would be loath to do. Had its recent offensive made major inroads, the military might have created impetus for a ceasefire: Naypyitaw would have avoided total capitulation, while the Arakan Army would have had a stronger incentive to freeze a front line preserving most of its gains. The failure of the campaign has instead left them deadlocked, and the violence unleashed over the past month, particularly the bombardment at Kyauktaw, are indicative of the military’s frustration. With a deal now even less likely, the most likely scenario in the near term is a war of attrition in which civilians bear the heaviest cost, deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis. Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt mloukili Thu, 10/08/2026 - 16:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Nigerien soldiers participating in a rally in support of General Abdourahamane Tiani (not seen) outside the former National Assembly in Niamey, on 2 September, 2026. AFP. Q&A / Africa 08 October 2026 11 minutes Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt A mutiny by Niger’s special forces in late August morphed into a coup attempt. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts explain how the unrest exposed growing discontent within the military’s ranks. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Niger What is happening? Niger’s military leadership continues to reel from a coup attempt that exposed serious divides within the defence and security forces. On 28-29 August, soldiers from Niger’s Special Forces began shooting in their barracks at Air Base 101, which lies within the compound of Niamey’s international airport and houses most of the country’s military aircraft, as well as army units and foreign troops. Unrest quickly spread: groups of soldiers attacked the state broadcaster and the presidential palace, both in the city centre. Whether the incident began as a mutiny or whether it was meant from the start to oust General Abdourahamane Tiani, who seized power in a July 2023 coup, remains unclear. But the ramification of an uprising by a group of well-trained soldiers unhappy with their conditions of service and recent battlefield setbacks could be significant – particularly if it deepens divisions within the armed forces and disrupts their operations at a time when jihadist threats are looming large across several parts of the country. Members of the Special Reconnaissance Battalion for Special Operations Command, known by the French acronym BSR-COS, appear to have been behind the coup attempt, although a small number of soldiers from other units may have joined. Loyalist forces, particularly the presidential guard that Tiani commanded from 2011 to 2023, fought back as gunfire and detonations shook the capital, while national radio and television temporarily stopped broadcasting. By midday on 29 August, the mutineers withdrew to Air Base 101, where they unsuccessfully sought to rally other units to join them in toppling the government. Their stand did not last long, however. By the evening, national TV was up and running again, broadcasting images of loyalist forces arresting dozens, including at least one female soldier. A few days later, the government organised a national funeral for three members of the presidential guard forces who died in the clashes, while media reported that at least 27 mutineers were killed. The clashes further unsettled civilians in the capital, where heavy gunfire and explosions had already jolted residents twice this year, in January and June, when jihadists attacked the international airport, leaving many increasingly anxious about their safety. Why did the soldiers rebel? Tensions had been building within the BSR-COS for some time. In the days leading up to the revolt some soldiers had reportedly refused to go on a mission, citing a lack of adequate equipment. The battalion’s commander, Major Boubacar Maïhatchi, was detained soon after in the town of Tera as he returned from a mission escorting supply trucks from neighbouring Burkina Faso. Social media platforms have portrayed Maïhatchi as popular among younger officers, who respect his bravery and concern for his troops. His arrest may have prompted the soldiers’ decision to turn against the military leadership. The BSR-COS is part of Niger’s elite special forces, trained and equipped to work specifically in high-danger zones. As jihadist violence intensified in western Niger starting in the mid-2010s, the government expanded these forces, creating additional battalions, often with training and equipment from Western partners such as the U.S., France, and Germany. Today, there are more than a dozen battalions of roughly 500 to 600 soldiers each. The BSR-COS is among the most recently established units, with its members receiving training in Morocco. These battalions are leading the fight against jihadist insurgencies in Niger, including Islamic State Sahel Province and Jama’ at Nusratul Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) in the west. From its headquarters at Air Base 101, the BSR-COS has frequently assisted units under attack from jihadists or escorted convoys travelling through dangerous areas. In November 2025, for instance, Niger sent 82 fuel tankers to Mali to ease shortages caused by a JNIM blockade on the city. Members of the battalion led the military escort that protected the vehicles during the 1,400 km journey. While special forces battalions are valuable to the fight against jihadists, they are also capable of posing a serious threat to the military regime. Since winning independence from France in 1960, Niger has experienced five coups and several failed coup attempts. The army has long held sway in politics. Seven of its eleven presidents have been military officers. Given that history, Niger’s leaders are understandably wary of powerful military units. Where to deploy the special forces often presents the authorities with a dilemma. As the jihadist threat draws closer to the capital, their presence is increasingly indispensable to protect strategic localities and sites. At the same time, their proximity to the seat of power also fuels concerns within the military regime about the risk of yet another coup. The BSR-COS was initially expected to deploy to Ayorou, a jihadist hotspot near the Malian border where the government is building a large dam crucial for electricity and irrigation. That deployment was delayed in part because of militant attacks on Air Base 101 in January and again in June 2026. Why are soldiers unhappy with Niger’s top military leaders? The incident revealed a widening gap between the military leadership and the rank and file. The July 2023 coup brought senior officers from various components of the defence and security forces to power, ranging from the presidential guard and the army to the gendarmerie and the national guard. Together, these senior figures formed the National Council for Safeguarding the Homeland, which shapes government policy and military strategy. Four generals wielded the most influence in the council: Abdourahmane Tiani, who had himself sworn in for a five-year presidential term in 2025; Defence Minister Salifou Mody, his second-in-command; Mohamed Toumba, who heads the interior and security ministry; and armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salao Barmou, who has since been removed. Yet beneath the military brass that had seized control of the country, discontent has been simmering in the lower ranks. The senior officers justified their power grab partly by accusing the civilian government they toppled of failing to tackle the jihadist threat. Three years on, insecurity has grown and spread to more parts of the country; the opening of new fronts has stretched the defence and security forces thin. Troops are deployed to the front line more frequently and remain there longer. Foot soldiers complain that they lack adequate weapons and equipment. They allege air or ground reinforcements are slow to arrive when needed, if they arrive at all. Combat vehicles and pickup trucks are often in poor shape and the government has been slow to replace them, which makes working in high-risk zones hazardous. Conditions in military barracks have added to soldiers’ frustrations. Some have posted images on social media of the poor-quality meals they are served; others pool their money and buy condiments to improve their rations. On top of that, a recent wave of jihadist attacks – in Diffa, Dosso, Tillabery and Niamey – has killed dozens, draining troop morale. Senior command seems aware of the rumblings. The defence minister, the chief of army staff and other generals have made multiple visits to military bases to listen to soldiers’ concerns. They often blame sanctions imposed by foreign powers after the July 2023 coup for hampering their ability to procure arms. Most of these sanctions have since been lifted, however, and many soldiers appear unconvinced by the senior leadership’s explanation for the lack of equipment. In several instances soldiers’ frustration has manifested in defiance. The August revolt was Niger’s fourth episode of military unrest in less than two years. In June 2025, after an attack in Banibangou in northern Tillabery killed over 70 military personnel, soldiers assigned to retake the position protested and beat the officer in charge, who was later evacuated for medical treatment. A few days later, soldiers in the Zinder region mutinied and tried to kill their superior. In August 2025, soldiers in Ayorou rebelled and opened fire on their commander. As one officer puts it, “A mutiny is first and foremost a failure of leadership”. What did the coup attempt and its aftermath reveal about military divisions? The incident broke an unwritten rule that has long guided Niger’s military: namely, it is essential to avoid internal confrontations between different branches of the armed forces. In 2023, various military units opposed Tiani’s move to detain then-President Mohamed Bazoum in order to remove him from office, but senior commanders ultimately decided to avert an open conflict and rally behind Tiani’s power grab. This time around, the mutineers fought the presidential guard, while the government asked Russia’s Africa Corps to help quell the revolt. Hours after the August revolt had subsided, Russia’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, told reporters that Russian forces had helped subdue the dissidents. Around 200 men from Africa Corps, the expeditionary force controlled by Russia’s defence ministry, have been deployed in Niger, including at Air Base 101, since 2024. They have assisted the regime with intelligence gathering, training on drone use, and operating air-defence systems. Russian forces reportedly used kamikaze drones that explode upon impact to force the mutineers to surrender. Some within the military found the involvement of foreigners in an internal confrontation particularly grating. Rumours have it that armed forces chief of staff Barmou may have been among those who voiced reservations about the Africa Corps’ intervention against the mutineers. In any event, on 11 September Tiani replaced Barmou with General Mamane Sani Kiaou, a move observers interpreted as aimed at reasserting control over the army. Barmou was also among the first generation of Nigerien special forces officers trained by the U.S. in the 2000s; he had reportedly threatened to resign previously over the army’s lack of equipment and his limited influence over military decision-making. Regime authorities, meanwhile, arrested over a hundred soldiers, while dozens of others, including special forces members, remain unaccounted for. Several civilians were also arrested, including two former ministers and a prominent journalist. The coup attempt could accentuate the resentment many troops feel vis-à-vis the presidential guard. The elite unit has long had access to the best equipment and the most talented recruits. It also foiled several coup attempts in the 2010s and early 2020s, leading some in the armed forces to perceive the guard as preoccupied with policing the military and protecting the regime rather than national security. Finally, the failed coup demonstrated that public support for the military regime is declining. The generals’ promises to restore security, overhaul governance, and assert Niger’s sovereignty on the international stage won a degree of sympathy from the public early on. But much of that enthusiasm has evaporated amid repeated security setbacks and an economic slowdown, partly attributable to the departure of Western donors and the closing of many NGOs by the government. On the afternoon of the coup attempt, regime supporters called on Niamey residents to turn out in support of the military leadership; notably, only a few dozen people did so. How did the incident reverberate in the region? The unrest had major diplomatic repercussions. The following day, a Nigerien officer speaking on national television alleged that he had received calls and messages from contacts in Chad, France, Belgium and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), informing him that several foreign countries – including Chad, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France – were prepared to intervene in support of those who had seized Air Base 101. He said they were operating with the blessing of the Economic Community of West Africa, the regional bloc from which Niger – alongside Burkina Faso and Mali – withdrew in 2025. On 3 September, the government spokesperson accused France of orchestrating the mutiny and alleged that “other African countries” had supported Paris. Some of these accusations were unsurprising. Tiani has repeatedly accused Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France of conspiring against him, allegations the countries have rejected. But the regime’s claims that Chad was somehow also intent on destabilising Niger were new. Niger’s relations with Chad have soured in recent months. Niger’s authorities and their counterparts in Chad have traded accusations of tolerating, or even supporting, armed opposition groups active in their common border zones. Chadian officials did not respond to the allegations, although President Mahamat Idriss Déby later posted Quranic verse on social media warning against mixing truth with falsehoods. At the same time, the failed coup brought northern neighbour Algeria closer to the Nigerien authorities. Algeria condemned the incident and sent its chief of army staff to Niamey along with four fighter jets and a refuelling aircraft. The deployment of the fighter jets was apparently aimed at sending a strong message of support and to deter any attempt by foreign interests to dislodge the regime. The gesture also reinforced a diplomatic thaw already under way between the two countries. Relations had deteriorated last year after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border, prompting Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – the three members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – to recall their ambassadors from Algiers. Niger and Algeria have since taken several steps toward rapprochement, culminating in President Tiani’s visit to Algiers in February. The episode has also reinforced Niger’s relationship with Russia. Moscow’s intervention demonstrated the growing importance of Russian security support to the authorities in Niamey. In turn, the episode could deepen the regime’s dependence on Moscow for its survival. Since the coup, most Western forces have left Niger, including U.S. and French troops, as well as German, Belgian and Canadian personnel involved in training the Nigerien armed forces. Today, only a few hundred Italian troops remain, making Italy the last Western country with a military presence in Niger. What should the authorities do next? The Nigerien authorities should exercise restraint during their ongoing post-coup crackdown. While those within the BSR-COS who instigated the mutiny will likely face sanctions, the authorities should spare the rank and file who simply followed commanders’ orders. Thus far, over a hundred soldiers have been arrested. A sweeping purge risks further weakening the armed forces, deepening mistrust between ranks and damaging troop morale at a time when Niger is under enormous pressure from jihadists and rebel groups. Restraint will not address the grievances that helped fuel the revolt, however. The authorities should tackle soldiers’ concerns about inadequate equipment, housing and food. A leaked 2020 defence audit exposed widespread corruption in procurement practices. In February 2024, however, Niger’s military authorities issued an ordinance exempting defence and security procurement from ordinary state contracting and public accounting oversight. Without compromising legitimate security concerns, the authorities could adopt a stronger approach to rooting out wrongdoing in the acquisition of military equipment, as well as improve living conditions in the barracks. The authorities should also tread carefully in order not to deepen divisions between different wings of the defence and security forces. Even symbolic decisions matter. The national funeral held for three presidential guard soldiers reinforced perceptions of double standards: regular soldiers who are killed in the line of duty are often buried quietly and rarely honoured publicly. A more equitable recognition of soldiers’ sacrifices could help reduce resentment across the ranks. More fundamentally, Niamey needs to reduce the mounting burden on its armed forces. The authorities should develop a comprehensive strategy for dealing with the proliferation of conflict fronts, giving greater weight to non-military approaches. Where possible, dialogue and diplomacy could help pacify restive areas. Even if such approaches do not produce sustainable peace, they could help demobilise combatants, achieve temporary ceasefires, and possibly reduce the number of simultaneous conflicts, providing relief to armed forces that show growing signs of fatigue. Finally, the authorities should recognise that military discontent is unfolding in an increasingly closed political environment. With political parties dissolved and civic space severely restricted, peaceful avenues for expressing dissatisfaction with the government have narrowed considerably. In such an environment, the armed forces risk becoming one of the few remaining channels through which opposition to the regime can erupt, and potentially in its most dangerous form. Reopening political and civic space would allow grievances to be expressed through less destabilising channels, even if doing so exposes the authorities to greater public criticism. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/09/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 09 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities.
